This paper presents an innovative technique to create spatial boundaries for navigation in dynamic environments. In dynamic environments, motion planning methods often rely on map-based constraints generated by global planners. However, the inaccuracy and outdated nature of these maps leads to navigation issues. To overcome this limitation, we developed a method that uses sensor data to identify movable areas and create maps with more accurate spatial boundaries. Additionally, we adapted a distributional model to describe navigation in dynamic environments. This allows agents to learn and represent spatial boundaries from sensor data. We tested and validated our method on a mobile robot in various dynamic scenarios, demonstrating its effectiveness and statistical significance. The results show that our technique outperforms existing methods, ensuring safe and efficient navigation in dynamic environments. Videos illustrating our method's performance are available online. Furthermore, we conducted field experiments to compare the safety and efficiency of our approach with that of a state-of-the-art method, which can be found on our GitHub page. We demonstrate that the rational function semifield of a tropical curve has a finite set of generators over a specific semifield. This involves identifying a particular finite set that generates the semifield. Furthermore, for curves with zero or one degenerate point, the generating set consists of functions that map the curve's non-degenerate segments to maximum values. Additionally, for curves with multiple degenerate points, the generating set includes functions that map these points to infinity in conjunction with rational functions over a finite set that generates the semifield of the curve's complement. These results have been shown to hold for any tropical curve, not just smooth ones. Lastly, it has been found that analogous properties apply to the rational function semifield of tropical surfaces, providing further evidence for previously proposed conjectures. These results were made possible through the use of a theoretical framework called a tropicalization, allowing for a natural mapping between algebraic varieties and their tropical counterparts. This framework was used to provide a new characterization of logarithmic meromorphic connections and to show that a particular property of meromorphic connections is shared by certain specific cases. These results have further implications for the study of other mathematical concepts, including hyperbolic surface singularities and Newton polyhedra. However, it is worth noting that the study of these surface singularities is a separate area of study from the one being explored here. These results were made possible through the collaboration of several mathematicians, including David Kaushansky and Amrami Rosenberg, who have previously worked together on the study of Newton-Okounkov body theory and its application to the study of meromorphic line connections on complex curves. Their most recent paper marks a significant departure from their previous focus on the study of meromorphic line connections as it applies to the curve itself, as opposed to its associated parabolic geometry. While in most FeSCs superconductivity arises close to a nematic and magnetic state, the iron-based compound LiFeAs exhibits unique characteristics, becoming superconducting below 18 K without undergoing a magnetic or structural phase transition. Some studies have hinted at the existence of nematic fluctuations and a nematic superconducting state in LiFeAs, but recent findings from this study indicate that pristine LiFeAs, along with LiFeAs doped with low levels of Co and V, show no signs of being close to a nematic instability, which contrasts with the findings in magnetically and nematically ordering NaFeAs. This is despite employing more sensitive tools for measuring fluctuations compared to previous studies. This data suggests that nematicity may not be necessary for achieving high-temperature superconducting phenomena in FeSCs. It shows the influence of electron-lattice coupling and spin-lattice coupling on the collective charge order and superconducting phases. This research introduces two modifications for enhancing the security of Loidreau's code-based cryptosystem.
Originally built using Gabidulin codes within the McEliece framework, it is susceptible to a polynomial-time key recovery attack under certain conditions. To counter this vulnerability, the proposed modifications involve substituting Loidreau's cryptosystem with two new variants leveraging parital sum (PS) and partial difference (PD) sums of vectors. Theoretical analysis confirms the improved security of the modified systems against known algebraic attacks. Furthermore, the portfolio includes an implementation of the new systems using top-performing field extensions for code-based cryptography. Experimental results indicate that the modified schemes can be combined with the widely adopted NTT-based matrix multiplication technique to increase their computational efficiency, thus making them more practical for large-scale deployments. As an extension, the researchers propose a public key encryption scheme based on the new modification-I construction, featuring high efficiency and strong security properties. The performance of this scheme is evaluated against contemporary schemes within the same framework, showcasing its superior performance in terms of key size and computation speed. Moreover, the proposed scheme is compatible with the quantum-resistant, public-key encryption algorithm PKCrypto, and its proposed PKCrypto-based variant is shown to be resistant to proven attacks, while outperforming other schemes in the same class. The research further estimates the cost of implementing the new scheme within the context of the planned quantum cryptocurrency PKCrypto, anticipating that the modified scheme will reduce the expected energy consumption by 22.64% while complying with the proposed energy constraints. The experimental findings are made publicly accessible through a verifiable code repository hosted on GitHub. The minimum weight spanning tree in graphs and its higher-dimensional equivalent, the minimum spanning acycle in simplicial complexes, were previously linked to a particular value by the zeta function. A recent study of these values by Newman and Widder proved a key insight into their growth. However, in practical applications, we often only have partial information about these values due to limitations of computational methods. To address this challenge, we study the characteristics of the empirical distribution of these values under various conditions. For trees and spanning acycles, we demonstrate that this empirical distribution converges towards an exponential distribution with a characteristic scale that is determined by the complex zeta function. A complementary aspect of this work involves analyzing the complex zeta function itself using techniques from analytic number theory. Furthermore, in cases where the complex zeta function exhibits polynomial behavior in a critical region, we observe a diverse empirical distribution that depends on this polynomial term. To establish polynomial behavior in this complex zeta function, we draw upon principles from Perko's theory on higher-dimensional analogues of catlin's theorem and apply them in conjunction with ideas rooted in classical techniques for evaluating determinants and multivariable analogues of the Gel'fand-Serganin theorem. Notably, our results extend Newman and Widder's theory, offering a more refined understanding that is applicable even in the one-dimensional context (i.e., trees). A significant aspect of this research involves the development of an efficient algorithm for evaluating the complex zeta function of a simplicial complex through the use of Perko's polynomial growth theorem. This algorithm leverages this polynomial growth theory to calculate and recursively compute partial moments of the complex zeta function. Furthermore, we provide a method for approximating probability distribution functions of minimum spanning acycles with a surprising connection to the generating functions of directed spanning acycles and the roots of controlled random walks. To facilitate these computational methods and algorithms, we created a publicly accessible software tool written in the R programming language. This tool allows users to calculate and plot various characteristics of the empirical distribution of these values for trees and acyclic simplicial complexes. By drawing on recent research from Pemantle and Watson regarding the complex zeta function's asymptotic behavior, we establish a lower bound on this function, demonstrating that its absolute value is limited from below by a function that decreases at a particular rate and is related to the complex zeta function's polynomial behavior. This text can be replaced with a structured summary of machine learning techniques called federated learning. Federated learning is an innovative approach where multiple parties collaborate on training machine learning models without exchanging sensitive data. There are two primary forms of federated learning, namely horizontal and vertical federated learning. In horizontal federated learning, multiple parties share the same attributes but differ in sample sizes, leading to the collection of a larger dataset. In contrast, vertical federated learning involves parties with distinct attributes and variables but shared labels through a aggregation process. As a result, the training process becomes aligned with the target distribution without compromising data security. The application of federated learning in healthcare is particularly promising due to its ability to address data security and privacy concerns. However, developing reliable evaluation metrics for federated learning remains a pressing concern. This concern stems from the existing gap between simulation-based and practical applications of federated learning, leading to a lack of dependable evaluation metrics. In healthcare, the effectiveness of federated learning is often measured by accuracy rates, with data utility serving as a primary benchmark. Nonetheless, the choice of benchmark often results in a failure to consider the intricacies of federated learning and privacy. Consequently, the development of a unified evaluation metric capable of addressing these concerns is a pressing requirement. The proposed algorithm, M-Diversity, aims to close the existing gap between simulation-based and practical applications and addresses the devil in the details of federated learning by developing an effective evaluation metric. This algorithm is equipped to measure the degree of divergence in representation learning between vertical and horizontal federated learning settings. Specifically, the algorithm capable of measuring representation learning in various settings often fails to consider a key aspect - the deviation from the target distribution. Consequently, the proposed algorithm provides a comprehensive and systematic approach to evaluating the divergence in representation learning while addressing the existing gaps in the literature. The algorithm's effectiveness was tested on the NCI-Kinase2 dataset and the results demonstrated its ability to enhance representation learning while ensuring privacy. Specifically, the proposed algorithm achieved an evaluation metric of 0.1581 - a 98% improvement over existing alternatives. The approach was found to outperform other algorithms in terms of precision, recalling, and F1 score, with results indicating its potential in diagnostics and other machine learning applications. The source code for the algorithm is available on GitHub at the specified repository link. In conclusion, the proposed algorithm offers an effective and reliable method to evaluate divergence in representation learning while addressing the existing gaps and concerns in the literature. In a Smart City environment with numerous agencies and interconnected cyber and social layers, safeguarding public safety is becoming increasingly complex. To address this challenge, this study develops a sophisticated mathematical model that simulates the interactions and resource allocations between agencies when faced with terrorist attacks on both physical and cyber-social targets within the city. The proposed model, Smart City Defense Game, is formulated as a multi-layered, multi-stage zero-sum game, requiring efficient solving to ensure optimal agency operations during attacks. The proposed model, taking into account the complexities of each layer, is still manageable for solving, thanks to the reduction of the solution space and the exploitation of the properties of the game's equilibrium solution. Computational results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed model, and a case study highlights the practical relevance of the model. Furthermore, this research will be further expanded by considering the dynamics of terrorist organizations. Its underlying theoretical framework can also be applied to other problems where multi-agent resource allocations are crucial. Finally, potential future research directions are outlined. Researchers studied the Schwarzschild and charged black holes' behavior in an expanded universe model.  They considered these black holes within a large empty sphere of radius $r_B$ in an expansive space environment. A related physical volume was created for black holes by considering the volume of a sphere with its own boundary, plus any void space outside it.  They then examined how thermodynamic properties of these black holes change when their temperature varies.  Using the canonical and grand canonical ensemble methods, they respectively investigated the impact of pressure on the black hole's phase transition and the relationship between the phase transition and chemical potential.  Study results of Schwarzschild, charged, and the charged version of the rotating black holes revealed that a phase transition occurs in all cases.  Finally, the research analyzed how the initial black hole temperature at the phase transition changes based on the values of $r_B$ and the void radius.  It also looked at how the phase transition relates to the relationship between the black hole and void radii.  Overall, the research found that black holes experience a phase transition when their internal energy over specific parameters equals the energy of the expanded space.  This discovery suggests that a phase transition occurs in black holes due to external environmental factors.  This new perspective on black hole properties has significant implications for understanding gravitational physics.  Future research goals include using a expanded-space model to study the behavior of other types of black holes.  These black holes include those that are rotating and charged, as well as those that are neutral in nature.  We plan to investigate their thermodynamic properties in an expanded-space model using the canonical and grand canonical ensemble methods.  We will examine their relationship to the extended phase space and phase transitions and explore how these black holes behave under rotation and charge conditions. One of the widely applied optimization methods in machine learning is Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), which tackles optimization problems by iteratively selecting and computing gradients of small data subsets before updating the solution. When executed in parallel, SGD demands communication among involved processes at each iteration. Our innovation is a communication-optimizing approach for utilizing SGD to solve logistic regression. This strategy organizes computations into a pattern where communication is required only every $s$ iterations, as determined by the $s$ tuning parameter. By deriving theoretical bounds on operations count, data transfer bandwidth, and latency, and accompanied by experimental findings, we demonstrate that the newly designed Communication-Avoiding SGD (CA-SGD) can reach speedups of up to $4.97$ on high-performance clusters, preserving the same convergence and accuracy as standard SGD. This method is versatile and easily integrates with existing SGD implementations, thus allowing existing SGD-based solvers to attain the communication efficiency seen in our results without the need for further modification. The open-source code underlying our results is accessible on the GitHub platform. Additionally, our design provides insight into the inherent trade-offs between computation and communication involved in optimizing SGD, a common optimization tool. Moreover, our work sparks curiosity about the practical implications of our design choice, which we plan to explore in a future work focused on integrating data compression to further reduce data transfer time. Moreover, our findings indicate that the optimization technique may not always lead to faster convergence, and we observed instances where it yielded the opposite outcome. In the near future, we also aim to extend our results to other optimization methods, such as variational auto-encoders, which is another area we plan to investigate. Lastly, our technique could eventually contribute to advancing the field of optimization towards data parallel methods, a method that was observed to be less effective in our experiments. Ultimately, we conclude with key insights derived from our findings and possible future research directions. Traditional architectures, requiring the calculation of all antenna pairs, become impractical for arrays with many antennas. The introduction of the FFT-correlator architecture reduces the computational complexity, making it more feasible, but still incurs significant costs, necessitating careful consideration of parameter settings. A novel implementation, using the FFT-correlator architecture and minimizing data input bandwidth, is presented, allowing for efficient calculations with lower complexity. The new architecture, already widely adopted by single dish experiments, offers further improvements when combined with data compression techniques, specifically the FFT-based HiTime approach, which allows for efficient global spectral calculations while reducing individual unit computational demands. The combination of this compression technique with the new architecture, significantly reduces computational complexity, making it more feasible to implement the cross-elevation mapping technique, previously limited by computational constraints. The study focuses on identifying Fermi-LAT blazar candidates, consisting of BL Lacertae objects and Flat Spectrum Radio Quasars. In contrast to traditional dense neural networks, Bayesian neural networks yield a dependable estimation of the network's prediction accuracy. The study investigates the similarities between conventional and Bayesian neural networks, along with the effect of data augmentation. It is discovered that Bayesian neural networks are ideal for classifying tasks reliant on limited and uneven datasets, producing reliable results. The outcomes of this classification are instrumental in informing studies on blazar population dynamics, aiding in refining blazar luminosity function constraints, and guiding multi-messenger observations. The method can be applied to other classification tasks involving rare or hard-to-study phenomena with astrophysical implications. Active participation and user engagement are crucial components of social networking, 
fueled in large part by user-generated content that comes in various forms like 
images, videos, and GIFs. However, this content remains inaccessible to many users, 
despite available solutions that aim to reduce this form of exclusion. Our research 
involved surveying 258 social media users and interviewing 20 participants to 
investigate their perceptions regarding content sharing and viewing difficulties. 
Through these studies, we gained a deeper understanding of users' online behaviors, 
noticing for instance that users are increasingly employing multimedia like 
images, videos, and GIFs for self-expression. Notably, these users feel that the 
main hurdle preventing them from sharing content is the inability to access different 
file formats. To address this issue, we developed an open-source browser extension 
that enables seamless conversion of various media formats. Our extension not only 
translates content but also provides users with a preview before sharing. 

By combining these capabilities, we aim to make social networking more inclusive 
and accessible to a broader user base. The extension successfully passed accessibility 
testing as per the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.1 and the Section 508 
standards. Our participation in the 2022 Google Accessibility Focus competition 
allowed us to receive valuable feedback from experts in the accessibility field, 
ultimately leading to the completion of our accessibility feature. Our extension has 
since been published on the Mozilla Add-ons repository and is awaiting review by 
Google. In line with our goals of promoting accessibility and raising awareness, 
we plan to donate our code to relevant organizations and share our research findings 
with them. Our research also highlights the significance of user perspectives in the 
design and development process, emphasizing that users should be actively engaged 
in these activities. Overall, our research aims to contribute to the creation of 
more accessible social media platforms for users with diverse abilities and 
perspectives. Our code is available for review at https://github.com/Ajay1999/

We establish that any hypergraph can be viewed as a composition of hypergraphs formed by a common tensor-based operation, and we identify the conditions under which a hypergraph can be decomposed into hypergraphs of a specific, fixed tensor-based structure. We also derive a condition for when a hypergraph can be expressed as the combination of two specific, tensor-defined subgraphs, and establish a relationship between this condition and a previously studied notion for hypergraphs. Specifically, we show that a hypergraph satisfies this condition if and only if its hyperedges consist of edges from a set of fixed-size hypergraphs. Furthermore, we introduce a hypergraph property related to a previously studied concept and demonstrate that a hypergraph possesses this property if and only if its tensor representation meets a certain divisibility criterion. We also investigate properties of the hypergraph tensor product and establish a duality between this product and a hypergraph projection operation that is analogous to a corresponding duality in the context of graph products. A novel computational strategy called Action-CSA is introduced, enabling the global exploration of reaction pathways via optimization of the Onsager-Machlup action using conformational space annealing. Action-CSA is capable of sampling multiple reaction pathways without initial guesses and successfully captures both the most dominant pathway and a variety of alternative routes. Pathway diversity is maintained through a crossover operation, facilitating the efficient sampling of pathway space. Action-CSA is evaluated through comparisons with transition path theory and molecular dynamics simulations on a low-dimensional model system and an $\alpha$-helix. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that Action-CSA can identify and accurately reproduce quasi-low-energy pathways via mutation of a small peptide fragment. These results indicate that Action-CSA is a reliable method for sampling reaction pathways across diverse systems. A Python 3.9 implementation of Action-CSA is available on the GitHub platform at https://github.com/Yoho-Lido/Action-CSA. Action-CSA has been implemented using the CUDA and OpenMP languages to optimize its performance on GPU and CPU platforms. Action-CSA is compatible with a range of molecular models, from classical to quantum mechanics. framework based on automata theory that relates to the study of implicit
computational complexity, much like how Church encodings connect to
polymathematical recursion theory.
In this framework, we will focus on two concepts: polyregular functions,
which are crucial in automata theory and pattern matching, and (semi)partial
algebraic theories, which allow for Church-style encodings in type theory.
Our study will examine how these concepts relate to one another, enabling us
to investigate questions such as: Can we use polyregular functions to
simultaneously encode and bound the complexity of a problem? Can we apply
Church-style encodings in a way that reflects partiality? Furthermore, these
inquiries will guide us in assessing the relative strength of the new framework
compared to other approaches like Typos, Quine-Russell, and Tybalt. Ultimately,
we aim to showcase the framework's power by demonstrating that some
fundamental problems in automata theory can be easily expressed within it. 
Significantly, we expect this framework to have significant value in other
domains like quasiregular languages, categorical semantics, and domain
specific programming languages, where polyregular functions and partial
algebraic theories are prominent. A shorter version of this paper has been
submitted to the 2022 Conference on Formal Epistemology for an extended

comprehensive solution to long-standing open issues in pattern matching,

approach this problem. A substantial portion of this work has been conducted
within the context of the project "Tybalt: Towards typed implicit computational

In massive machine-type communications (mMTC), reducing access latency through grant-free connections is crucial, but highly dense mMTC networks face significant interference challenges. To mitigate these challenges, a novel grant-free random access method is introduced in this paper, utilizing a comprehensive understanding of random vector properties to minimize interference and improve the downlink capacity of mMTC. Specifically, this method involves selecting reliable uncorrelated devices to transmit, pre-processing, and scaling signal power to create distinct signal patterns for each device, and leveraging extended discrete Fourier transform (DFT) to maximize desired signal reception while minimizing interference. Simulation results show that our proposed method achieves superior downlink capacity performance with minimal overhead and is highly resilient to channel uncertainty. Moreover, this method facilitates efficient rate matching and scheduling at the base station, ultimately enabling higher sum-rate and sum-log2(|B|/ρ) performance compared to traditional grant-free techniques. As a result, this method is highly suitable for mMTC networks, particularly those with dense mMTC configurations and severe channel uncertainty. As such, it holds great promise for near-future wireless communications. Despite this method's initial focus on downlink operations, it is equally applicable to uplink operations. Furthermore, this work also paves the way for further research into overcoming specific uplink-downlink asymmetries, thereby enabling the development of more efficient communication strategies for future wireless networks. The proposed method has been publicly shared through its inclusion in an open-source repository at the following URL: https://github.com/hariszhen/2022-NCWMS-MmTC-Methods. Additionally, our work contributes to the advancement of mMTC research and development by participating in the NCWMS-2022-MmTC competition. A detailed description of our participation and methodology can be found at the following URL: https://github.com/NCWMS/2022-NCWMS-MmTC-results. The proposed method demonstrated robust performance across various scenarios, ultimately ranking 3rd out of 72 competitors across all testing phases, specifically securing 1st place in Phase 1, 4th in Phase 2b, and 12th-13th (tie) in Phase 2a. The top-ranking teams' implementations are available online at the following URLs: https://github.com/NCWMS/2022-NCWMS-MmTC-results/tree/1st-place/CEDAR-MmTC, https://github.com/NCWMS/2022-NCWMS-MmTC-tree/tree/3th-place

This paper explores an alternative framework, drawing on confusion networks from ASR research to expand the potential models available for interpretation. It explores the use of confusion networks, develops an efficient sampling algorithm, and evaluates the feasibility of using them in place of a large set of fixed ASR hypotheses. Results show that a dynamic selection of confusion network hypotheses, based on model likelihood, yields better measures such as WER and response delay, than both the top N ASR hypotheses and fixed CN hypotheses. In addition, the paper examines the impact of varying the size of the CN hypothesis set on system performance and finds that even a small set of 10 CN hypotheses can achieve a lower WER than the top 10 ASR hypotheses. Finally, it is observed that proposing a small set of complete sentences, derived from CN hypotheses, can lead to better system performance than proposing the transcribed text of the single best ASR hypothesis. This research suggests that leveraging confusion networks can provide a flexible framework for an intelligent dialogue system to trade off performance and response time. In general, the larger the CN hypothesis set, the better the system's performance, but at the cost of a longer response delay. This makes CNs an attractive option for applications where a fast response is not crucial, such as when running on a resource-constrained device. In contrast, when a quicker response is essential, the cost of larger CNs may be too high and a more efficient sampling algorithm may be required to achieve the desired balance between performance and speed. Overall, the outcome of this investigation depends on how the CNs are used to facilitate communication between the user and the system. In turn, this ultimate performance result relies on various factors like the size and the structure of the CN hypotheses chosen to best serve the system's purpose. A critical factor in secret sharing schemes is the count of minimal qualified subsets, as knowing this value results in the smallest possible size of the access structure. Specifically, when the number of these subsets equals one, the access structure becomes universal - applicable to every secret sharing scheme. 

We focus on the pivotal parameter - the size of the minimal qualified subsets - and how it relates to the access structure. We define a critical graph for every secret sharing scheme, where vertices represent subsets and edges connect those capable of sharing a secret. We prove that if the access structure is universal, the critical graph has a specific property - it can be divided into connected subgraphs with equal edges per vertex. 

Consequently, a boundary exists for this property and the size of the minimal qualified subsets; specifically, this boundary equals $\_O(n) = \log^n(n)$ for $n$ subsets. We further investigate, using a probabilistic approach, the occurrence of scheme universality given the size of the minimal qualified subsets. 

Universality has been a crucial factor in evaluating the security and efficiency of secret sharing schemes. We hope our findings provide valuable insights into their evaluation. We also examine fundamental issues in secret sharing schemes - their recoverability, redundancy, and consistency, and the connection between universal schemes and recoverable schemes. The long-lived palm tree modes (PTM) found in the JET tokamak's edge plasma remain somewhat enigmatic despite detailed documentation. A recently investigated explanation suggests that these structures form when magnetic field eddies caused by edge-localized modes trigger the development of a PTM seed island. However, this study instead seeks to provide an alternate explanation based on observations of edge plasma turbulence. A distinct feature of plasma turbulence is the existence of persistent structures known as blobs and holes in the scrape-off-layer. Measuring the currents within these coherent regions has shown that they follow the direction of the magnetic field. Here, the relationship between these turbulent filaments is likened to level sets, which form distinct islands within the magnetic field. Using data compiled from the JET experiment, this study presents images of these turbulent islands, known as QGIs, during the time leading up to the onset of a PTM. By examining the evolution of these islands, it is possible to see how they grow and develop into PTMs, providing a more complete understanding of these phenomena. Furthermore, examining the growth rates of these turbulent islands has shown that they correspond with experimental measurements of PTM growth rates. By deriving a strike-line from analyzing the magnetic field snapshot data using a vector magnetic field algorithm, it is possible to see how these turbulent islands, or palm tree modes, evolve from distinct structures along the magnetic field. A strike-line is a plot of the magnetic field, or equivalently the electron density, along a straight line in the plasma. Recent years have seen increasing interest in Automatic Program Repair (APR) with
numerous approaches being explored. One area of research focuses on search-based
methods, generating potential repairs through syntactic analysis and systematic
exploration of feasible solutions. Conversely, we investigate an innovative
approach inspired by the concept of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), 
aiming to directly produce high-quality repairs without searching. Our method
involves training a textual GAN to learn the repair pattern of faulty programs,
thereby producing accurate fixes for unknown programs. Despite initial
difficulties, our experiments show that this GAN can effectively fix programs in
the industry-standard benchmark path. Nonetheless, our results also reveal that 
most generated repairs are unsuccessful, thereby undermining the efficacy of GAN
approaches. Consequently, we propose a novel search-based integration technique,
utilizing generated repairs as initial guidelines for a more targeted search. 
Experimentation demonstrates that this hybrid strategy significantly outperforms
existing methods in the path evaluation benchmark. Our research suggests that GAN
techniques are still in their nascent stages and that combination with search-based
techniques may be required to achieve high-quality repairs. Moreover, our work 
identifies new avenues for search-based repair research and sheds light on the
underlying challenges and limitations of textual repair generative methods. 
Furthermore, our project is accessible at https://github.com/jpereira/jp/mtextrepair. 
We anticipate that textual repair generative methods will accelerate the 
automatization of repair processes and stimulate discussions about new ideas and 
algorithms for APR. Our findings will be made available at https://arxiv.org/.

We propose InDistill, a novel model compression approach, combining the principles of knowledge distillation and channel pruning to effectively transfer critical information flow from a powerful teacher model to a more efficient student model. Unlike previous techniques that collapse this information, InDistill leverages layer-wise pruning of the teacher's intermediate stages, aligning their widths with those of the student, thereby enabling direct information distillation without an intermediate encoding step. To facilitate knowledge transfer, we employ a curriculum learning strategy that prioritizes layer-wise difficulty and critical learning periods. Through these advancements, InDistill significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, achieving enhanced results on a range of benchmarks, including ImageNet and CIFAR-100. We examine a mechanism design problem for selling $k$ items to unit-demand buyers with private valuations for each item, who can choose between participating directly in the auction or being represented by an intermediary. The aim is to develop robust auction designs that don't rely on the buyer-demand distribution and work well across diverse contract scenarios between intermediaries and buyers.

Initially, we focus on the case of $k$ identical items where buyers draw private valuations independently from a specified distribution, known as a $\lambda$-regular distribution. By designing a linear auction that pays buyers $p_i f_i$ dollars for item $i$, where $f_i$ is determined in advance, we can design mechanisms that don't rely on the demand distribution and work even when the buyers can select the price for each item. We also create mechanisms that accommodate contracts that only boost revenue while preserving these beneficial traits.

For the case of distinct items, achieving similar results is more complicated and challenging due to the vast number of possible demand distributions, known as $P_2$ distributions. By modeling the distribution over these demands as a $\lambda$-regular distribution in a transformed space and employing a technique for creating linear programs from convex body representations, we can design linear auctions that don't rely on the demand distribution, effectively applying the result to the case of distinct items. By combining this with existing research on converting these linear auctions into non-linear mechanisms that boost revenue, we can develop sophisticated auction designs that integrate both cases. Furthermore, we can design mechanisms that incorporate pre-computed prices or require minimal computational effort to generate non-linear prices at auction closing time. These designs preserve the benefits of the linear auction and address potential issues associated with its bindingness at closing time. By testing these designs with data on online book purchases, we can evaluate their performance and efficiency in real-world market environments. These experimental assessments highlight several market distortions resulting from the linear mechanism's bindingness, which might go undetected in theoretical analyses based on expected valuation distributions. These additional gains stem from the complex, non-uniform distribution of user valuations in market practices. In market situations where intermediaries play a prominent role, we observe that price manipulation can lead to revenue augmentation. Building on this concept, we develop a significant typing discipline within this quantum lambda calculus by selecting a particular set of typing rules, which effectively restricts typing for numbers to only those that have been explicitly encoded. This typing discipline allows for a direct correspondence with linear time bounding PSPACE, which signifies a stricter set of typing conditions compared to the original typing system. It has also been demonstrated that another typing discipline corresponding to polynomial time bounds can be achieved through the introduction of an additional semantic condition. This new typing discipline highlights the distinction between these two approaches and points out that simply adding more rules does not yield the desired typing discipline for polynomial time bounds. Instead, it requires a significant change in the way we use typing rules. These findings involve the first use of a particular typing technique in the context of the WKL theorem. Furthermore, we establish a relationship between this typing discipline and the size of space used during computation by comparing it with the WKL theorem. This achievement marks the first integration of a typing discipline that corresponds to polynomial time bounds into a full fledged quantum lambda calculus. Ultimately, we establish a significant distinction between the expressive power of the full quantum lambda calculus and that of quantum linear time bounded functions. This distinction points out that while quantum lambda calculus may capture the essence of all quantum linear time bounded functions, it possesses a much broader and more general approach. Which ultimately points to the possibility that a quantum extension to linear time bounded aggregation may not be feasible. The model's output indicates that the initial anisotropy is directly passed on to particle azimuthal asymmetry after particle interaction. Notably, we discovered that while initial anisotropy may vary with centrality, it is maintained throughout the particle evolution process. This allows the final particle flow asymmetry to be directly influenced by initial conditions. Unlike elliptical flow (centrality dependent) and quadrupole flow (highly sensitive to partonic effects), we found that triangular flow is largely insensitive to partonic effects. Instead, it mirrors the initial anisotropic geometry. This understanding can serve as a valuable reference point for deciphering the source of anisotropic flow. Furthermore, our investigation of anisotropic flow in isobaric collisions has shown that isobaric symmetry does not necessarily translate to zero final flow asymmetry. This is because initial flow asymmetry can persist throughout particle evolution, and subsequent particle interaction may not fully eliminate it. Therefore, even though collisions are isobaric, we may still observe a non-zero flow asymmetry. This conclusion sheds light on why isobaric symmetry collisions often reveal non-zero $v_2$ but not necessarily $v_3$ in similar studies. These findings hold key implications for future experiments. Deep neural network training for semantic segmentation requires considerable effort,
so many researchers opt for pre-training their model on a different task before
further refining it using a smaller annotated dataset. Top-notch approaches
traditionally rely on image classification for pre-training, a method which can
be marred by uncontrollable biases. To investigate a more effective method, we
proposed that depth estimation using untagged videos might be a better choice
for pre-training. Although this method lacks any meaningful scene details, we
assert that calculating the three-dimensional geometry of scenes is closer to
the goal of semantic segmentation than assigning broad image classifications.
Lacking an analytical method for validating our hypothesis, we conducted an
experimental evaluation that demonstrated our pre-training scheme produced an
improvement of 5.7% mean intersection over union and 4.1% pixel accuracy in
comparison to classification-based pre-training. Notably, although we were able
to bypass the need for ground truth depth maps by training our initial network
with misaligned video frames, the best results were ultimately achieved by using
ground truth depth maps in the training process. Overall, our work suggests that
depth estimation is a suitable choice for pre-training and that our scheme is
generally effective when implemented. The code and models for our work are
publicly available online. 
Ultimately, while fine-tuning with a smaller annotated dataset yielded better
results, the improvements obtained through pre-training with depth estimation were
still modest. The modest gains made were primarily due to generalizing low-level
features like edges and textures from the pre-training stage to the segmentation
task. This insight implies that the additional resources required for pre-training
are largely unnecessary in the current state of the art in semantic segmentation. 
Despite our findings, using depth estimation as a pre-training method does offer
several advantages over image classification. For instance, calculating three-dimensional
geometry is essentially a form of supervision that, while broad, is still
meaningful and helps to guide the initial stages of deep neural network training.
Moreover, although our experimental evaluation demonstrated that the pre-training
scheme that yielded the best results relies on ground truth depth maps, it is
possible to leverage recent advancements in monocular depth estimation, which
can provide reasonable estimates of scene geometry without the need for labeled
data. Combining these technical developments with our experimental results leads
us to believe that the future use of unsupervised depth estimation is likely to
become a more prominent component of deep neural network training

Our objective is to quantify the magnitude of off-shell and non-resonant influences on the forms of various differential distributions that will be crucial for top quark mass determination via template fitting techniques. The susceptibility of facial recognition systems to fraudulent presentations restrict their adoption in highly secure contexts. However, the validity of these systems in detecting identity manipulations at scale remains uncertain. To address this gap, we investigated the resilience of state-of-the-art face recognition algorithms against impersonation using 3D-printed faces, employing both printed faces alone and combining them with purchased masks. Our results, obtained over two institutional networks with over 65,000 subjects, demonstrate that these algorithms can easily mistake artificially created identities for real ones, even when the impersonator has access to limited information. Moreover, our findings indicate that 80% of inter-agency searches yield false positives. These outcomes imply that established face recognition systems are imperfect and sometimes exploitable. Although the technology is still developing, the reverse approach of using 3D printed faces to create detailed facial replicas in conjunction with a purchased mask has significantly lower error rates when searching across different datasets. Consequently, these findings highlight the pressing need for continued research in this area. Additionally, we outline potential strategies for further enhancing the accuracy of face recognition systems and present a new dataset comprising similar-looking individuals. Our work has important implications for high-stakes community safety scenarios such as crime prevention, surveillance, and identity fraud detection. Moreover, our research highlights the pressing requirements of enhancing user privacy while minimizing unjust bias in these systems. Lastly, our findings suggest that system performance may rely on the quality of the impersonator's mask rather than the accuracy in creating the facial replica, which poses the risk of spreading false information about facial recognition technology. As such, our results offer valuable insights for government agencies, researchers, and other third parties to develop reliable and transparent facial recognition systems. Ultimately, our research outcomes may alarmistically reveal the flawed state of facial recognition systems but hopefully prompt significant advancements in this area. The concept of an effective, time-independent Floquet Hamiltonian underpins the Floquet engineering of isolated systems, describing their evolution over driving periods and often obtained through analytical high-frequency expansions. However, extending these ideas to open quantum systems, modelled by a Markovian master equation of the Lindblad type, poses a significant challenge. In systems with only two energy levels, distinct phases arise where the Floquet generator may be either a linear operator on state space or a matrix of rank two. In this context, a high-frequency approximation is made and numerical computations are conducted to identify the phase boundary, which is determined by the relative strength of red- and blue-shifted terms in the Lindblad form. These numerical results are refined using a mathematical approximation method. Importantly, in the phase where the Floquet generator is a matrix of rank two, its exponential solution can be found, allowing for a generalised Floquet engineering of driven-dissipative systems. Furthermore, conditions for guaranteed existence of this solution are derived and examined. These findings show how Floquet engineering can be used to achieve coherence, exemplified by an approach to create robust, time-independent peirles phases, where opposing dissipative effects are balanced. Importantly, in systems with stronger dissipation, a phase shift can be triggered by reducing the driving frequency, demonstrating the Floquet engineering's ability to extend the stability of quantum phases previously inaccessible under strong driving frequencies. Moreover, it has been found that the Floquet engineering can be applied not only to model the generator but also the entire time-evolution of an open quantum system, under certain conditions. Specifically, in systems with composite systems separated by a significant thermal gap between their spectral densities, a phase transition can occur and the solution to the time-evolution of reduced systems can be found, which may exhibit a form of temporal Floquet engineering. In exemplary scenarios, these findings show that temporal Floquet engineering can be used to achieve coherence of entire systems, which may otherwise be destroyed by dissipation, but for reasons other than phase noise can remain stable under strong driving frequencies. Despite recent advancements in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), explaining their predictive decisions remains an unresolved issue. Current methods primarily address the interpretation of individual cases by visualizing the importance of graph nodes and edges. Nonetheless, there are limitations to their approach including relying on relative ratings instead of absolute measures, using simplified representations, and offering only case-by-case insights rather than global understanding. To address these challenges, we present LKDA, an innovative method for explaining GNN predictions that provides an in-depth, graph-level comprehension. LKDA quantifies critical features affecting predictions through Lasso Linear Regression with additional covariates, specifically identifying key nodes and edges. Experimental results demonstrate LKDA's capability in accurately pinpointing important nodes and edges while surpassing other interpretation methods in predictive performance. Moreover, we show that integrating the features derived from LKDA with the original GNN model yields a substantial improvement in downstream tasks using few-shot learning with transfer learning. The code for LKDA is available at https://github.com/quantifiedintelligence/LKDA. This research benefits from significant contributions from the DeepGenius team. Moreover, we are grateful for support from the DeepRoots program and the DeepSense project. Additionally, LKDA is hosted on https://deepintelligence.ai/lkda for user accessibility and easy deployment. Furthermore, LKDA has been applied to real-world scenarios in the field of Computer Vision by analyzing a community question-answer forum. Ultimately, the distinct features of LKDA facilitate its utilization across a wide array of graph-based applications in machine learning. As part of the paper, we include an additional appendix with more implementation details, figures, and analysis, and are available for contact at [ai4iq at gmail.com].

Recently, the Legendre Memory Unit (LMU), a novel type of recurrent neural network, was developed and has demonstrated superior performance on various benchmark datasets. In this work, the linear component of the LMU is optimized, resulting in a simplified variant that can be trained in parallel, thus overcoming the obstacle of GPU training limitations on RNNs. Our modification allows training times to be reduced to less than 10 minutes for the MNIST dataset. Initially, the performance of the variant is evaluated on MNIST, CIFAR10, and CIFAR100 and is shown to be competitive with the original LMU. Two additional image classification datasets, CIFAR100V2 and Tiny-ImageNet, are also used for evaluation purposes. Furthermore, the proposed model is used to analyze the performance of the LMU on the Tiny-ImageNet dataset over varying filter sizes and dataset sizes. Our results indicate that the LMU can successfully capture the hierarchical nature of image classification tasks when properly tuned. Finally, the proposed model is successfully applied to the 50-class version of Tiny-ImageNet, resulting in a 0.64% improvement in accuracy over the baseline LMU. It is worth noting that the proposed model consistently underperforms compared to the transformer-based neural network throughout our experiments. It is suggested that the potential drawbacks of the LMU can be mitigated through adjustments in the number of neurons in the first linear layer, with our results indicating that the LMU can significantly benefit from a larger number of neurons in the first linear layer, particularly when trained for longer periods. Moreover, the proposed parallel training method is successfully applied to the LMU, simplex network, and transformer models, demonstrating superior performance on RNNs due to its ability to efficiently utilize GPU resources. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/kunlspar/parallel-rnn-training/tree/main/lmu. Our research aims to explore the potential of the simplex network as an alternative to the LMU and indicates that the simplex network may not learn hierarchical information effectively, but our results suggest that the LMU can be simplified while retaining its performance. Additionally, our results imply that the simplex network could outperform both the LMU and transformer-based neural networks when properly tuned. Our final goal is to establish the simplex network as a viable option for the classification of hierarchical data, particularly for the LMU, and our near-feature model is successfully applied to the classification of 10-digit images, resulting in a 4.64% improvement over the baseline LMU. By intensely driving a mode within the microring that's coupled to an external waveguide, we can induce a significant amount of quantum squeezing in two fundamental modes within the cavity. We can achieve this by having the strongly driven mode undergo a strong nonlinear interaction with a high-power optical field, thus generating a highly squeezed state for one of the modes. Our theoretical model reveals that the presence of this squeezed mode enables us to attain an extremely high degree of optical nonreciprocity, with optical powers within the linearly coupled waveguide decreasing by as much as 15 dB when transmitting signals in the reverse direction. Furthermore, we've found that the level of nonreciprocal transmission is directly proportional to the logarithm of the input power in the high-power regime. Additionally, we've explored the possibility of achieving nonreciprocity without relying on external waveguides by exploiting the differences in power loss between two fundamental modes within the microring. This difference in power loss arises due to the nonlinear interaction with a high-power optical field, resulting in one of the modes experiencing a greater decrease in power than the other. The fundamental tone induced by this process acquires a phase shift of approximately 180 degrees relative to the fundamental oscillation, thus allowing us to attain optical nonreciprocity between modes within the microring. Our findings contribute to the growing field of nonreciprocal photonics and hold significant implications for developing future photonic circuits and networks. Furthermore, the studied system shares similarities with other systems that leverage strong nonlinear interactions for generating quantum squeezed states, such as double-cavity systems or those incorporating superconducting components. Therefore, our research opens the door to exploring other systems that leverage strong nonlinear interactions for quantum applications. The CRESST experiment is one of the leading projects for directly detecting dark matter particles weighing less than GeV/c$^2$. Its ability to analyze numerous isotopes within its target material is an advantage in exploring dark matter interactions. This research focuses on dark matter interactions with $^{6}$Li protons and neutrons, made feasible through updated nuclear matrix calculations for this specific lithium isotope. By utilizing data collected by a CRESST prototype using LiAlF$_4$ and tested above ground in Munich, Germany, we demonstrate the effectiveness of incorporating $^{6}$Li into our calculations to improve our detection of spin-dependent interactions between dark matter and neutrons, particularly significant for particles weighing less than 1 GeV/c$^2$ where improvements of over two orders of magnitude are seen compared to previously published results with the same data. Furthermore, we show that even with the current prototype's shortcomings, CRESST is capable of providing competitive constraints for dark matter particles weighing less than 1 GeV/c$^2$ in exploring neutrons. Future upgrades aimed at reducing the prototype's heat sensitivity will significantly enhance our detection limits for such dark matter weights. Ultimately, incorporating $^{6}$Li into our calculations represents an important milestone in CRESST's capability to directly observe dark matter particles weighing less than GeV/c$^2$ and possessing properties governed by spin-dependent interactions.

Distributed consensus is crucial for various distributed systems, such as distributed databases and blockchains, to function correctly. The Canopus protocol efficiently manages large-scale distributed consensus without the need for a single leader, achieving this through a virtual tree network structure and a two-phase consensus approach. However, Canopus may experience poor performance when dealing with small-scale networks of eight or fewer nodes due to the cost associated with tree maintenance. To address this issue, a new scalable distributed consensus protocol, ScalCanopus, has been developed to effectively function within small-scale networks. The proposed protocol converts the Canopus tree structure into a ring structure and introduces a new leader election process to minimize the need for network updates, resulting in improved scalability and efficiency across various network sizes. The ScalCanopus protocol demonstrates better performance than Canopus, especially in networks of eight or fewer nodes, while its consistency and energy consumption metrics remain comparable to Canopus. The proposed ScalCanopus protocol effectively combines high scalability with efficient performance, making it suitable for a wide range of distributed consensus applications. The protocol's source code has been made publicly available on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/autoant/ScalCanopus. The protocol's open-source status allows for further testing, evaluation, and refinement to handle real-world distributed consensus challenges. This paper examines the loop quantum cosmological model generated from the ADM Hamiltonian. It looks at a spatially homogeneous, flat FRW model and finds that its modified Friedmann equation can be characterized as a quadratic equation in terms of density. The model's support interval for matter density is identified and its lower critical density is determined at which the scale factor becomes infinite. Additionally, the paper determines the upper critical density beyond which the model's matter density reverts to zero and a new, ancillary matter sector emerges at the quantum gravity scale. It was found that the model's gravitational action has a limited area corresponding to the model's parameter range, which indicates the model's stability due to its high kinetic terms. This model's behavior was further compared with the standard matter-filled FRW cosmological model and its cosmological implications were explored. This investigation discovered that the model's matter density distribution during density bounce surpasses its classical expectation. The paper also explores the model's equivalence to the de Sitter spacetime at high-density states and determines the model's minimum proper time at such high-density states. It was discovered that the quantum gravity effects caused by loop quantum cosmology have a significant impact only when the matter density in the system approaches the critical density at the onset of quantum gravity effects. This discovery can potentially pave the way for a deeper, systematic analysis of the quantum gravity effects in the universe and its consequences. Overall, the paper provides a systematic understanding of the quantum gravity effects in the homogeneous, flat FRW loop quantum cosmological model. It was realized throughout this investigation that the loop quantum cosmology framework presents a considerable obstacle when attempting to forge a universal theory combining quantum mechanics and general relativity. This knowledge can pave the way for the integration of quantum gravity effects in inhomogeneous spaces, which may further shed light on the loop quantum cosmology framework. Lastly, the paper proposes that a novel quantum gravity model with two interdependent matter sectors could emerge at the quantum gravity scale, which might be explored in greater detail in the inhomogeneous spaces discussion. However, this topic will be explored in a separate study.

The integration of advanced traffic forecasting technology significantly affects urban transportation systems.
The traffic4cast competition pushed the limits of short-term traffic prediction, leveraging high-resolution traffic volume and speed data, available in five-minute intervals. 
To adapt to new cities, as the 2021 challenge demanded, a more effective approach is suggested: predicting local sections of a map rather than the entire system.

In recent years, rewriting theory has been used to create systematic approaches to proving coherence in strict higher categories. We're taking this theory further by applying it to Gray categories, which can be thought of as a specific type of tricategory. To achieve this, we need to adapt rewriting theory to the more challenging framework of Gray categories, which involve categories with binary bispecies objects that support both composition and Gray homotopy. Our approach involves defining a strict monoidal rewriting system for the elements of these Gray categories, which allows us to prove that the original categories are coherent. We've successfully applied this method to prove coherence in several well-known categories, such as the categories of functors from spheres to spaces and the categories of colored perturbation invariant paths. We also used this method to prove coherence in bicategories, which are a specific type of 2-category, and recovered a key result from reference given by Loday and Valette. Our work has further reveals the significant overlap between rewriting theory and the more advanced theory of Gray categories, which are essentially tricategories with certain limitations. We then took this theory yet another step further by adapting it to the framework of weak $SSSS$-multicategories, which are a specific type of SSSS-categorical object. Interestingly, we found that defining a rewriting system in this new framework is much more challenging than in the others studied, as it requires at least the use of two different systems. Nonetheless, we were able to successfully demonstrate that the original system reduces to the latter. We believe this work has significant implications for rewriting theory in the realm of SS-categories, as it challenges the long-standing assumption that defining a rewriting system in this field is a relatively simple task. Our findings also highlight the importance of using advanced mathematical tools to establish coherence in the presence of higher-dimensional data. We further explored the relationship between rewriting theory and the more advanced theory of elementary $SS$-bimodules, which are a specific type of SS-categorical object. Through this investigation, we developed an algorithm that allows us to translate the former into the latter. Automatic hippocampus segmentation on magnetic resonance imaging is a critical factor in diagnosing and treating neuropsychiatric disorders. Current deep learning-based methods primarily utilize data from patients with healthy or Alzheimer's disease. This raises concerns about their performance in other domains, such as patients with epilepsy. We present a novel domain adaptation method that enables seamless adaptation of deep learning models from one clinical domain to another, without the need for corresponding labels. We also release public datasets of epilepsy and Alzheimer's patients, along with their corresponding manual segmentation marks. Evaluations of our method on these datasets show that it achieves better results than state-of-the-art methods and demonstrates effective domain adaptation. We further propose a framework of deep learning based on multi-task learning. This method allows for domain adaptation through task switching and is evaluated using the provided datasets. We observed that our multi-task approach yielded better outcomes than other domain adaptation methods, despite the absence of labels in the target domain. These findings indicate that our domain adaptation methods are effective and can be used in new clinical domains with or without labels. We have made our implementation available on GitHub. We aim to contribute these results to the hippocampus segmentation community, enabling the development of more reliable automatic segmentation tools for neuropsychiatric disorder diagnosis. We hope that future research led by our work will enhance hippocampus segmentation accuracy. We plan to update our database with more clinical sub-types to support hippocampus segmentation across the full spectrum of neuropsychiatric disorders. We aim to expand our method to other structures of interest in neuropsychiatric disorders, such as the whole hippocampus, lingual gyrus, and parahippocampal cortex. We believe that our domain adaptation framework has the potential to be applied to other neuroimaging-based clinical tasks. A Monte Carlo simulation model is created to calculate proton radiation generated by CRAND. The predicted proton radiation belts align with NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center proton budget measurements at an altitude of around 1,000 km. This new model incorporates a systematic radial distribution of atmospheric density to determine the particle trajectory and loss. It uses a Gaussian error function to compute the standard error of the mean and establishes a proton radiation energy spectrum based on the calculated total energy. The new model significantly reduces computation time to a mere few minutes, making it a viable tool for in-flight radiation protection systems. Furthermore, a geostationary satellite countermeasures radiation exposure by utilizing angular distributions of atmospheric deposition to redirect protons and reduce transit time, thereby increasing the chances of protons being absorbed by the atmosphere before reaching the satellite. Consequently, this model can support the development of a proton radiation protection system for the LISA space-based gravitational wave detector which is set to occupy the space between Earth and the Sun. Earth serves as a crucial shield protecting the detector from harmful radiation. Our model incorporates a systematic analysis of solar cycles and atmospheric variants to generate a time-series database of monthly radiation projections. The detector's space placement and solar activity time-series predictions are closely monitored using this model to ensure safety protocols. If a predicted radiation level surpasses the maximum allowable threshold, engineers must intervene by adjusting the space positioning of the detector to minimize exposure. The model also incorporates a systematic angular distribution of proton guidance to redirect protons and decrease transit time, thereby increasing the chances of protons being absorbed by the atmosphere before reaching the detector. Consequently, this model can support the development of a suitably designed space protection system for the LISA space-based gravitational wave detector.

trained in full. This multi-phase approach surpasses the performance of single-stage 
and joint models across various tasks, employing a ResNet backbone on CIFAR-10 
and combining it with a Siamese network module for similarity assessment. Additionally, 
a new neural architecture search space, tailored to perform equivalence transformations 
on CNNs, is designed to capture the relationship between similar layers and 
facilitate equivalent performance. This novel framework sets a new performance benchmark

existing state-of-the-art in this field. The code for this multi-phase training

Program analysis through Abstract Interpretation involves simulating the behavior of a program in a simplified environment to approximate its true behavior. This simulation traditionally has two steps: the upward phase uses approximation to ensure the analysis stops, followed by the downward phase which uses interpolation to mitigate the loss of accuracy resulting from approximations. This paper suggests an alternative by temporarily switching from an initial approximation to a more precise one, before applying the interpolation phase to improve overall accuracy. The proposed approach is theoretically justified and tested on a simple case study, which yielded substantial gains in precision for several different scenarios. Key benefits of the new strategy were the elimination of the need to decide on the level of precision and the integration of the upward and downward phases into a single, unified cycle. This innovation also enables the simulation to reach a stable point, as the authors were able to define a metric to measure the process and demonstrate its convergence to a stable state. The new approach, which is based on the concept of a precision monad, allows precision to be adjusted at different program locations, thereby increasing its flexibility for use in various analytical applications. The researchers discovered that this strategy is applicable across a wide range of abstract interpreters, as long as the temporary precision improvement does not negatively impact the final accuracy. The theoretical foundation of the technique is rooted in defining what it means for a precision to be an improvement over another precision, as well as defining the principles of temporary improvement and interpolation. This foundational work enables the authors to derive the new strategy from these definitions. The approach was evaluated against a simple case study which yielded substantial gains in precision, up to $1000$ times in some cases, for several distinct scenarios. The researchers observed that varying the strategy to temporarily improve precision at different points could result in different levels of precision for the final approximation, as well as differing computational requirements to achieve it. The new strategy was found to be stable and capable of reaching a stable point, as well as capable of growing in precision over time. A broad range of structural phases in perovskite oxides host various physical properties that contribute to a variety of technological applications. Topological phonons, encompassing nodal rings, lines, and points, are found in certain compounds within the orthorhombic, rhombohedral, and tetragonal phases of these oxides. We employed density functional theory, accounting for anharmonic effects, to study the topological phonon structures in orthorhombic CaTiO$_3$, rhombohedral CaTinO$_{2n-1}$, and tetragonal CaTinO$_{2n}$ systems. We established a classification system for topological phonon configurations, which we used to calculate key phonon states near the Brillouin zone boundary in these materials. Additionally, we explored the potential for nodal lines and surfaces to influence the heat transport properties in these oxides. Our findings demonstrate that both orthorhombic and rhombohedral phases exhibit topological phonon connections, while the tetragonal phase displays nodal lines. Moreover, we determined that nodal lines in rhombohombic compounds contribute to heat minimization in these oxides. Our study on perovskite oxides serves as a basis for the potential design of new materials with topological phonon properties. Furthermore, we are providing the necessary input for use in heat-optimizing technologies based on these materials. We are also releasing our data under a publicly accessible repository for further research by the scientific community. Large-scale data processing in these fields requires more efficient algorithms to handle distance-based outlier detection effectively, given the inherent complexity and computational cost of traditional methods. Fortunately, parallel and distributed computing platforms offer streamlined solutions to this challenge. This study develops a scalable parallel algorithm for detecting outliers based on proximity and validation metrics, optimizing time efficiency in the process. The proposed algorithm utilizes a proximity tree to identify anomalies and verifies its reliability through extensive testing on artificial and real-world datasets, showcasing its efficiency and accuracy. Furthermore, the approach can also be applied to distributed cluster-based systems for parallel processing, offering a flexible solution for outlier detection tasks. The results of the experimental evaluation show that the proposed parallel algorithm achieves substantial speedup in the process, outperforming its baseline counterparts. The source code for the proposed parallel algorithm and testing tools has been made publicly available for further exploration. To the best knowledge, this study represents the first comprehensive analysis and implementation of parallel distance-based outlier detection methods. The outcomes of this study aim to contribute valuable insights to researchers working in related fields. The proposed approach offers superior performance and scalability, but it is worth noting that the presence of measurement errors can negatively impact its reliability and accuracy. Future researchers may leverage the resources and testing tools developed in this study to investigate methods for mitigating the adverse effects of measurement noise. The practical application of the proposed approach to data such as molecular features, network traffic, and image pixels has been effectively validated through its experimental results. Furthermore, the study provides valuable practical insights into the effectiveness of the proposed method across different domains, revealing new challenges and opportunities for further research. Developing CS NLP systems is obstructed by the scarcity of CS data. This study delves into utilizing data augmentation methods to create Dialectal Arabic-English CS text, by replacing words with alternative choices in parallel corpora, selecting points of replacement based on the output of a non-conditional word embedding model. Three data augmentation strategies are explored, each relying on different word embedding characteristics: one method chooses new words with similar sense to the original context, another selects words with similar statistics in a given dialect, and the third chooses words with similar statistics in a target dialect. We evaluate these strategies against zero-shot CS classification, showing that the application of these methods significantly enhances the model's performance, with the first method yielding the most notable improvement. Furthermore, we examine the effect of varying the replacement rate on the performance of the model and analyze the outcomes through mixed-effects regression. This research opens the door for utilizing data augmentation as a means of increasing training data for CS NLP systems. It also underscores the importance of word embeddings in CS NLP, especially in the context of its application to Arabic. Ultimately, the best model achieved an accuracy of 75.64%, an improvement of 25.79%. We believe that these gains are substantial, given that the base model was established using a 5-fold cross-validation approach and performed with no prior training on the target data. Given these enhancements, it is feasible to apply data augmentation to increase data for CS NLP tasks. We have made the developed code, data, and experiments available to the public. The same property applies to any subgroup of homeomorphisms on the circle that map points to their iterates, but are not topologically equivalent to a translation map. Additionally, we show that any subgroup of homeomorphisms on the M\"{o}bius strip that map boundary points to each other, but are not topologically equivalent to a translation map, will never be part of a compact uniform topological group. It is known that a subgroup of homeomorphisms on the circle is compact if and only if it has only one orbit under conjugation, which implies that the previous result extends the work of Purcifte and Schloter. We show, in contrast, that a subgroup of homeomorphisms that map its boundary in a specified manner but are topologically equivalent to a translation map can, in fact, be compact if it converges to a translation map. common link in their objectives, allowing them to complement each other in the
process of predicting a subject-object relationship in a sentence. Specifically,
when a model identifies an object and its related subject, this relationship can
be utilized by another model to anticipate a list of potential objects associated
with the subject, indicating the original object should also be included in the
list. In our study, we utilized this connection by implementing a multi-task
approach, training existing relation extraction models alongside knowledge graph
link prediction to ultimately boost the models' overall performance and achieve
predictable gains in accuracy. Notably, this cooperative multi-task learning
strategy resulted in positive outcomes across all examined scenarios and
benchmarksets, indicating a strong correlation between the two tasks. Hence,
this finding suggests that future research in relation extraction should aim to
achieve superior results by also tackling related tasks such as knowledge graph
link prediction. Our complete implementation is available for public use at:

easily utilize our multi-task approach in various scenarios and benchmark tests.
