Recent searches for supersymmetry at the classical level have not provided any conclusive signs of new physics. In response, the CMS is implementing specialized searches aimed at more complex and precise supersymmetry scenarios. This contribution will focus on three new searches using 13 TeV proton-proton collision data recorded with the CMS detector between 2016 and 2018: a heavy gluino search involving the decay of heavy neutralinos and resulting in boosted Z bosons and undetected energy; a search for supersymmetry compression in final states featuring soft tau particles; and an investigation into compressed, long-lived charginos in final states characterized by abundant jet activity. Each of these searches is based on more than 35 pb^-1 of data collected during 2016, with updated results presented using up to 35.9 fb^-1 of 2015 and 2016 data, with the latest findings presented using 35.9 fb^-1 of 2015 and 2016, and 41.5 fb^-1 of 2016 data respectively. In addition, these results are presented in relation to existing models, with certain parameters suggesting the presence of certain supersymmetry scenarios based on model independent likelihoods. Finally, the discussion will conclude with an examination of the relevance of these results to existing searches, and how these new findings compare to existing data. In particular, it has been determined that the decay length of charginos resulting in displaced tracks at the muon system of the CMS is typically less than 0.1 cm under standard conditions. In certain situations, however, the decay length can reach as high as 55 cm, thereby indicating the necessity for the implementation of new and sophisticated tools in order to cope with the extreme difficulties posed by the challenges faced in these new searches. In general, it is clear that the complexity and precision of these new searches are pushing the boundaries of detector capabilities, and the necessity for the development of cutting-edge algorithms in order to master these exceptional difficulties. In certain instances, however, the difficulty of these new searches is not entirely within the realm of what is technologically possible with current detector design. In particular, the state of the field is clearly indicated by the following: in the case of the search for supersymmetry compression where the tension has reached a point that marginal significance has been achieved with the current dataset; in the case of the search for heavy gluinos where the tension has reached a point that upper bounds have been placed on new physics at a 2.2 Tevat

Temporal sequence analysis typically employs spectrometric or gene expression profiles with limited time points and a high number of variables. Due to this, existing methods face significant challenges, often relying on classical expression differences or wrapper techniques for predictive variable identification. A key issue lies in the small sample size common in such studies. In contrast, our proposed supervised learning approach, Supervised Topographic Mapping Through Time, successfully tackles these challenges by creating a low-dimensional grid mapping for temporal sequences. A hidden Markov model and relevance learning technique allow it to handle time-dependent data, prioritize predictive feature dimensions, and prune irrelevant dimensions that introduce noise. As a result, our system excels in efficient learning for temporal sequences. Compared to conventional techniques, incorporating simultaneous supervised learning and metric adaptation enhances prediction accuracy in both synthetic and real-life scenarios, according to our results. Furthermore, the features identified by relevance learning show impressive comparisons to those of alternative methods. They demonstrate that simultaneous feature importance learning and metric adaptation can produce valuable features for temporal sequence analysis. Additionally, the features identified through relevance learning outperform the features obtained from alternative methods. They show that feature importance can be learned and metric adaptation performed successfully, providing valuable insights for engineers and biologists. They can be used in engineering for dimension reduction in temporal sequences and in biology for understanding the underlying genetic mechanisms related to trypptic protein degradation in gut flora. Reinforcement learning seeks to develop the most effective strategies through interactions with complex systems, even when the underlying rules are unknown. Many successful methods use a valuation function approximation to determine near-optimal approaches. However, in partially observable systems, these valuations are dependent on an extensive sequence of past events and previous actions. Recent research demonstrates that neural networks specifically designed to approximate these valuations are found to internally calculate a probability distribution of the present system state given its history, or belief. Notably, studies have revealed that, as these networks learn and adapt, their hidden states increasingly become intertwined with key environmental markers, recapitulating important physiological processes in living organisms. Furthermore, our own investigation using the variant environment with the name 'Gridworld Navigation Continuous', which requires the estimation of a belief distribution over grid locations and navigation direction, confirms the crucial role of the network's hidden states in achieving optimal outcomes. Through this, we uncover a fundamental link between key environmental markers and the internal states of these networks, thereby improving their overall performance. Finally, our analysis also compares the efficacy of the recurrent architecture in achieving effective strategy development in various complex environmental conditions. The investigation into these connections aims to propel the development of more efficient reinforcement learning systems and shed light on the essential design features, moving towards creating more agile and effective agents. As these learning systems, which are dependent on the underlying principles of their environment, continue to improve, our understanding of their potential use in various applications will evolve, paving the way for a broader range of adaptations. The research findings are set to contribute meaningfully to both reinforcement learning methodologies and the design of agent intelligence. However, we believe that understanding an action involves also considering its context - objects and individuals within a video scene - so we've developed a novel model integrating self-attention and graph convolutional networks to better model context like actor relationships and object interactions. This self-supervised method aims to reduce annotation dependency using the minimum amount of bounding box annotations, offering clear explanation of actions through visual attention maps, even for actions with multiple actors. We've also used our approach to generate new, hidden action semantic spaces which we believe can serve as common representation framework across different action classification paradigms and datasets. This is further exemplified by our successful cross-domain action classification, yielding a 6% higher accuracy than baseline methods. We believe our approach yields new insights into action understanding through self-supervised learning and graph-based object interaction analysis. Our research involves analyzing stochastic differential equations with rapidly changing, periodic coefficients. We consider a mathematical model described by diffusion equations with small variations in the diffusion coefficient and a potential function that change in a correlated manner. Under certain conditions, the diffusion model converges to a problem involving the transport of a substance, known as a drift-diffusion equation. However, this ordinary differential equation has a property called metastability, where the equilibrium positions of its solution change under different parameters. We investigate how this metastability affects the entire diffusion model and show that the probability distribution of the diffusion converges to a specific probability measure as the variations in the diffusion coefficient approach zero. Our research involves showing the convergence of the diffusion model to an optimal mix of the metastable states, either unique or multiple, depending on the equilibrium points of the ordinary differential equation. To demonstrate this convergence, we establish upper limits on the difference between the expected values of the diffusion model and the ordinary differential equation. We also show that the model meets the requirements for the law of large numbers by proving that the model's expected values converge to the mean of the metastable distribution. Our research involves adapting and expanding existing mathematical models of supercooling and the behavior of solitons in the micelle-endosome transport process. We demonstrate that the metastability affects both general and singular degenerate cases. Our work provides a more precise explanation of the metastability effects observed in the general case and the key factors that influence metastability, as found in previous studies. Additionally, we show that the model degenerates into different types, including periodic and boundary instability. Showcasing the applicability of our research, we utilize the metastability effects to analyze specific ordinary differential equation problems, revealing new insights into the general case. Furthermore, we develop a probability distribution model to describe the metastable equilibrium positions, providing a more accurate account of soliton trapping in the degenerate case. Our findings reveal that degenerate metastability can lead to both periodic and boundary instability in the ordinary differential equation. Our research involves examining specific mathematical models where the metastability has remarkable effects, including supercooling and soliton trapping. As the small variations in the diffusion coefficient approach zero, the metastability reveals unique and intriguing behaviors of the ordinary differential equation problem. Our work indicates that the metastability will play a crucial role in understanding the initial-stage dynamics of supercooling, showing the likelihood of the system avoiding homogenous nucleation by reaching a stable equilibrium between the metastable equilibria. This study focuses on the characteristics of nuclear matter at zero temperature within the influence of intense magnetic fields by applying the lowest order constraint variational (LOCV) method, utilizing the $AV_{18}$ nuclear potential. We discovered that the absence of a magnetic field results in an energy per particle symmetrical function in relation to the spin polarization parameter. As a result, our calculations indicate that no spontaneous transition to a ferromagnetic state occurs in nuclear matter under this condition. However, our analysis shows that this symmetry is disrupted when intense magnetic fields are applied, making it possible for the energy per particle to minimize with rising spin polarization. We found that the energy per particle reaches a minimum at magnetic field strengths of approximately 8.95 $\times$ $10^{18}$ G for different neutron-to-proton ratios. Additionally, our calculations indicate that the spin polarization parameter reaches its lifetime limit at a neutron-to-proton ratio of zero. We found that nucleon density decreases with rising magnetic field intensity, while quark-level parameters, which are drawn from the $AV_{18}$ nuclear potential, remain consistent across varying magnetic field intensities and neutron-to-proton ratios. Moreover, our analysis shows that the magnetic field effect causes the quark-level parameter $m_d$ to deviate from its free neutron value, while the quantities $m_s$, $g_\sigma$, $g_{\omega}$, $g_{\rho}$, and $h$ remain unchanged. Overall, our calculations reveal that the presence of strong magnetic fields leads to substantial spin polarization in nuclear matter. The calculated spin polarization parameters are found to be consistent with theoretical estimates from other studies. Moreover, our LOCIV method suggests that the symmetry is disrupted when magnetic fields interact with matter, making it possible for the spin polarization parameter to reach its lifetime limit. The research conducted provides an in-depth exploration of nuclear matter under the influence of intense magnetic fields, focusing on its energy per particle, lifetime limit, nucleon density, quark-level parameters, and spin polarization. The studies may lead to new insights into the magnetic behavior of exotic states like hypernuclei, quark matter, and strange quark cluster, which can only be stabilized in a regime with intense magnetic fields. The results of the calculations are displayed in figures 1-7. The research can be further expanded by applying magnetic fields to studies of quark clustering, which has been left for future work. Balancing communication efficiency and data privacy is a critical concern in distributed neural network training. To address this gap, we introduce an innovative approach, Privacy-Chaining Vector Quantization (PCVQ), a distance-preserving quantization technique that can be combined with intermediate data transmission (IDDT) to substantially reduce communication overhead. PCVQ leverages the security of differential privacy and its compatibility with intermediate data transmission, thereby enabling faster convergence while maintaining data privacy. Our experiments demonstrate PCVQ's efficacy across various federated learning scenarios, yielding a 33.75% reduction in communication costs on average, when compared to conventional quantization methods paired with intermediate data transmission. Moreover, PCVQ surpasses the recently proposed PrPriQuant approach in achieving better convergence speed and top-1 accuracy on the CIFAR-10 dataset, averaging a 10.33% improvement in top-1 accuracy and 34.33% reduction in communication costs. PCVQ's performance can be further optimized by integrating it with intermediate pruning (PCVQ+IP), resulting in an enhanced convergence speed and top-1 accuracy on the ImageNet dataset at a global iteration 100. The PCVQ source code is freely available at: https://github.com/QuantifiedCuriosity/PCVQ. Our research shows PCVQ's potential in achieving robust federated learning results. A comprehensive far-ultraviolet continuum map of the Taurus-Auriga-Perseus complex was created by combining the observations from GALEX and FIMS, which provided data at nearly identical wavelengths. The UV intensity in the area exhibited significant variation, with diffuse UV radiation largely resulting from dust particles scattering starlight. A UV background intensity of around 1000 CU was measured, with a portion potentially attributed to scattered light in the foreground of dense clouds. Fluorescent hydrogen emissions constituted roughly 10% of total UV intensity across the region, generally corresponding to local continuum levels. A customized radiative transfer model was employed to determine the optical properties of very small grains and their abundance in the Taurus-Auriga-Perseus complex, yielding an optimal fit. Specifically, the best-fit very small grain albedo was approximately 0.3, with a range of 0.2 to 0.5, and their cross-section per H2 molecule was about 50,000 square angstroms, with associated uncertainties. Furthermore, it was found that the optical properties of very small grains do not appear to be uniform across the complex. Considering the observed diffusion of UV radiation due to its weak intensity, extensive datasets, including those from the James Webb Space Telescope, could be used to explore the UV environment in similar complexes, allowing for a more precise model constraint. Structured tables in various documents effectively present complex information, making research in scientific papers easily accessible to scholars by compiling experimental outcomes and highlighting novel discoveries. Current table analysis techniques can fall short due to recognition errors stemming from the conversion of PDFs into document images, resulting in information loss. This study develops a solution to table extraction by leveraging Graph Neural Networks and incorporates tailored representation embeddings that improve differentiation between tables, table headers, and other document components. An experimental assessment was conducted on a combined dataset consisting of the CMTK and TableBank datasets to evaluate the proposed approach's efficacy. The results indicate that this solution outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques, achieving a recall of 83.79% and precision of 81.02%. In addition to evaluation results, the paper discusses methods to increase the precision of the final model by adjusting the number of GRU iterations and varying the number of GRU layers. The proposed approach demonstrated promising outcomes, showing considerable potential for improving table extraction by incorporating sophisticated machine learning architectures. The code for the proposed approach is publicly available on the GitHub repository located at: https://github.com/QuantNow/Table-extraction-with-GNN. An additional document detailing the analysis is provided as supplementary material.

This work delves into the dynamic cognitive hierarchy theory, introduced by Lin and Palfrey (2022), within the context of multi-stage incomplete information games. In such scenarios, players simultaneously uncover peers' relevant characteristics and problem-solving abilities over the course of the game. Building on this concept, our study provides a complete characterization of the dynamic CH equilibrium for games featuring two-stage incomplete information. Furthermore, our findings are applied to a series of two-stage games. Firstly, we examine a modified version of the linear demand model as proposed by Bertoletti and Tamura (2020), aiming to explain international income disparities. Secondly, we investigate a modified version of the gift-game model, enabling the detection of cognitive differences between individuals. Finally, both models are permitted to be incomplete. Crucially, our paper develops a direct link between the solution to these strategic problems and the main characteristics of the dynamic CH equilibrium, thereby facilitating computable equilibrium construction. Such a breakthrough is accompanied by two computable and easily implementable tests for distinguishing between different levels of cognitive abilities within each of the specified models. Moreover, our study provides a control function to assess how changes in specific model variables influence key outcomes. Finally, our findings are confirmed through the results of a Monte-Carlo simulation experiment. In terms of practical applications, our work has potential implications for understanding economic inequalities within society. By analyzing data on income and education, for instance, it may be possible to distinguish between different cognitive levels as described by the dynamic CH framework and, through this, gain a better understanding of an individual's problem-solving abilities. Lin and Palfrey's (2022) root node equilibrium is applied to the three tested models in a separate appendix. Moreover, our study presents additional analyses, such as test results for cognitive differences, dynamic CH equilibrium estimates, and sensitivity tests for the main models. Such supporting material is presented in an online supplement available at linzechong.github.io/2022/dch2.pdf.

Precise and continuous population estimates are crucial for policy decisions surrounding vaccination initiatives and infrastructure development planning. As censuses fall short of providing the necessary spatiotemporal detail, researchers have been turning to independent approaches combining satellite imagery and geospatial data. The main limitation of such strategies lies in their inability to continuously monitor population changes over time. We address this issue by developing an advanced population estimation framework leveraging multi-source data. Our approach pairs a neural regression method with a geometric data representation and incorporates diverse information from multiple perspectives. The efficacy of our technique was assessed through comparisons of its accuracy across seven diverse cities. The results show that it performs comparably to the estimates derived from census data, thereby enabling the creation of high-fidelity population maps. Furthermore, we demonstrate the potential of our approach by applying it to previously unobserved regions like Kashmir, thereby facilitating informed decision-making. The framework, comprising both code and data, is publicly accessible at https://github/popformer. The data utilized for training, validation, and testing purposes consists of a comprehensive dataset spanning 112,107 squares covering 28 countries, 50 states in the US, and 4398 counties in the US. The dataset is divided across 28 European countries, featuring 28 initial channels. The framework was developed under Python 3.7, employing the PyTorch 1.9 deep learning library. The neural network training process requires approximately 3 days on 32 GPUs, while the total data volume amounts to 2 TB, with a data size per square of approximately 0.28 MB. The time needed to predict population squares is approximately 0.005 seconds on an NVIDIA V100 GPU. The framework incorporates 23 million model parameters, with a memory requirement of approximately 3.5 GB per square. This research focuses on solving spatiotemporal object-based reasoning challenges in videos by employing object persistence principles. A crucial element of our approach is recognizing how to track objects throughout a video by identifying their movement and transformation, thus efficiently utilizing memory resources. Currently prevalent deep learning-based methods exhibit spatiotemporal biases when employing low-level features, resulting in inadequate video understanding. Furthermore, existing memory-based architectures lack the capability to learn effective memory queries. To overcome these limitations, we developed a novel model named ObjectPermanence (OP) that learns object-based queries to accurately interpret spatiotemporal relationships in videos by employing object persistence principles. Overall, OP achieves enhanced performance compared to the top-tier methods on multiple video benchmarks, including the large-scale video benchmark ImageNet-Video-Captioning. Additionally, we introduced a novel video benchmark named OP-Benchmark, featuring 10,000 images divided into three sections, to assess video-based object persistence understanding. The images in this benchmark are sourced from Labyrinth, a well-known video analysis benchmark. We observed significant performance improvements when our model was fine-tuned using the OP-Benchmark training dataset derived from Labyrinth. This enables our model to learn object persistence by employing object-based queries and thus enhance the accuracy of video understanding. The game "Mafia," also known as "Werewolf," is a party-based competition between two opposing groups. Citizens and mafia members are the main groups. Each phase in the game, consisting of day and night segments, allows for various actions to be taken, with lynching occurring during the day phase. Mafia members possess special abilities that distinguish them from the citizens, who are the dominant group due to their higher numbers. Researchers have developed a mathematical model that represents the game's progression as a discrete-time pure death process. They have found precise equations describing the mafia's chances of winning and the overall game's progression, also exploring their discrete properties and continuous-time approximations. Studies have shown that only a small number of mafia members, equivalent to the square root of the total player count, can grant the mafia and the citizens an equal probability of winning. Additionally, the outcome of the game heavily relies on whether the total number of players is even or odd. Investigation into the approximated equations reveals interesting behaviors at critical total player counts that occur at specific thresholds. Furthermore, these findings have been verified through simulated trials. The researchers have also kept the mathematical model's simplicity and the game's basic characteristics intact, while obtaining a solution that accurately represents both groups' winning chances. They have further analyzed and compared the mathematical model's results with other variants of the game "Mafia" that include additional elements. Those variants involve the addition of three special citizen roles - seer, detective, and double-mafia - whose detection or identification by these roles yield different outcomes but do not alter the fundamental characteristics of the game. Researchers have derived mathematical models for these variants, representing the seer and detective as discrete-time Markov chains and the double-mafia as a discrete-time birth and death process. They have derived equations relying on simpler linear algebra methods. They have found that approximating these variants resembles the basic "Mafia" game's progression, also observing interesting behaviors at critical total player counts that occur at specific thresholds. Therefore, this research contributes unique insights into the mathematical representation of the "Mafia" game by utilizing pure death and Markov processes to explore the game's characteristics. In doing so, it opens a new avenue for researchers to analyze the game as a scientific subject, also establishing a connection between discrete-time processes and continuous-time Markov chain approximation methods. Further studies can utilize these findings to explore more intricate game variants. The code used to simulate trials and derive mathematical models has been made available online. Several planetary systems have multiple giant planets, and research aims to
understand how their formation is affected when planets develop in tandem. Our
study uses long-term computer simulations of planetary growth from a shared gas
disk, and the results reveal a link between the planets' relative sizes and the
formation of gaps in the disk. However, when both planets form simultaneously,
their masses converge to a narrow range over a relatively short period of time.
Delaying one planet's development slightly increases their size disparity but
ultimately yields a similar mass ratio. To replicate observed exoplanet mass
variations, models suggest planets form and grow at different times and then
either disperse quickly from the gas disk or have gas supply interrupted early. 
Simulations also indicate systems with inner, less massive planets are the
result of extended gas supply, and ratios of inner-to-outer planet masses fall
within a narrow range. These findings align with observed exoplanet mass ratios. 
Additional simulations with varied planetary proximity consider how close
planets need to be to stay in a shared gas disk. Proximity of less than 2 astronomical units separates planets in most cases,
and a simulation of 28 Earth-mass planets reveals wide separation requires a
large disk or early gas supply interruption. These studies provide a framework
for understanding exoplanet masses and planetary spacing. They predict systems
with inner, massive planets and tighter spacings than observed, unless planets
are given extended gas supply, and consider how close planets need to be to
develop in tandem. These findings also imply most observed exoplanets are not
as spaced out as Earth and other inner planets. 

These simulations provide a framework for understanding and interpreting
exoplanet masses, and predictions based on the models suggest planets in the
observable universe should exhibit mass variations consistent with recent
findings. However, delayed planetary development in tandem requires early gas
supply interruption or dispersion to replicate spacings wider than observed,
and further exploration into early life and planetary systems is necessary to
fully grasp planetary formation and evolution processes.

and other inner planets. To better grasp planetary development and evolution,

be better understood.

The electrical conductivity of an ensemble of nanomaterials on a macroscopic scale
depends on intricate electronic transport mechanisms involving the constituent
nanoscale objects. Heat units known as phonons exhibit a dual influence on
conductivity: by scattering electrons, they can hinder it but can also enhance it
by facilitating temperature equilibrium among electrons in conducting paths.
Investigating these nanoscale components therefore necessitates a comprehensive
analysis of electronic transport mechanisms. This paper presents an asymmetrical
heat transfer model to demonstrate the biphasic effect of phonons on electronic
conductivity in nanomaterials. This model establishes that the temporal and spatial
distribution of phonons directly impact electrical conductivity and emphasizes the
importance of synergistic electron-phonon interactions in electronic transport. 
Phonons can not only lower the system's electrical resistance by reaching thermal
equilibrium but also improve the system's overall conductance by creating a pressure
that tightens filled electrons. This phenomenon provides novel insights into the
electrical properties of nanomaterials and serves as a potential starting point for
designed conductivity enhancement at the nanoscale. Moreover, this paper discusses
potential applications and experimental implementation of the proposed concept. 
Lastly, it forecasts a promising future for aspherical nanoparticles, in particular,
ellipsoidal particles, and suggests that these shapes may hold the key to achieving
desired conductivity levels in electronic devices. This research outcome can therefore
be used as a guide for the designed creation of nanomaterials with optimal electrical
conductivity based on their unique geometry. 
Simultaneously, this paper presents an innovative method of asymmetrical heat
transfer that can extend the application of the Lorentz model, which was initially
designed for one-dimensional systems, to systems of varying dimensions. This novel
approach effectively combines multiple heat transfer methods in a systematic
model that can be readily extended or modified to suit systems of any dimension. 
According to the proposed model, in lower-dimensional systems, phonons exhibit
unidirectional movement, and as a result, heat transfer is restricted to the primary
direction. Conversely, in higher-dimensional systems, the influence of the Lorentz model
diminishes whilst phonons with varying directions and velocities contribute to the
asymmetrical heat transfer in multiple directions. Hence, this paper presents a

The goal of deep transfer learning (DTL) is to empower deep neural networks (DNNs) with the ability to draw from past experiences like humans. This capability is referred to as knowledge transferability. Typically, the process of DTL begins by initially training DNNs on general knowledge and then utilizing them for specific tasks through a refinement process called fine-tuning. There have been two commonly observed patterns of transferability among pre-trained DNNs: one being that larger gaps between pre-training data and downstream information result in lower transferability and another indicating that transferability tends to be higher for smaller tasks. There is, however, no consensus on a unified explanation for these patterns. To address these issues, we suggest a new framework that links pre-training data to downstream performance and downstream capacity. Within this framework, one dimension measures the distance between pre-training and downstream data, and another measures the amount of information required to accomplish a downstream task. Different from previous studies, our framework offers a more comprehensive understanding of transferability and its limitations, and it also suggests that dimensions extracted by DNNs correlate with our framework's dimensions. As proof, we show our framework's results align with common transfer learning methods. Additionally, we discovered that incorporating a new refinement process called data refinement could enhance transferability and explained data refinement's mechanisms. Lastly, by leveraging our framework, we were able to achieve a greater GEM-MOT score of 70.1 compared to 68.9, on the MOTT benchmark for video object detection. The code for our framework can be found at https://github.com/la-ml/dtlt.

The widespread adoption of Android as the global leading operating system makes it an appealing target for malware. To counter this threat, security experts continuously develop advanced detection systems based on machine learning and deep learning. However, skilled hackers counter these systems by adapting their malware samples to bypass detection through a variety of evasion attacks. This study focuses on problem-space evasion attacks on Android devices, where malicious actors modify APK files directly to evade detection. The study examines the recent advancement in this area by analyzing 11 such attacks discovered in the last five years. Each attack is assessed based a set of established metrics that consider factors like detection rate, accuracy, and computational resources required. The analysis reveals that existing evasion attacks can bypass Android malware detectors up to 100%, with an average increased in accuracy of 70%, all while increasing processing time by 3 times. Based on these findings, future research directions are proposed, including implementing more sophisticated evasion attacks that utilize dynamic and semantic analysis of Android malware. The investigation also provides insights for Android developers and users on how to defend their devices against such attacks. Finally, the challenges associated with a specific form of problem-space evasion attack that uses code padding are discussed. The study is presented in two parts: Part I focuses on a literature review of existing Android malware detection methods, including a comprehensive analysis of problem-space evasion attacks, while Part II showcases a novel approach to detect code padding attacks that achieves high detection rates with efficient resource usage. The final objective is to integrate the proposed approach with existing malware detection systems to enhance overall system robustness against various evasion attacks. Service-oriented computing utilizes services as building blocks for constructing distributed systems. Traditionally, orchestrating cloud-based services centered around business process execution, particularly with BPEL's focus on services as processes. However, recent shifts towards alternative service motivations such as XaaS and RMAD require a revised approach. Although conceivably, diverse services can be converted to WSDL/SOAP formats, such a strategy is overly complex and impractical for industries to adopt. As a result, treating a service solely as a business process proves restrictive. Conversely, we view a service as a procedure that is agnostic to specific technologies, decoupled, and transparent to locations. Underpinned by these ideas, we introduce Ozy, a generalized orchestration framework, enabling us to redefine the orchestration of modern service-based applications. Our definition encompasses traditional process services, technology-aware microservices, SaaS-based service compositions, and RMS-driven, service-based approaches. Ozy redefines its orchestration through its deconstruction into constituent services, applied via specialized operators that reflect services' native modes of operation. We showcase Ozy's application in various use cases spanning all four service types. Ultimately, we conclude that a revitalized approach to service understanding and service orchestration is necessary to tackle the challenges of modern service-oriented computing. Our aim is to renew the way we comprehend and utilise service orchestration in Service-Oriented Computing. This study addresses the dial-a-ride problem within large urban settings where residents have a range of transportation options at their disposal. To meet the needs of riders who do not own cars, a service known as ridepooling has emerged - it works by grouping multiple riders traveling along the same route and transporting them efficiently. However, ensuring that ridepooling services remain attractive to customers has become a complex issue. On one hand, a high percentage of riders in a pool can make the service more appealing, but on the other hand, groups with an excessive number of riders can be costly and time-consuming as they involve extra stops along the way. Furthermore, customers may take detours to pick up fellow riders en route, which can also drive up costs. To tackle these challenges, we have developed a computational model aimed at minimizing the costs associated with picking up riders, maximizing the number of riders per pool, and accounting for pre-existing social connections within the community. By incorporating these factors, we have modified the classic multi-department vehicle scheduling problem into a more dynamic and ride-sharing friendly scenario. This study explores multi-modal pretraining techniques for product data in E-commerce, addressing limitations in current methods which struggle with modality-noise and modality-missing. We introduce K3M, a novel method incorporating knowledge modality to mitigate noise and supplement missing modalities in image and text data. K3M utilizes a modal-encoding layer and a modal-interaction layer that combines features of individual modalities with a structured aggregation module fusing knowledge, image, and text modalities. Through pretraining with MOM, MLM, and LPM tasks, we demonstrate K3M outperforms existing methods in handling modality-noise or modality-missing scenarios in E-commerce product datasets and related downstream tasks. The code and model weights are freely accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/Ai4Eteam/K3M. This research benefits from substantial real-world E-commerce product data provided by our collaborator, Jingdong Inc. (99tests.com). We believe K3M offers substantial improvements in multi-modal E-commerce applications and may serve as a foundation for future developments. Furthermore, our investigation reveals an unusual phenomenon in E-commerce product images characterized by both high textual knowledge density and lexical simplicity, contributing knowledge to the AI research community. Similarly, our analysis of known brand logos in the data reveals a typical representation, sparking an idea for future brand logo recognition applications. We are eager to share K3M with the research community, anticipating valuable discussions and possible enhancements. We believe K3M may be adopted in related fields and look forward to collaborative discussions. Unlike other machine learning techniques that rely on labeled data, unsupervised learning discovers natural groupings within a dataset. A novel approach to this issue is presented in a paper by Theodore G. Moran et al., focusing on the principle of energy minimization through a network called Deep InfoMax (DIM). In this paper, the authors review relevant theory, assess the applicability of DIM in brain imaging, and evaluate the use of pooling methods with deep neural networks in medical brain imaging. Three of these methods are tested on two brain datasets: primary glioma and multiple sclerosis. Compared to standard dimensionality reduction techniques, DIM is shown to produce groupings that better align with clinical understanding. However, the application of DIM in brain imaging is found to be challenging due to its large dimensionality and the lack of a comprehensive theory of brain function. As a result, a comprehensive framework for brain imaging analysis is proposed, incorporating not only unsupervised learning but also semi-supervised learning, pooler training, and an attention-based classifier. This framework achieves superior performance on a multiple sclerosis dataset, earning an award from the 2020 MICCAI Grand Challenge Tracking and Semi-supervised Segmentation of Temporal Lobe Epilepsy. These potential applications require a more in-depth analysis of brain data than what is currently provided by the unsupervised learning approach. An effective spin-orbit constant $\lambda_{\text{eff}}$ is considered in the wave function, focusing primarily on quarter-filled electrons. We find that $\lambda_{\text{eff}}$ correlates directly with the bare $\lambda$ and depends on electron interactions represented by the parameter $(U'-J')$. In the paramagnetic region, $\lambda_{\text{ext}}$ increases as interactions increase, however this effect diminishes in the antiferromagnetic phase where $\lambda_{\text{ext}}$ reaches a maximum. Additionally, we identify the development of an exchange interaction between electrons in planes parallel to each other as a factor contributing to $\lambda_{\text{ext}}$. This interaction, referred to as $t'^{\perp}$, amplifies the magnitude of $\lambda_{\text{ext}}$ and creates a cross-linking effect within the 2-dimensional structure. Our investigation further suggests that a higher $\lambda_{\text{ext}}$ could lead to the formation of a uniaxial ferromagnetic component alongside the existing antiferromagnetic characteristic in the exchange interaction between the two orbitals, while a higher $t'^{\perp}$ may enhance this uniaxial ferromagnetic property. Finally, we conclude that, even though $\lambda_{\text{G}}$ is very low (approximately 0.004 eV), it does not disappear completely, indicating that $t'$ plays a significant role in the formation of a uniaxial ferromagnetic component in the exchange interaction between the two orbitals. The Asymmetric Numeral System (ANS) was a significant innovation in entropy encoding developed by Duda, revolutionizing data compression by surpassing the capabilities of arithmetic and Huffman coding. Despite its optimality being studied by Duda et al., the asymptotic redundancy of ANS, relative to entropy, remained unclear. This paper provides a precise bound on the redundancy by which ANS falls short of optimal entropy compression, using the findings of Deleuil et al. on the characteristics of ANS distributions and its implications for sequences. Additionally, we show that the table-based version of ANS (tANS) does not substantially improve the situation, as it incurs the same redundancy. This result has practical significance, suggesting that tANS is not a substantial achievement. This study relies on recent findings regarding the range of frequencies for which ANS is efficient in computing, a topic previously investigated by Deleuil et al. and further analyzed in this work. In contrast to other studies on ANS redundancy by Codinhas, Deleuil, and Nekrich, this research uses a different mathematical framework, focused on set theory rather than a Markov process model. The findings of Cid-Falcon and Rivas indicate that ANS's poor performance for certain distributions can be attributed to its discrete nature, suggesting the superiority of continuous encoders like the arctangent encoding. This research also analyzes the situation for the binary search-based ANS (bsANS) encoder, showing that it incurs only a small negative redundancy, thereby exemplifying a situation where a continuous encoder, bsANS, has a lower redundancy than its table-based counterpart, tANS. This study finally demonstrates the positive redundancy of the binary range partitioning-based ANS (brANS) encoder, thereby confirming the asymptotic optimality of this continuous encoder under certain conditions. Theoretically, this research validates the performance superiority of continuous encoders based on the analyzed cases, implying the potential for further compression improvement using continuous encoding schemes. On a practical note, this research shows that the continuous ANS encoders, bsANS and tANS (with Duda's precise initialization), do not substantially outperform their table-based counterpart in terms of redundancy. The study concludes by examining the related open issues and challenges that could facilitate deeper research on the topic, especially highlighting a fundamental question regarding the related binary range partitioning problem that has been put forward in this research. The dielectric characteristics of micro- and mesoporous materials are heavily influenced by the dielectric properties of the liquid phase. For electrolyte solutions, these properties are significantly affected by the salt concentration and the dielectric response of the liquid phase is determined by short and long-range ion interactions with the dielectric environment. In order to gain a deeper understanding of the dielectric properties of liquid phases in contact with a dielectric solid, we have conducted experiments and computer simulations. Specifically, we have measured the dielectric response of potassium chloride solutions at high concentrations using dielectric spectroscopy, in addition to performing molecular dynamics simulations that model the dielectric properties of these solutions. The results of these experiments and simulations reveal that, in the frequency range of 0.1 - 1 MHz, the dielectric response of potassium chloride solutions is predominantly determined by the movement of ions. In a further development of this research, we have conducted a theoretical analysis of the dielectric properties of potassium chloride solutions, incorporating experimental results from dielectric spectroscopy and comparing them with the outcomes of molecular dynamics simulations. The results of this research show that ion-pair dielectric behavior is prevalent at high salt concentrations and high frequencies, however, as temperature and frequency variations occur, the dielectric response of the solutions changes from dielectric permittivity reductions to dielectric permittivity enhancements via dielectric relaxations. Moreover, the results reveal the dielectric contributions given by individual ions, with an emphasis on the dielectric response given by the chloride ions. In a comparative evaluation, the results of this research showed that, in concentrated solutions, the dielectric response is predominantly determined by the movement of the ions, whereas in dilute solutions, the dielectric response is predominantly determined by the movement of the ions and the dielectric properties of the solvent can no longer be ignored. The results of this research further demonstrate that, in certain scenarios, hydrogen bonding between the chloride ions and the solvent can significantly contribute to long-range ion interactions, leading to a decrease in the dielectric permittivity in the lower frequency range. When performing cosmological inferences based on the Lyman-$\alpha$ correlation functions, standard analyses usually only consider a specific feature related to baryon acoustic oscillations. In this research, we investigate whether these standard analyses adequately capture the relevant cosmological information. To address this, we directly fitted synthetic Ly$\alpha$ correlation functions, including cross-correlations with quasars, without compressing the data, and then compared the results to the conventional method. Our approach provided significantly more precise measurements of the cosmological parameters with smaller uncertainties of 0.3%, 0.2%, and 0.2% for the matter density, neutral hydrogen density, and Hubble constant respectively. The inclusion of these additional information led to reduced uncertainty in parameters such as the distance to the surface of last scattering, neutrino density, and Planck mass, with their respective uncertainties becoming 4%, 8%, and 25% smaller compared to the conventional method. Furthermore, there was a 0.03 increase in the likelihood value when using the full information compared to only considering BAO signals. To take full advantage of these constraints in future Ly$\alpha$ feature-based experiments, we suggest adopting a more comprehensive analytical model that can accurately capture the rich information contained within the Ly$\alpha$ correlation functions. Our research paves the way for the utilization of these high-quality data, enabling the detection of subtle signals related to early dark ages, and potentially yielding constraints on the standard model with a 1% precision. Given the anticipated statistical precision expected in future surveys such as DESI, we anticipate our approach to be essential for the analysis of Ly$\alpha$ correlation functions in the near future. To facilitate the use of our findings, the code used for the analysis has been made public at https://github.com/Researcher/FUZZLYA/tree/main/ code/ lyafit. Additionally, the Ly$\alpha$ correlation functions and their cross-correlation with quasar data have been made public at https://www.sciel.br/ph/_rcd/ ead/ rcc/. Our code is written in the HEALPix framework and the fast Fourier transform was applied during the analysis to enable the evaluation of the correlation functions at multiple radii. To establish a basis for comparison, the results obtained here are consistent with those from the earlier work as intended. Our research was performed within the framework of a collaborative global challenge held at the 2019 '20th International Conference on Computational Methods in Physical Sciences hosted by the University of California

Over the past thirty years, various theoretical models have been introduced to analyze intricate systems. This research aims to compare and contrast these measures objectively by exploring their core similarities, disparities, and limitations. To achieve this, a comprehensive analysis of four renowned metrics is conducted through case studies, including complexity metrics based on network topology, dynamical systems, mutual information in neural networks, and information integration theory. By examining these metrics step by step, the underlying assumptions and mathematical rigor of each one are evaluated systematically. Additionally, the methodological links between these metrics are highlighted, and their common criticisms reviewed. However, existing methods for determining these potentials rely on the requirement that they be piecewise affine, which limits their application to only certain systems. In order to overcome this limitation, a new approach is presented here, describing how to construct continuous gauge potentials from the given driving potential without any geometric constraints. This method is then demonstrated using the example of driving a qubit with a magnetic field, where it is shown that its results match those of existing methods when the system is linear, and also enables the creation of more complex driving mechanisms for qubits. Additionally, a new technique for implementing the counterdiabatic control, not previously achievable with conventional methods, is developed. This method involves the generation of artificial gauge fields by combining optical Raman and dipole interactions, which is shown to be effective in driving two-level systems in free space. These developments offer the potential for applying counterdiabatic protocols in a broader range of systems, facilitating the manipulation of quantum systems. Color-neutral images are a cornerstone in various image processing domains, such as image compression, restoration, and enhancement. However, color information can be detrimental when working with sensitive images or medical data, requiring a conversion to grayscale. Currently, widely-used grayscale creation methods original or rely on predefined filters, often failing to adapt to diverse image types. To address this, this research introduces an unsupervised neural network capable of converting color images to grayscale in a data-driven manner. The proposed approach utilizes contrast perception to generate an initial color sensitivity map, followed by a tailored network that adapts to diverse image types, including computational art forms. The framework also incorporates contrast preservation, ensuring the resulting grayscale images maintain optimal contrast levels. Comprehensive evaluations have been conducted on the state-of-the-art Witkin-Fries algorithm and four additional datasets, yielding superior results in terms of MSE, SSIM, MS-SSIM, and UIQI metrics. Furthermore, the approach demonstrates versatility in multiple applications, including color filters, computational art forms, salt and pepper noise removal, image compression, medical data conversion, and super-resolution, showcasing its robustness and versatility across multiple image domains. Overall, the proposed method successfully enhances existing grayscale creation methods, offering a valuable tool for diverse image processing domains. The implementation of this research can be accessed at the following GitHub repository: https://github.com/filipezai/UnsupervisedGrayscale. KEYWORDS: Grayscale conversion, Unsupervised conversion, Data-driven conversion, Neural network, Computational art, Image processing domains.

This research develops an expression to decompose infinitely differentiable complex-valued functions into a sum of exponentials along with a corresponding error term. Building upon this, a corresponding infinite series is derived for functions in $C^\infty$, which converges to the original function under specified conditions on the remainder term. Subsequent applications of these results enable the computation of certain infinite series connected to Stirling numbers. Moreover, this formulation enables the introduction of a novel representation of transcendental functions like $\sin z$ and $\cos z$, given in terms of the Stirling numbers just mentioned. Finally, the text examines the convergence of the series representing $\cos z$ and $\sin z$ in various regions of the complex plane. Notably, this investigation demonstrates that each convergence region corresponds with a particular set of directions in the complex plane. Ultimately, the text demonstrates that this new representation allows for the derivation of certain inequalities for $|\cos z|$ and $|\sin z|$. In particular, this formulation enables the creation of a novel minimum-maximum inequality for $|\cos z|$. Similarly, this new representation yields a novel minimum-maximum inequality for $|\sin z|$. To facilitate further research, this paper leaves several open questions at the conclusion. Chiefly, it is sought to determine whether the series representing $\cos z$ and $\sin z$ might also converge in the entire complex plane except for a modified version of the negative real axis, similar to known cases with the exponential function. We create a vacuum state and observe the formation of both continuous and discrete spectra resulting from the interaction between photons and electrons. Employing a quantum electrodynamics (QED) approach, our research focuses on the Breit-Wheeler process, converting two photons into an electron-positron pair. Through analysis of an electron's scalar function in a dressed formalism, we identify pairs of discrete spectral modes that contribute to the electron's momentum. Our findings show that the Breit-Wheeler process produces two electron spectral modes: a continuous 'pair-production' mode and a discrete 'dress-to-dress' mode. This research reveals the Breit-Wheeler process as a source of electron spectral strength. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the electron's strength is predominantly attributed to the process's discrete spectral mode, occurring early in its temporal development. To facilitate experimental identification, we also compute the electron's spectral strength generated by the Breit-Wheeler process across various energy settings. Our research sheds new light on the Breit-Wheeler process as a significant linear process in QED and quantum field theory photoelecton spectroscopy. As a photoelectron's interaction with the electron's magnetic moment is exceptionally weak at low energies, the observed 'dress-to-dress' mode can be indirectly probed through measurements focusing on the electron's charge. This offers an innovative experimental approach for identifying the Breit-Wheeler process at various energy settings. Nonetheless, the electron's spectral strength is exceedingly tiny at high energies, making experimental identification extremely challenging. Nevertheless, the discrete spectral mode can be crucial in modeling black hole information paradox, the electron's magnetic moment, and quantum radiation. Consequently, the problem of the electron's spectral strength remains unsolved, but our research brings it closer to being understood. Our study primarily employs the Breit-Wheeler process in its classical form; a subsequent study will examine the process in its quantum form, examining the quantum nature of its 'dress-to-dress' mode. Research is currently underway to investigate the electron's spectral strength using laser-based approaches, including strong-field QED, as well as nonlinear photoelectron spectroscopy. These studies can be found at arXiv:2103.04427, arXiv:2103.04428, and arXiv:2104.03993. Our research aims to ultimately explore the quantum nature of the electron's spectral strength in highly excited states. In a forthcoming letter, we examine how sensitive the Two Higgs Doublet Model is to a crucial parameter, $m_{12}$, which breaks the symmetry softly and impacts the Higgs boson decays significantly. Along with other vital model parameters like the Higgs boson masses and the Higgs vacuum expectation values ratio, $m_{12}$ determines how effectively Higgs bosons decay into Standard Model particles and each other. By focusing on the lightest Higgs boson decaying into two photons, we develop a method to restrict the model by depending on the mass of the other Higgs bosons. This model's ability to explain a recent anomaly in its role in decaying the top quark is also investigated. After running a Monte Carlo simulation of Higgs production and decay processes using the LHC's data, we establish boundaries for $m_{12}$ based on the Higgs boson's observed mass and energy, 125 GeV and 7, 13 TeV respectively, and find a best fit for $m_{12}$ to be around 170 GeV in the model variation where the Higgs boson decays preferentially. However, our analysis shows that choosing an optimal set of model parameters is challenging due to the available data not strongly constraining it. Nonetheless, we obtain at the 95% confidence level the following restrictions for $m_{12}$, which corresponds to various masses of the other Higgs bosons: $m_{12}$ corresponds to $m_H$ = 300 GeV as 190 GeV, 270 GeV, 210 GeV, 450 GeV; $m_H$ = 450 GeV as 170 GeV, 190 GeV, 210 GeV, 270 GeV; $m_A$ = 300 GeV as 190 GeV, 270 GeV, 190 GeV, 190; $m_A$ = 450 GeV as 170 GeV, 190 GeV, 270 GeV, 190. Additionally, we find that choosing an optimal set of model parameters is difficult when considering all possible model variations. Nonetheless, we discover at the 95% confidence level the following restrictions for $m_H$ - $m_A$ mass pairs: $m_H$ - $m_A$ pairs as 90 GeV - 170 GeV, 90 GeV - 190 GeV, 90 GeV - 270 GeV, 150 GeV

Pre-trained language models possess the ability to capture syntactical information, as established in previous studies [Tenney et al., 2019, Jawahar et al., 2019, Hewitt and Manning, 2019]. This work presents two unsupervised constituent parsing models, UPOA and its enhanced version UPIO, both of which use the syntactic distance from self-attention weight matrices in pre-trained language models to evaluate sentence structures. Further experiments demonstrate the significance of linear projection matrices for queries and keys in self-attention for accurate parsing. Consequently, the unsupervised models were transformed into few-shot parsing models, FPOA and FPIOA, to learn better parsing matrices with less annotated data. On the Penn Treebank dataset, the unsupervised model UPIO achieved parsing performance on par with supervised models having only 16 labeled trees. Importantly, the few-shot parsing model FPIOA reached parsing performance on par with the best supervised model with as few as 500 labeled trees. These results show that the unsupervised and few-shot parsing models have a considerable amount of predictive power in their current state. It is suggested that the linear projection matrices for self-attention in language models can serve as a pre-trained component for future parsing models. Additionally, the results provide an answer to a question posed by Adi Shmueli and Aryeh Kontorpi in 2019: Can a "naturally" self-supervised language model produce a parse tree that accurately represents the structure of a sentence? The current study offers an affirmative response. All source code is available at https://github.com/kuo-ling/UA. As the self-attention mechanism in pre-trained language models possesses the ability to capture syntactical information, the study envisions the future integration of self-supervised models with linguistic rules and constraints for enhanced parsing performance. Ultimately, the study serves as a stepping stone for the development of future self-supervised parsing models. The study proposes the term Syntactic Pre-trained Knowledge (SPK) to describe the syntactical information embedded in pre-trained language models. The SPK has the potential to be further developed for applications beyond natural language processing, such as code analysis. The study presents a new paradigm for the understanding of pre-trained language models. The accuracy of speech-based applications heavily relies on high-quality Automatic Speech Transcription. Although German acoustic models perform well, they can benefit from additional training data, specifically spoken language corpus from various domains and dialects. We introduce a new dataset, Spoken Wikipedia, comprising 24,007 hours of speech from 2,685 speakers across 78 distinct dialects, offering a wide range of regional accents and expertise. We then assess the effectiveness of incorporating this new data into existing German acoustic models, using Wav2Letter2 and the Sennheis as baseline models. Our results indicate significant improvements when incorporating Spoken Wikipedia data at both the feature and final output stages. Notably, using Spoken Wikipedia data yields an absolute WER reduction of 2.6% and 4.6% for the baseline models Wav2Letter2 and the Sennheis, respectively. Although the new data poses challenges due to varying speaking styles, tone, and pronunciation, our models demonstrate resilience and efficiently incorporate this information without requiring adjustments to the loss function. Interestingly, our experiments reveal that using a smaller subset of the Spoken Wikipedia corpus, totaling 250 hours, is sufficient to yield optimal results, providing an efficient solution for continuously improving German acoustic models. In our research, we conducted a comprehensive review of NTK, focusing on its applications in reinforcement learning, which is rarely documented. Our study covers the essentials of NTK, examines both visual and non-visual AI tasks where NTK methods have been employed, and provides insight into challenges associated with training NTK models. Furthermore, we highlight the significant advancements achieved by NTK methods in reinforcement learning and explore the prospects of incorporating kernel learning in reinforcement learning. Ultimately, our review outlines existing obstacles that must be overcome in reinforcement learning and identifies promising avenues for further research. Review articles are an efficient means of disseminating knowledge and save readers time, as they enable them to swiftly become acquainted with the latest research in reinforcement learning and deep learning. As such, we encourage researchers in visual AI to adopt more structured survey methods and incorporate automatic summarization techniques to facilitate future reviews in the field. In contrast, we recommend that researchers exploring understanding in deep learning utilize detailed surveys and wait for subsequent updates, allowing these updates to complement previously-cited sources. The possibility that our Universe undergoes a periodic cycle of expansion, driven by ΛCDM models separated by phases of inflation and radiation dominance, is investigated. The ΛCDM periodic cosmology is based on the hypothesis that both inflation and the current accelerated expansion could be caused by the same dark energy component. When plotting the matter density parameter Ωm against the radiation density parameter Ωr in phase space, a closed trajectory is observed that would allow the Universe to repeat the cycle indefinitely. Consequently, the acceleration of the ΛCDM phase expansion is replaced by the onset of a new inflation phase. Analyzing the simplest variant of ΛCDM periodic models reveals that the acceleration of the ΛCDM phase is replaced by the transition to the inflation phase earlier than in the standard ΛCDM model. However, the predicted pattern of the multiple microwave background anisotropy acoustic scales differs only slightly from that of the standard ΛCDM model, with the ΛCDM periodic model exhibiting a smaller discrepancy in this context. A future large project that measures the position of galaxies at far distances, called DESI, may search for signs of the transition from the ΛCDM phase to the inflation phase by studying how galaxy distributions change over time and using their redshift values to locate their positions within the predicted periodic expansion path. If successful, such a search could confirm that our Universe behaves according to the predicted periodic expansion path. On the other hand, the absence of the predicted transition or discrepancy in the multiple microwave background anisotropy scales observed in the DESI project would rule out the ΛCDM periodic model in favor of the standard ΛCDM model. Overall, the proposed search using DESI observations offers the potential to confirm or rule out the ΛCDM periodic model at high precision.

In recent years, the needs of embedded systems have grown more complex.  These systems not only require reliable, hard real-time capabilities but also diversified functions like network capabilities.  Implementing virtualization using hypervisors has emerged as a suitable solution to address these demands.  Unfortunately, existing hypervisors, which were designed with general-purpose computing in mind, come with a considerable system overhead that is not suitable for mixed criticality embedded real-time systems.  Moreover, the schedulers within embedded hypervisors fail to account for the diversity of real-time demands as well as the rapidly evolving nature of scheduling principles.  
  This paper presents T-Visor, a custom-made hypervisor designed for mixed criticality embedded real-time systems.  Built from the ground up to support embedded systems, T-Visor implements a minimal set of functions to meet the requirements of embedded systems.  This includes a hypervisor-based virtualization framework with real-time capabilities that leverage the principles of embedded real-time systems.  This paper also outlines our approach to integrating virtualization with embedded real-time systems, which focuses on loadable scheduling models.  Furthermore, T-Visor implements a device driver-based memory management scheme with expandable and embedable capabilities that leverage the principles of shared memory.  The schedulability analysis of the scheduling model is also discussed. When two coupled populations of oscillators have synchronized and asynchronous elements respectively, a chimeric state can arise in such networks. We've analyzed chimeras in systems where one parameter influences an oscillator's behavior, drawn randomly from a uniform distribution, for oscillators in dimensions d ≥ 2. Our investigation reveals that the emergence of robust chimeric states depends on the degree of internal population synchronization, which is particularly evident when the oscillators' mean interaction strength is above a certain threshold proportional to d^{-1/2}. Furthermore, to assess the robustness of these chimeras, we considered small-world and complete networks, finding that internal synchronization's sensitivity and the overall network's structure play crucial roles. Our research offers a new perspective on chimeras in complex networks and contributes to our understanding of collective oscillators. Additionally, we provide an estimate for the region of parameters where stable non-trivial solutions can occur, complementing existing theories with specific numerical and analytical findings. Finally, we verify the stability of these chimeras through local bifurcation analysis. Our work opens up further areas of investigation regarding the phase transitions that occur in multiverse systems, where robust chimeras may exist. Moreover, our research suggests that the emergence of these chimeras may be influenced by factors such as population size, network complexity, and the distribution of oscillator parameters. Future studies could explore these dynamics and provide a deeper understanding of multiscalar systems. Our mathematical framework can be applied to various experimental scenarios, enabling the observation and analysis of chimeric states in practical contexts. As an example, we discuss how chimeras can occur in systems of coupled Stuart-Landau oscillators, commonly used to model different physical systems. Our work notably demonstrates that, in certain circumstances, chimeras can occur even when the oscillators' mean interaction strength is quite small, a phenomenon that could potentially be observed in experiments involving weak coupling. Our study's novelty lies in the fact that, to the best of our knowledge, it is the first to investigate chimeras in systems drawn from the uniform distribution in dimensions d ≥ 2. Our research may contribute to a deeper understanding of complex multiscalar systems, leading to the discovery of additional intriguing phenomena, particularly in systems where parameters vary across different scales. The clock registers two tunneling times,  $\tau_y$ and $\tau_z$, corresponding to particles approaching a potential barrier in the $y$ or $z$ direction. There is a discrepancy between the definition of tunneling time by B{\"u}ttiker and Steinberg, with the latter identifying the actual tunneling time (ATT) with the Larmor clock reading for the $y$ direction. Research, however, has shown that ATT is influenced by spin fluctuations in non-commuting spin systems. Consequently, we have established an ATT based on fluctuations that takes into account spin fluctuations in tunneling particles. The findings reveal that tunneling times measured by B{\"u}ttiker and Steinberg are approximately 34.6% apart on average. The research also shows that as tunneling probability decreases, so too does the range of times averaged across these different measurements. Furthermore, we have discovered a notable similarity between tunneling dynamics and the behavior of an event horizon in cosmology, with the average tunneling time amounting to its radius. The global spin fluctuations underlying this work also enable the development of an ATT that is less sensitive to local spin strength in tunneling processes. The findings are corroborated by applications to various physical systems. However, the current understanding of BECs relies on complex descriptions, often through quantum field theory or nonlinear differential equations. These descriptions sometimes conflict with the principles of quantum information science. To clarify the situation, we examine BEC interferometry in the context of two parallel paths and reveal that a critical decision hinges on whether to employ linear or nonlinear quantum mechanics. If the system can be accurately modeled using linear dynamics, it may lead to enhanced precision and elevated visibility in the interferometry. Conversely, if linear dynamics are insufficient, leveraging nonlinear effects can still yield first-order quantum interference. Furthermore, by exploiting BEC's ability to engage with external fields, researchers can detect these interference signals without compromising stability. Consequently, even in systems requiring nonlinear descriptions, BEC interferometry may serve as a reliable tool for evaluating linear quantum mechanics. Ultimately, our analysis points to the efficacy of combining multiple measurement approaches to fully describe the capabilities of quantum systems. Moreover, our findings potentially pave the way for the development of BEC-based devices capable of detecting linear changes in phase shifts, as small as π/2 radian. Nonetheless, in systems exceeding mean-field regimes, the described interferometry loses its precision and visibility. Hence, in these instances, external control may be necessary to ensure stable operation within the linear quantum mechanics regime. Interestingly, in the context of quantum information science, BEC systems offer versatile opportunities for processing information that is partially linear and partially nonlinear. To further explore these capabilities and detection limits, we examine the functionality of entanglement-swapping in BEC systems, revealing that despite BEC systems typically being resistant to decoherence, entangled pairs may experience degradation due to local measurements. Nonetheless, when external fields interact with BEC condensates, they may induce sufficient mixing to enable entangled pairs to remain stable, given the appropriate timing and interference wave function orientation. Consequently, demonstrating the entanglement-swapping process in BEC systems hinges upon the balance between the system's internal dynamics and external interactions. Learning with an ever-growing number of categories poses significant challenges. The task becomes particularly demanding when models need to learn online after seeing each example only once. Current techniques struggle to adapt or require memory, making the problem nearly impossible to tackle in scenarios like image classification with diverse datasets drawn from various fields. To overcome this issue, we propose a new approach, called One-Shot Forgetting-Free Learning (OSFFL), which eliminates the memory issue and allows models to continually learn without forgetting previous classes. The proposed method works by maintaining a stationary neural network and using a reversible module to create adaptable features for new classes. The reversible module utilizes a novel rating loss that prevents feature retention and a reconstruction loss that ensures minimal change to previous features. The proposed method, called one-shot reversible framework (OSRF), achieves the desired objective and has been tested using multiple benchmarks such as Caltech-256, MiniImageNet, and combined datasets of MiniImageNet and FMoW/ILTS. The experiments show that the proposed method outperforms existing baseline methods in one-shot learning scenarios. Additionally, we developed a new method, called progressive one-shot freezing learning (POSFL), for learning with numerous examples across multiple fields by applying a new approach called FrostLearn. The proposed technique outperforms existing baseline methods in multiple experiments. The proposed code and models are available at the website cited above. The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, tracking particle interactions resulting from high-energy collisions. As part of the CMS system, the silicon pixel detector forms the innermost component responsible for navigating the trajectory of particles. Although initially operational between 2009 and 2016, it has been replaced with an upgraded variant in 2017. During a preceding period of shutdown for the LHC, an upgraded forward pixel detector prototype featuring a novel readout system and third disk was introduced, integrating eight pilot blades built using advanced digital readout chips. Through pilot module testing, researchers obtained practical experience in operating the upgraded detector. This study reports the results of analyzing data captured with these new components, including a detailed explanation of the reconstruction process and an assessment of the newly achieved hit efficiency. Furthermore, the study demonstrates how these modules can accurately track the movement of charged particles. Finally, the results illustrate the effectiveness of these upgraded modules in enhancing the accuracy of particle tracking. These outcomes are set to influence the development of the detector's full upgrade, which is set to take place by 2026. Moreover, the study discusses prospects for forward detector upgrades that could significantly increase its capabilities, such as the addition of an electromagnetic calorimeter component that could enhance the detector's ability to quantify energy levels. When gluon distribution becomes saturated, it establishes a distinct gluon density threshold per unit rapidity per transverse area known as the saturation momentum.  In certain large-energy situations within the context of the factorization framework for hadronic processes, the saturation momentum plays a crucial role and functions essentially as an intrinsic momentum threshold to the hadronic system.  As an example, it plays a pivotal role in the rapidity gap processes where it determines the upper limit to the mass of the emitted particles outside the main hadronic body.  In light of this, researchers investigated direct photon production in the diffractive collisions of large hadronic systems such as protons and lead-lead ions.  In these systems, factors such as the saturation momentum of the emitted photons and the quantum numbers of the incident and emitted hadronic systems play a pivotal role in the photon spectrum distribution.  Monte Carlo-based rapidity gap process simulation demonstrated that the diffusion of the saturation momentum around its average value might significantly influence the observed photon spectrum distributions, especially in the low-photon pseudorapidity regime.  Consequently, researchers might obtain insight into the quantum characteristics of the hadronic system by studying photon spectrum distributions in such diffractive collisions and, in turn, gain a deeper understanding of the hadronic system itself.  Furthermore, researchers found that the diffractive photons emitted during coherent $^{16}$O-oxygen nuclear collisions could potentially be directly observed at the LHC.
