Baryon creation is investigated using a quantized fragmentation model based on QCD strings. Baryons are generated through a process that is straightforward to understand, which involves an initial QCD string breaking up into monopole-like components. A simplified model, called the CNF-MOT model, has been found to be effective in describing the masses of various types of baryons. This model has been successful in replicating the masses of well-studied particles such as the proton, neutron, and various isobars composed of nucleons, lambda particles, and sigma particles. Additionally, it has also provided insights into the masses of strange baryons, including the lambda, sigma, and xi particles. Using this framework, the CNF-MOT model has made predictions about the masses of unknown baryons. This work includes an analysis of the properties of strange baryons, including the lambda, sigma, and xi particles. It also discusses how the CNF-MOT model relates to the classification of unknown baryons observed in heavy-ion collisions. A list of the masses of unknown baryons, including those predicted to have masses less than 3 GeV, is included in this paper. This work includes a discussion on how the CNF-MOT model relates to the classification of unknown baryons observed in heavy-ion collisions. Such information could be beneficial in helping physicists to identify and analyze particles discovered in recent high-energy heavy-ion experiments. A computer code that demonstrates how the CNF-MOT model achieves its results has been made available for public use. This code includes all of the equations that underlie the model, as well as a detailed description of an simulation method called the contour-consistent string break-up technique. It also includes a detailed description of an algorithm, referred to as MOT, which is used to optimize parameters in order to fit observed data accurately. This code is compatible with public quantum computer simulators and is written in a way that allows it to run on clusters, supercomputers, and quantum computers. It includes pre-calculated solutions to certain differential equations that describe the mass spectrum of QCD theory. A potential application of this code is to use it to analyze data from experiments at the Large Hadron Collider. Such information could provide insights into whether quantum chromodynamics is satisfied at energies corresponding to protons that have been accelerated to levels approaching the energy threshold of the LHC. A detailed description of future work that aims to use artificial neural networks to analyze data using this code is included in this paper.

In the present investigation, variations in the breadth of five oscillation modes, encompassing degree values between $s=10-150$ and spanning the 23- and 24-year cycles of the solar active periods, are examined through data obtained from Michelson Doppler Imager (MDI) and Highly Sensitive Camera (HSC) instruments. Active region observations conducted every 5 days reveal a significant relationship between surface velocity flows and oscillation frequency alterations. Notably, the broad-based mode ($l=2, m=2$) exhibited increased narrowing during the cycle's ascending phase, which could be attributed to surface magnetic field fluctuations. To further analyze this phenomenon, two-dimensional surface magnetic field maps of active regions were studied. In-line with theoretical predictions, it was found that the oscillations converge towards the interior of the sun in areas with strong magnetic fields, which may also explain the observed decrease in the broad-based mode's frequency. Utilizing a one-dimensional hydrodynamic model, the relationship between the turbulent convective flow and its inverse energy cascade was explored, which provided additional insight into the issue. By differentiating between local versus global flows within the convective turbulence, a possible explanation for the observed decrease in the broad-based mode frequency has been identified. In the local turbulent convective flow scenario, faster moving fronts induce slower moving moving plasma against the background, which is moving towards the sun's surface. However, the oscillations are prevented from reaching the sun's interior by the magnetic field. Consequently, the issue of the broad-based mode frequency narrowing during the cycle's ascending phase remains unresolved, as it is found that the oscillations are either trapped at the sun's surface or in the shearing layer. Furthermore, the magnetic field strength needs to be less than $10^{3} G$ for the sun's surface magnetic field to play a significant role. It is also found that the solution to the issue is dependent on the degree of helioseismic sensitivity, which is defined as the degree to which the oscillations are influenced by the sun's surface magnetic field fluctuations. In a $150\le s\le 200$ degree of helioseismic sensitivity, it is found that the oscillations are either trapped at the sun's surface or in the shearing layer. However, for higher sensitivity levels, the solution becomes more complex, which is consistent with theoretical predictions. In the most extreme scenario, the oscillations are found to be completely absent, which is consistent with theoretical predictions based on sunspot magnetic field fluctuations.

The remarkable effectiveness of deep learning has sparked various concerns regarding ethics, encompassing skewed predictions and data security risks. To address these problems, experts employ fairness metrics, decentralized machine learning methods known as federated learning, or differential privacy. A pioneering approach, this study creates a unified ethical federated learning framework, seamlessly integrating all three techniques in harmony. Experimental results based on the Adult, Bank and Dutch datasets showcase the "interplay" between precision, equity, and confidentiality that occurs when incorporating differential privacy in federated learning settings for classification tasks. Moreover, this study provides practical guidance on how to effectively balance fairness and privacy by adjusting the trade-off between them. Our findings also reveal that, in practice, the use of differential privacy may result in enhanced fairness, contrary to initial expectations that it would solely increase the risk of misclassification. A newly developed metric, known as EDP-mrp, is introduced to efficiently quantify risk in this context. Our work presents the first-ever systematic investigation of the intricate relationships between deep learning techniques, focusing on classification tasks. Our comprehensive analysis sheds light on the intriguing connections between precision, equity, and confidentiality, which are crucial considerations in themselves. Our approach offers a versatile and generalizable methodology, capable of handling diverse datasets, including the German KAGGLE ActiveMLL dataset. Our results show that there is still unexplored potential for applying differential privacy in practice, as it may lead to increased fairness. Our work outlines a new direction for research, exploring how various ethical metrics influence one another through concrete empirical results, which can be used to inform design and policy decisions. We investigate a smart reflecting surface-aided wireless-powered communication network where a multi-antenna energy transmitter broadcasts an exclusive energy signal to a powered transmitter that initially absorbs the energy, then sends an information signal to the destination despite potential external interference. To optimize this setup, we've formulated an analytical problem focusing on maximizing throughput through the simultaneous optimization of energy absorption duration and reflecting surface phase shift matrices, despite this being a highly complex non-convex problem. To address this complexity, any advanced optimization algorithm can be used but we suggest an efficient method using a deep learning network, as a significant performance-complexity advantage can be obtained without the time-consuming task of manually labeling data. Our results show that this approach significantly outperforms conventional methods, such as beamforming without energy harvesting or intelligent reflecting surface assistance. A detailed numerical analysis was also provided to confirm the effectiveness of the proposed scheme. Overall, this research presents a pioneering solution utilizing a deep learning-based scheme to optimize a smart reflecting surface-aiding wireless-powered communication network. Furthermore, this approach enables the efficient collection of data for the design of interesting machine learning-based architectures, thereby contributing to the development of AI. A key benefit of this technique is that it eliminates the need for any form of manual data labeling involved in the training process, thereby making it a compelling solution. We explore the intersection of dark matter and leptogenesis within a unified theoretical framework, which includes three right-handed neutrinos, a fermionic dark matter particle, and two additional scalar bosons beyond the Standard Model. We establish that dark matter and right-handed neutrinos share a common origin, which is crucial in accounting for the asymmetry between $\tau$ and light leptons during leptogenesis. Our analysis reveals that in the vicinity of the $h$-$X$ resonance, the relic dark matter and right-handed neutrino pairs contribute significantly to the total asymptotic abundance, which may satisfy the Planck experiment's requirements for dark matter. Moreover, the resonance enhancement of the dark matter annihilation rate can explain the observed density of dark matter, resulting in a self-consistent solution for both dark matter and baryon asymmetry within our theoretical model. Our findings represent the first description of dark matter and leptogenesis in a unified theoretical framework, which includes three right-handed neutrinos, within the effective field theory framework with masses for right-handed neutrinos below $5 \times 10^2 \, \mathrm{GeV}$. Our research demonstrates that in the near future, it may be possible to test the gauge boson associated with dark matter, which results from the relic dark matter momentum distribution near resonance. Our results represent the first description of dark matter and leptogenesis in a theoretical framework, which is consistent with the existing experimental data, and demonstrates that dark matter can be leveraged as a tool to probe the physics associated with the Standard Model. Despite significant advancements in producing realistic images with GANs, a primary concern persists, particularly for high-resolution inputs and intricate datasets, due to training instability caused by a mismatch between the real and randomly generated distributions, leading to a common issue of vanishing gradients during GAN training. In order to mitigate this problem, previous solutions employed practical techniques, such as weight clipping and gradient penalty, to constrain the capabilities of the discriminator. In this research, a more systematic approach is presented as an alternative to tackle this problem by focusing on relationships between paired samples rather than classifying them as real or fake. Specifically, a relation network architecture for the discriminator is explored along with a specially designed triplet loss that yields superior generalization and stability. Extensive evaluations conducted on benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method, consisting of a relation discriminator and novel loss function, results in notable enhancements in a variety of applications, such as image super-resolution, particularly when the input resolution is higher and the data complexity increases. A novel approach for practical quantum communication over long-distance fiber has been introduced in the form of Twin-field quantum key distribution (TF-QKD). This method presents a significant improvement by circumventing the necessity for the phase locking technique. Instead, our approach identifies a suitable reference state through the collection and post-selecting of data from a main channel, thereby facilitating the determination of the phase in the return channel. Our work validates that the phase in the main channel can be accurately reconstructed by leveraging the data from the data collection process, eliminating the need for phase locking. Additionally, our approach for establishing the phase in the main channel yields a substantial increase in the data efficiency when compared to previous methods. Consequently, our approach serves as a valuable foundation for practical quantum communication over long-distance fiber, including a proposed TF-QKD system with a reach of 620 km. Furthermore, our approach can be extended to the field of quantum teleportation, allowing for the efficient determination of the phase in a quantum signal using a large number of data collections, thereby enhancing the data efficiency in this field. In the context of TF-QKD, our approach allows for the implementation of a potentially game-changing technology known as blind TF-QKD. This method involves the selective collection of data from the main channel, thereby eliminating the need to estimate the probability of a photon being detected in order to establish the phase in the return channel. In a proposed blind TF-QKD system, our approach yields substantial improvements, including an increase in the distance capable of being traveled of over 30% when compared to previous methods. Furthermore, our approach yields a substantial enhancement in the security of the system, eliminating the possibility of a photon being selectively detected in order to establish the phase in the return channel. As such, our approach represents a significant advance in the field of practical quantum communication over long-distance fiber. In particular, our approach allows for the first instance of blind quantum key distribution being implemented, thereby constituting a significant enhancement in the field of practical quantum communication. In the context of TF-QKD, our approach yields substantial improvements, including an increase in the distance capable of being traveled of over 30% when compared to previous methods. In particular, our approach constitutes a significant improvement when said methods require the probability of a photon being detected being explicitly calculated in order to establish the phase in the return channel, a process that constitutes an invasion of privacy. As such, our approach constitutes an significant improvement in the field of practical quantum communication over long-distance fiber, representing a substantial enhancement of the security of the system.

Mortality forecasting models built on the classical factor framework, such as the Lee-Carter model and its variants, often oversimplify real-world conditions. The models assume factor loadings remain static over time despite the significant influence of variables such as advancements in medical treatment and environmental shifts. We expand the classical model to create a factor model that accounts for the evolution of factor loadings over time. We introduce two methods for forecasting factor loadings and apply them to a model that effectively captures the changing relationships in mortality datasets and improves forecasting accuracy for various timeframes and regions. Moreover, a new technique based on analyzing critical points is developed to identify optimal forecasting intervals for long-term and short-term predictions, and simulated studies verify the performance of the model in multiple scenarios. The model's success is further demonstrated through applications to mortality data for England and Wales, the US, and a synthetic dataset. Finally, additional theoretical investigations and a maximum likelihood estimation algorithm are provided to complement the model's development. As a result, this factor model offers enhanced flexibility, flexibility-accuracy tradeoffs, and flexibility-management by incorporating various forecasting methods and analysis techniques. Potential variables for consideration include lifestyle factors, environmental conditions, socioeconomic indicators, dietary preferences (such as the impact of COVID-19 on mortality trends), and advancements in medical care, among others. Reducing the cost of neural architecture search (NAS) by sharing weights among different child models is a popular strategy. However, due to interference from other models, there is often a poor correlation between predicted accuracy and actual performance of the child models. This study investigates the cause of interference by comparing how similar the effects are when child models are trained with shared weights and reveals that the level of interference depends on the diversity of the other models being trained, and also the differences in the data inputs. Based on these findings, two methods to reduce the impact of interference have been proposed. First, instead of using a one-size-fits-all architecture for all child models, a tailored architecture specific to each model is defined, reducing the interference. Secondly, to reduce the interference caused by the differences in the data inputs, a technique to balance the data input distribution among the different models is used. Compared to using a one-size-fits-all architecture alone, or the method that used performance prediction to guide the search with data balancing, we show with our results that the combination of these two methods significantly reduces the interference and leads to better top-performing child models on image classification tasks. This is confirmed by our results using the Search-BALANCE algorithm on a dataset of image classification tasks, and we show that it leads to better top-performing child models compared to other methods. This is confirmed by our results using the Search-BALANCE algorithm on the CIFAR-10, CIFAR100 and ImageNet datasets. This work highlights the need to reduce the interference that occurs when different child models are trained with shared weights in NAS. This is supported by our findings that more diverse the other child models that are trained with shared weights, the worse the top-performing child model will perform if the interference is not reduced. Moreover, our results show that the proposed method Search-BALANCE leads to better top-performing child models at a reduced computational cost compared to other methods. This is because it reduces the impact of interference that occurs when different child models are trained with shared weights, and leads to more effective search. We identify concrete, infinitely precise criteria under which a proper geodesically complete CAT(0) space has a semistable fundamental group at its boundary. Building on this foundation, we prove that any relatively hyperbolic space with a boundary consisting of more than two points admits a boundary group. Furthermore, when the space is proper and finitely generated, we show that the boundary group corresponds to its Euler characteristic, yielding a significant consequence for the Haar length spectrum of the space. This spectrum is, in fact, proportional to the Novikov density of the space when the latter is assumed to be proper, connected, locally compact and semi-simple. This finding affirms a long-standing conjecture initially proposed by Gromov, specifically that the Novikov density can be captured through the change in volume density as the time parameter progresses along a proper, semi-simple group action. It's also worth noting that our results extend and complement previous works conducted by Mohapatra--Tsai and Sambale--Wingate. Ultimately, our methodological approach demonstrates that our semistability framework is versatile and can be adapted to accommodate spaces with boundary curves possessing positive width in the Gromov-Paulsen sense. In a broader context, our results are relevant within the realm of 3-manifolds, worldviews, and other geometric and topological structures, opening doors to potential cross-connections and generalizations that extend beyond the proper and complete CAT(0) space framework presented herein. A concise, illustrative example describing a boundary group is included, detailing how it can be utilized to establish a geometric interpretation of invariance theorems, specifically highlighting its relevance within the context of Gromov's theorem, which asserts the equality between the trunk's Hausdorff dimension and the Novikov density of a proper, cocompact discrete group. A similar example is also given for proper, discrete hyperbolic group actions, illustrating how boundary group invariance can be utilized to establish a discrete analogue of the TRB theorem, thereby paving the way for a discrete equivalent of Gromov's theorem, with the boundary group playing a pivotal role in its discrete realization. Detailed, step-by-step explanations are provided, detailing how the Paulsen density of a discrete group is related to its trunk's Hausdorff dimension, based on the TRB theorem. A comprehensive, alphabetical list of terms and concepts is included, along with a list of references cited throughout this work. A preface is appended at the end

Human-assisted Translation Quality Assessment (TQA) is an extensively utilized method that helps gauge machine translation efficiency, negotiate translation contracts, and evaluates human translator proficiency.  Despite its importance, little research exists using quantitative methods to determine TQA's reliability.  In our investigation, we examine TQA as a multi-component process using complex system physics and Bayesian analysis, with the aim of exploring the concept of reliability.  Employing Translated SRL's error-annotated translation evaluations, we develop two Bayesian models to assess various TQA-related attributes - translation difficulty, translator expertise, and reviewer strictness.  Through validation of these attributes, we are able to evaluate translator reliability based on their overall performance and create a reliable translator ranking system.  Importantly, our results indicate that translator expertise is the primary factor contributing to reliability, with translator experience resulting in improved translation quality when working on difficult translations, suggesting that human translator expertise is a decisive factor in achieving high-quality translations.  Furthermore, our study yields new insights into reviewer characteristics and their impact on translation assessment.  Overall, our approach provides an original framework for translating a set of texts into multiple languages, resulting in accurate assessment of translator reliability, accurate ranking of translators, and an understanding of remaining challenges to be addressed in order to further refine TQA's reliability assessment capabilities.  Future applications of our methodology may involve translating texts into multiple languages, generating data for new translation projects, and investigating the effects of various TQA parameters.  Importantly, our methodology lays the groundwork for building large-scale models of translation processes, suggesting that human translation may be a suitable starting point for developing models of complex translation processes.  Ultimately, our approach may pave the way towards creating sophisticated digital tools for managing human translation, facilitating automated translation assessment and simulation. We've found that using pruning methods on artificial neural networks significantly
reduces their size while maintaining their performance, and can even reveal smaller
sub-networks with higher accuracy than their full counterparts. Our study focuses
on analyzing the structural properties of the sub-networks obtained by iteratively
applying a filter to the original network's connections. Notably, we found that
the resulting sub-networks tend to exhibit shorter path lengths. Additionally, we
observed that the surviving connections in the original network often form dense
clusters, and pruning them results in the disappearance of these clusters. Moreover,
we found that the pruning process can uncover smaller sub-networks with higher
accuracy in classification tasks. Interestingly, we found that the structural
characteristics of the sub-networks vary greatly from those of the original network,
exhibiting smaller diameter, lower average degree, and fewer nodes. Our findings
shed light on how to effectively prune artificial neural networks, and highlight the
significance of using statistical mechanics to analyze complex neural systems. 
Key words: neural networks, pruning, graph theory, statistical mechanics, gradient descent.

The large-charge expansion technique opens up a new possibility for calculating critical properties of high-charge operators $\phi^Q$, where the charge $Q$ is fixed. For operators of a given charge, the mathematical structure of their critical properties can be determined in the weak coupling regime by focusing on the properties of the operator itself, such as self-interactions and interactions with the vacuum and other external operators. When calculating these properties at the six-loop level for operators of charges up to $Q=5$, new optimized strategies for evaluating diagrams graphically were developed, including the use of distinguished variants. The results obtained for the critical properties of $ \phi^{2Q}$ operators are consistent with predictions from the stochastic tensor product representation of their critical properties at all orders in the coupling. Furthermore, the critical properties of high-charge operators cannot be accurately predicted using lower-order approximations, such as those obtained via the renormalization group flow in the vicinity of a given fixed point when the number of external operators included in the approximation is insufficient, including when the inclusion of five- or more-legged operators is required at the six-loop level. The results also show that the difference between the critical properties of an operator obtained under the large-charge expansion and those predicted by the renormalization group depends on the ratio of the critical exponents of the operator and the bremsstrahlung time. When the ratio of the critical exponents is small, the difference between the two approximations becomes proportional to the square of this ratio, while the bremsstrahlung time is inversely related to the power of the coupling constant with which the operator's self-interactions contribute, thereby facilitating a general understanding of when the large-charge expansion may yield more precise results than other approximation strategies. The optimization of strategies for evaluating diagrams graphically was based on the availability of general results from perturbative quantum field theory that allow for the identification of general scaling laws for diagrammatic expansions relevant to the critical properties of quantum field theories. Furthermore, the results obtained at all orders in the coupling for operators of charges up to $Q=5$ are consistent with predictions across multiple scales in the coupling, while the inclusion of the bremsstrahlung time in the optimization strategies for evaluating diagrammatic expansions at all orders in the coupling effectively accounts for the difference between the critical properties obtained from these expansions and those predicted by the renormalization group flow, such that the former may yield more precise results than the latter. Our research systematically explores how different mechanisms affect the valley Hall response in a two-dimensional, plain silicon material under the control of a magnetic field. t-SNE is a widely employed method for reducing high-dimensional data to lower-dimensional representations, particularly in data visualization. Its core assumption relies on non-constrained data within Euclidean space, with proximity determined by Gaussian distributions. However, this premise doesn't always apply in real-world scenarios, as evidenced by data such as points on the surface of a sphere, which adhere more closely to von Mises-Fisher distributions. In response, this study develops a novel vMF-SNE algorithm tailored for embedding spherical data efficiently, leveraging the Gaussian-based t-SNE framework. Experimental findings showcase the superiority of vMF-SNE over traditional t-SNE in preserving the intrinsic structure within spherical data. These advancements also enable more accurate von Mises parameters to be extracted, particularly in dimension 1, where significant enhancements are achieved. As a result, vMF-SNE outperforms vMF k-means and t-SNE in achieving consistent results for dimension 2. These improvements are confirmed through empirical analysis and further validated by promising future research directions on adapting t-SNE to accommodate diverse data distributions, as the developed approach resolves the limitations seen in the earlier method. vMF-SNE has been implemented and made available on GitHub, served up by the CDS project. Additionally, the issue of handling data with mixed priors may be a challenge for the algorithm, as the developed approach is singularly focused on spherical data, analyzed under the von Mises-Fisher distribution. In the future, the method may be expanded to accommodate data with mixed polyhedral anisotropies, as the developed approach is generally applicable, beyond its singular focus on spherical data. We derive an expression for the pullback of the Hitchin connection, extending from the moduli space of genus two curves to a 10-fold cover of a Teichmueller curve, which was first found by Veech. Subsequently, we develop an expression in terms of iterated integrals that describes the monodromy representation of this connection. Over time, the trend of companies adopting remote working has been on the rise, leading many to adapt Agile methodologies such as Scrum to cope with distributed teams. However, the global shift to fully remote working brought on by the COVID-19 pandemic was a unprecedented phenomenon. This research involves a two-phase, multi-method approach. Initially, it investigates how working from home affected Scrum practitioners through a qualitative survey. Subsequently, it proposes and empirically tests a theoretical framework using PLS-SEM with data from a sample of 200 software engineers who collaborated on Scrum projects from home. Our results demonstrate the reliability of all key constructs and the validity of all hypotheses, while also highlighting the importance of meeting fundamental psychological needs during remote working. Furthermore, the study identifies specific psychospatial design elements required to support these needs, ultimately leading to enhanced remote working well-being. Conclusively, the study contributes towards addressing the challenges associated with remote working by providing insights for managers and practitioners. Additionally, it offers practitioners valuable solutions to implement in such an environment. Finally, the study highlights key research areas and questions that merit further examination. Numerical studies have shown that in many instances of medium-scale networks, binary power control is near-optimal. Contrasting this, the GDoF investigation reveals the extremal gain of optimal power control grows exponentially with the number of users, while a binary power control approach is incapable of harnessing this gain. As such, it can be inferred that in medium-scale networks, binary power control is near-optimal due to the slow emergence of this extremal gain. This leads to the development of new extremal GDoF bounds for networks employing optimal power control, which can be seen as a hybrid of linearity and nonlinearity. Furthermore, extremal network theory is applied to establish a lower bound for the extremal gain, which is found to be substantial, potentially allowing for significant performance enhancements in networks of moderate size. Lastly, extremal GDoF analyses are conducted for MIMO systems, revealing that in some cases, enabling only one antenna per user can yield the utmost extremal gain. As such, it can be assumed that in medium-scale networks, enabling only one antenna per user is near-optimal. Extremal GDoF studies for MIMO networks are inherently intricate and unforgiving, making a mathematical proof challenging, but this work provides a comprehensive insight into its constraints and limitations. Lastly, the mathematical model used for the extremal analysis of MIMO networks is validated by demonstrating that it closely matches a computational optimization approach, an extremely resource-intensive and computationally demanding method. Computational results show a 3dB difference in GDoF gain between these two approaches. In addition, the mathematical model used in this work is capable of uncovering new insights into the extremal nature of MIMO networks, while a computational optimization approach is often too cumbersome and resource-intensive for real-world implementation. As such, the mathematical approach offers a suitable alternative, requiring relatively lesser computational power. Nevertheless, both methods fail to provide an exact analysis, leaving some ambiguity about the precise GDoF values, despite achieving a satisfactory insight into its constraints and limitations. Ultimately, the mathematical model used in this work is a suitable tool for assessing the extremal nature of MIMO networks, achieving approximately 90% accuracy in GDoF values. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. By comparing the robot's performance on various ground types, it was demonstrated that the proposed control system efficiently adapted to discrepancies between predicted and actual ground reaction forces. Our results show that the local self-energy's imaginary component, which governs the decay rate of initially localized states, can serve as a probabilistic rule for detecting signs of a many-body localized phase. Moreover, we establish that, in the thermodynamic limit, this phase is characterized by a non-zero, disorder-independent local self-energy, whereas in a thermal phase, this value asymptotically approaches zero. This finding paves the way for a novel approach to detecting many-body localization via measurement of the local self-energy's real part. Our approach also facilitates the exact calculation of long-term survival probabilities of localized initial states, which diverge from the thermodynamic limit with growing disorder strength. Specifically, we find that the time-dependent survival probability exhibits an abrupt, nonlinear transition from from the thermodynamic limit to a plateau-driven exponential decay. Moreover, we establish that this plateau is essentially a pre-asymptotic phase transition phenomenon. Moreover, we found that the time taken to complete this nonlinear transition increases with growing disorder strength and eventually reaches a horizontal asymptote. Specifically, the time taken to complete this transition, which we term $t^*_\Delta$, grows in proportion to the square of the disorder strength normalized by the hopping energy. Importantly, $t^*_\Delta$ corresponds to the time taken for the localized wave packet's delocalization across the entire system and its subsequent re-localization due to interactions with all available states. The exploration of quantum machine learning has demonstrated the potential for
groundbreaking insights in both areas of research. Experimental findings indicate
that quantum computers could significantly outperform traditional machines in
specific machine learning tasks. However, our study reveals that these quantum
advantages can be replicated using hybrid learning methods, even on conventional
computing devices. We observed that these methods excel in learning the binary
linear-sparse model when employing BERT-like neural networks. Moreover, our study
involves analyzing various feature encoders in both traditional and hybrid learning
settings to understand their performance. We found that these encoders excel in
low-dimensional data but struggle in higher dimensional data. Instead, using
maximum likelihood encoders leads to optimal results. We provide theoretical justifications
for these findings through analysis of the population loss function. Our study
also investigates the impact of the target predicate's characteristics on classifier
performance. We discovered that predicates with distinct degree distributions lead to
better performance. We observe that our proposed feature encoders achieve superior
outcomes when learning these predicates. We conduct an in-depth empirical analysis
of these findings across multiple datasets and conclude that these methods excel
in NLP tasks, especially for datasets with distinct degree distributions. Our study
also demonstrates the potential for hybrid learning to achieve state-of-the-art
results in information retrieval tasks. We compare the performance of these methods
to existing baseline techniques. We observe that hybrid learning produces superior
results in terms of both accuracy and F1-score. Notably, the differences in
performance are more pronounced when evaluating the models using the Deepscore
metric. We provide additional insights by analyzing the F1-score scores and
corresponding confidence intervals to understand when hybrid learning is beneficial.
Overall, our study offers a comprehensive empirical analysis of hybrid learning's
potential applications in both machine learning and quantum machine learning contexts.

We examine Steklov eigenvalues in nearly spherical domains of three dimensions. 
Building on our earlier research, which demonstrated the eigenvalues to be analytic functions of domain perturbation parameters, we calculate the first two terms of the Taylor expansion. 
The result stems from a Mercaj-Caldirova representation formula for the Steklov eigenfunctions, which we resolve for three-dimensional domains. 
The proof involves a novel approach in perturbation theory and spectral decomposition. 
The outcome can be visualized as a surface on three-dimensional space representing how changes in a domain's shape affect its boundary oscillations at a given frequency. 
This research expands our previous work on dimension two and addresses an unresolved issue from (Buzano et al., 2020). 
Additionally, we investigate the spectral properties of the Steklov problem on manifolds with boundary, showing that the eigenvalues exhibit local-analytic dependence on parameters involving domain shape, boundary curvature, and spatial coordinates. 
The proof relies on the Mercaj-Caldirova representation and a reduction of dimensions in the spectral decomposition. 
The approach provides a detailed, invertible mapping from eigenfunctions to boundary distances and curvature, offering a novel geometric interpretation. 
The research also derives the Mercaj-Caldirova representation for two-dimensional manifolds, showing that it differs from known results for Laplace eigenvalues, as it involves a different combination of scalar curvatures rather than the Gaussian curvature alone. 
A numerical example is presented to demonstrate the dependence of Steklov eigenvalues on boundary geometry. 
The research has implications for almost spherical domains and dimension three, displaying a distinction from the known result for dimension two. 
The results can be extended to dimension one, displaying an analogy with known results for dimension two. 
The research can potentially be applied to studying dynamical systems on domains with oscillating boundaries. 
One possible application is to central bank policies, revealing a connection between eigenvalue dependence and financial indicators such as the inflation rate. 
The research provides a global surface showing the effect of changes in a domain's shape on its boundary oscillations at a given frequency. 
The result can be extended to dimension one, revealing a novel surface representing curvature dependence, which may have applications in investigating dynamical systems on domains with oscillating boundaries. 
The research can be extended to nearly spherical domains of dimension three and manifolds with boundary, offering a novel method for studying dynamical systems in physics, engineering, and other fields.

Accurate prediction and simulation of radio wave transmission are essential for optimizing systems using antenna, waveguide, and propagation components. Existing propagation models can be broadly classified into two types - empirical and deterministic models. Empirical models, such as those based on Rayleigh, Lognormal, and Loo & Clancy equations, are simplified approximations often used in initial system analysis phases. In contrast, deterministic models, like those based on physical optics and uniform theory of diffraction, provide more precise predictions but are typically reserved for detailed design consultations. This paper aims to bridge the systemic disparity between these models by proposing a novel combination of these methodologies, poised to yield more accurate results than conventional methodologies. The paper also compares the efficacy of varying model combinations, such as combining an empirical line-of-sight model with UTD, or pairing two empirical models together, depending on the unmasked area fraction. Notably, this proposed methodology holds promise even in terahertz frequencies, where other methods may fall short. In conclusion, the performance of this radio propagation model is evaluated and assessed in various scenarios. The study's findings suggest its viability for terahertz frequency applications. The proposed model is compatible with computational software such as MATLAB, and relevant codes are included in the paper's appendices for user reference. Furthermore, a graphical user interface, provided in appendix 5, allows users to input various system parameters and generate output based on this radio propagation model. The conclusion highlights the benefits of integrating simulation and analysis models to enhance accuracy and efficiency. The proposed model is particularly pertinent to six terahertz communication systems. The systems considered include phased arrays, dipole arrays, rectangular and square antennas, fixed wireless links, and systems utilizing the uniform circular array. A general tutorial outlining the path to achieving successful radio wave transmission was given in the introduction. The paper's success can be measured by identifying the optimal balance between array and space efficiencies, active and passive components, direct and indirect signals, and so on. A straightforward semantics is proposed for temporal planning. We define and formally establish the logic within the interactive theorem prover Isabelle/HOL, and then obtain a validation algorithm based on that semantics. By using a formal Isabelle/HOL proof, it is shown that the validation algorithm faithfully represents the developed semantics. We also demonstrate through practical experiments that the verification of our algorithm is useful. Specifically, we use the validation algorithm to test and verify a classic algorithm for temporal planning, originally proposed by Giunchiglia and Yang. Our Isabelle/HOL formalisation offers a novel and advanced approach to understanding the temporal planning domain. We expect that our Isabelle/HOL formalisation will facilitate the analysis of verification algorithms for temporal planning, allowing for the creation of reliable and high-performing algorithms. We anticipate that these algorithms could be used directly in applications without needing to be re-implemented. Our formalisation also provides a valuable tool for educating students in automated planning and temporal logic. We observe that, despite temporal planning being a relatively old area of research, there has been limited focus on formally verifying verification algorithms within the domain. Our work is the first to formally verify a verification algorithm for temporal planning, providing insights into the complexities of automated planning. Our paper is structured to provide a comprehensive overview of the temporal planning domain, beginning with an explanation of planning and temporal logic, followed by a formalisation of planning and temporal logic within Isabelle/HOL, and then the validation of a specific verification algorithm. We then present a general verification method that can be applied to any verification algorithm for temporal planning, with the algorithm for temporal planning of our choice being a simple example. We conclude by discussing future research opportunities inspired by our Isabelle/HOL formalisation. Our work builds primarily on the seminal work by Giunchiglia and Yang, as well as related research by Pelanek and others. Power system expansion planning models, used to integrate renewable resources, rely on complex optimization problems involving various economic and technical factors. These factors carry significant uncertainties, yet their impact on model accuracy is poorly understood. This study introduces a new approach to assess the sensitivity of power system models to specific parameters by measuring the increased costs resulting from inefficiently allocating generation capacities. Through case studies involving capital costs, varied weather conditions, and differing spatial and temporal resolutions, we demonstrate the method's value and reveal that models are most susceptible to temporal resolution. Additionally, we clarify the limited influence of spatial resolution and stress the importance of selecting appropriate weather data. Ultimately, our approach provides an effective tool for power system expansion planning, enabling planners to pinpoint critical factors affecting model reliability and make more informed decisions. This method may be particularly valuable for planners seeking to accurately allocate renewable generation capacities across different time periods. By incorporating our approach, planners can minimize costs corresponding to inefficiently allocating generation capacities, ranging from 0.3-1.7 EUR/MWh, dependent on the specific parameter in question. Furthermore, incorporating our approach within optimization problems can yield efficient solutions with costs 4-14% lower than optimal baseline solutions. With further research, incorporating our approach within optimization problems may lead to reduced efficiency costs and increased model reliability. This research may also be applied to other fields of engineering involving planning and design under uncertainty. Furthermore, the approach may be expanded to other factors such as technological advancements, diversity, and stochasticity, and further research is needed to explore this area of study. The corresponding code for this research is available upon request. The models used in this study were based on scenarios from [1] and the data was from MSK [2]. The approach may be applied to planning for the integration of electric vehicles, heating, cooling, etc. and further research is needed to explore this area of study. When conducting software maintenance, developers typically receive numerous, loosely written requests for change, described using everyday language and involving relevant technical terms. The task requires identifying key terms related to the request's technical context, allowing developers to locate relevant sections in the source code and update them accordingly. Unfortunately, developers often struggle with extracting these critical terms, as they lack the necessary domain expertise. This study explores the possibility of employing machine learning algorithms to analyze change requests, pinpointing terms that are highly related to the request's context. The research focuses on two areas: identifying general technical vocabulary associated with the request and determining which parts of the request are heavily influenced by technical terminology. The investigators collected a substantial dataset consisting of 1,398 change requests submitted to 12 Apache projects hosted on GitHub. The analysis revealed that the vast majority of change requests characterized as technical contain a prominent technical term. Additionally, the researchers found that around 61% of change requests heavily featured technical terminology. Finally, the study examined several popular request types submitted to GitHub and observed that while most are written in a non-technical manner, some, such as those requesting configuration settings, require a strong technical presence. The evidence suggests that while most change requests may not be predominantly technical, they still benefit from the extraction of crucial technical terms. The researchers aimed to achieve this by employing machine learning algorithms trained on projects using technical vocabulary, such as Apache Spark. The analysis revealed that the algorithms were able to accurately pinpoint relevant technical terms, achieving an average weighted average precision of 0.13. Furthermore, when evaluating multi-term extraction algorithms, the researchers noted that the addition of each relevant term increased precision by a factor of 10. The investigators believe that these findings indicate the potential of using machine learning algorithms to assist developers in extracting critical technical terms from the request and understanding their underlying project framework. The research, therefore, recommends incorporating these algorithms into developers' toolkits, especially when working with technology-rich domains. The evidence obtained also highlights several potential applications for future research, such as distinguishing between project types with varying levels of technical terminology and developing more targeted data collection strategies. Researchers have discovered a class of materials called "rheo-acoustic" gels that are uniquely affected by ultrasonic vibrations. This phenomenon was observed in traditional ergoline gels, a common type used in pharmaceutical applications, which showed a significant decrease in viscosity under specific high-frequency conditions. To explain this behavior, researchers turned to theoretical models of fluid-like materials that account for the interaction between particles and fluid dynamics. By applying these models, they were able to reproduce the observed changes in gel behavior in response to ultrasonic vibrations and made predictions about how the gels' microstructure changes under different conditions. Additionally, they were able to create a new phase diagram that takes into account the combined effects of thermal energy and ultrasonic frequency. This work has important implications for the development of new rheo-acoustic gels made from soft, fragile molecules. To confirm their findings, researchers tested the ergoline gel system and observed changes consistent with the predicted phenomena. Finally, they discussed potential applications of controlling gel behavior through ultrasonic vibrations, such as creating smart materials that can adjust their flow resistance in response to frequency changes. Furthermore, they proposed ideas for designing new rheo-acoustic materials that can provide new possibilities for controlling gel properties and engineering novel material behaviors. Overall, this work sheds light on the complex interactions within colloidal gels and provides a theoretical framework for understanding and predicting the effects of mechanical vibrations on viscoelastic materials. Moreover, it opens doors to the development of new materials with programmable viscosity and unprecedented mechanical properties. Finally, it inspires new ideas for material design and smart technology with a low energy footprint.

This research paper explores the validity of the Collatz conjecture for a certain set of odd sequences with an infinite number of elements, which is then generalized to encompass all positive odd integers. By applying the principle of mathematical induction, this extended set is used to prove the conjecture. A second verification of the conjecture is provided for sequences whose odd components are defined by a recurring formula with a multiplicative structure. This verification is based on a different approach, again employing mathematical induction. A final consideration examines the efficiency of the algorithm used to verify the conjecture for sequences of length N, as well as how the results from these verifications can be used to find potential counterexamples to the conjecture. A finding is presented: for any prime number p greater than 2, it is possible to identify a Collatz sequence of length less than or equal to p^2, in which the first number of the sequence is p. This result is further generalized to the category of odd numbers. Additionally, the research provides an explanation for why the existing verification routines used to test the conjecture are inefficient for large inputs. As earlier research by Betchov predicted decades ago, this scale is equivalent to the Kolmogorov length. Although the original analysis was based on order-of-magnitude reasoning, modern understanding of turbulence has improved since its publication in 1961. Reevaluating the problem using the concept of scaling and considering the nonrandom, statistical nature of geophysical turbulence, we arrive at a refined conclusion that supports Betchov's initial finding. Furthermore, we apply this approach to examine the statistical persistence time in turbulent flows and derive an estimate for the statistical length scale based on that time. This E-layer length scale concept might be particularly relevant for the upper oceanic layer, given that turbulent flows there often lack clear boundaries and tend to be in a state of quasi-geostrophic balance. We explore the implications of this idea and others, such as the presence of superpersistent edies at scales larger than the overall size of the domain. We also examine the possibility that turbulent flows could reclaim from thermal fluctuations, for instance, by reestablishing the hydrostatic balance in layers where stratification is not sufficient. Ultimately, we examine the geometric properties of eddies, such as the likelihood of encountering non-deterministic, statistical persistence in turbulent flows of different sizes within the geophysical turbulence domain. We use the E-layer length scale and the duration of statistical persistence in turbulent fluctuations to define the geometric properties of the fluctuations. This concept, developed over decades, is now viewed in a new light with the addition of this reevaluation. The statistical persistence time and the E-layer length scale concepts, derived analytically, are now seen through the eyes of the "present day theory" of turbulence. Previous studies on laser propagation through a heated fluid employed simplified thermal diffusivity and heat transfer models, neglecting their respective characteristic times. These studies found that the spatial distribution of temperature affects beam energy transfer and the threshold for damage contraction. However, they failed to reveal the influence of heat transfer on beam dynamics. In the present study, it is demonstrated that heat transfer changes laser propagation and dynamics by altering the interaction between the beam and its surroundings. To investigate this, a beam propagating through a heated fluid is simulated using advanced models for thermal diffusivity and heat transfer. Results indicate that heat transfer modifies beam dynamics, accelerating its damage contraction and reducing its energy transfer efficiency. Furthermore, it is found that incorporating heat transfer and fluid motion is necessary to accurately study laser interaction with materials. Consequently, it is suggested that including these factors in beam propagation simulations could be beneficial. In addition, it is observed that heat transfer can be utilized to control beam dynamics, for example by using the thermal gradient to expand the beam. It is hoped that this could lead to the development of an innovative technology utilizing these effects. Potential applications of such a technology could be the manipulation of laser pulses and plasma formation, as well as the improvement of laser beam coherence through controlled passage through a turbulent medium. It is also proposed that incorporating laser field and fluid motion in turbulent systems may lead to the discovery of synergies between laser fields, plasmas, and turbulent fluidic motion. To expand our understanding of laser interaction with matter, it is suggested that incorporating these factors in beam propagation simulations could reveal novel applications and effects. In addition, it is observed that turbulent fluidic motion induces turbulent laser field behavior, leading to the stochastic decay of the laser field. It is also found that incorporating these factors in beam propagation may lead to the discovery of more effective methods for manipulating laser pulses and improving coherence by leveraging the interactions between the beam, the fluid, and an external influence. Consequently, it is suggested that these factors should be explicitly incorporated into advanced laser propagation simulations in order to discover novel applications and effects. In the final instance, it is hoped that these findings may contribute to the discovery of new applications for directed energy technology. Discussions among developers encompass various interactions, encompassing in-person conversations and online comments, which are beneficial to label as relevant to software design for documentation and improvement purposes. This is made possible through a process known as design mining, which applies machine learning to categorize discussions as pertaining to design. This paper introduces an automated method for design mining, employing discussion threads from Stack Overflow to train various models. When put through testing, this method successfully classified non-design and design posts with 92% and 88% accuracy respectively. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that focusing on a post's single text sample yields comparable results to examining the full discussion thread. This outcome suggests that design mining can be efficiently and cost-effectively implemented for various discussion platforms. Additionally, the study provides insight into several advantages and limitations of the method, potentialening its usability for guiding developers working in collaborative environments. Ultimately, the method shows promise in facilitating cost-effective automated design mining, which can be readily accessed through an accompanying tool. This analysis proposes a method for identifying vector-like quark partner production through additional gluons without using explicit mass terms. The methodology aims to find distinctive signs in final observables that indicate the presence of these vector-like quark partner partners, like the TL quark, which would result in asymmetric broad mass distributions in their respective two-body decay products, as opposed to the expected symmetric patterns observed in pair productions involving Higgs or Z bosons. To this end, we simulate the production of TL quark pairs along with one or two gluons and examine their broadening effects in energy distributions of their energetic outputs, which could serve as key indicators of these vector-like quark partner partners in theoretical models beyond the Standard Model, especially useful in the context of remaining uncertainties and ambiguities in the Higgs and Z boson production patterns. The study specifically focuses on the energy patterns of the energetic b jets produced during the decay of TL quarks into b quarks and light gluons. The effectiveness of this approach has been verified through extensive Monte Carlo simulations using two distinct parton distribution functions, namely CTEQ6 (MUF = 1/T MUF = 1 TeV) and NNPDF3 (MUF = 1/T MUF = 1 TeV), showing that it remains relatively insensitive to the choices of these parton distribution functions. Furthermore, to ensure accuracy, we compared the results with those obtained through an automated automated systematic matching approach, finding the two methods to be in agreement with each other. The proposed method displays remarkable sensitivity to the broadening effects, even at the level of individual events, enabling researchers to identify the vector-like quark partner partners even when they are produced in relatively low numbers, thanks to the distinct signs in their energy patterns. On the other hand, it was found that the study's findings were influenced by certain assumptions regarding the duration of the vector-like quark partner lifetime, highlighting a need for deeper theoretical understanding of the underlying processes. The method can now be used to analyze experimental data from colliders like the LHC to provide more precise measurements of energy patterns, which in turn can serve to tighten the existing experimental limits on the vector-like quark partner partners. A recent breakthrough in translating English to SPARQL using neural machine translation (NMT) models holds great promise for automating SPARQL query generation, but these models have a major limitation: they can't connect related queries by their semantic meaning. Our proposed Semantic Query Graph (SQLooNet) enables the link between NMT models and semantic query networks, allowing the transfer of features to improve performance. Our experiments using the dataset of translated SPARQL queries showed that adding semantic features significantly boosts the results of various baseline models, surpassing the state-of-the-art performance in open-domain query generation. Furthermore, we've developed a novel application that lets users create and customize semantic query templates with drag-and-drop widgets, demonstrating the potential of these linked models to generate meaningful queries. Our project currently faces a data imbalance issue, and we're exploring approaches to rectify this to enhance the models' overall performance. Ultimately, we envision the development of sophisticated models like SQLooNet to be instrumental in widespread adoption of SPARQL-based data access and automated query generation in the future. This work introduces a novel method for systematically assessing the prestige 
of individual researchers and institutions based on their publication history. 
A comprehensive dataset of over 142,000 authors and 14,000 institutions from 
55 countries has been established, along with an estimated 1.8 million author 
prestige scores and a database of over 65,000 institutional prestige 
scores. These scores are derived from a broad range of 4,500 venues, 
cross-referenced with millions of papers from the Scopus database (2021). 
Moreover, an innovative index is proposed for evaluating venue prestige 
based on factors such as impact factor, journal age, and publishing volume. 
Building upon this framework, this approach can serve as a foundation for 
developing a standardized and country-neutral research performance evaluation 
system. Current applications of this method are presented in the fields of 
intelligent systems, artificial intelligence, and automated performance assessment. 
The associated code and data can be accessed at: https://github.com/jprieto/flares. 
This research also faces challenges, which are outlined in the paper, intending 
to stimulate further investigation on assessing research quality using big data. 
In the future, this approach can potentially be expanded to incorporate 
additional complex evaluation criteria, encompassing new fields and types of 
scholarly produce, such as social media and software development.

This study builds upon three significant lines of research related to dissimilarity-based clustering and integrates them into a unified framework that provides a principle-driven approach to clustering. Specifically, it draws from Jardine and Sibson's concept of overlapping clusters, Carlsson and M\'{e}moli's functorial approach to partition-based clustering, and the injective envelope theory of Isbell and Dress. Carlsson and M\'{e}moli's idea of treating clustering methods as functors that map metric spaces to clusters, subject to functoriality, has desirable implications. The study's initial outcomes extend the existing functorial clustering theory to incorporate overlapping clusters, resolving issues related to chaining, commonly associated with single-linkage clustering. By analyzing the order structure influenced by morphisms, the research demonstrates that these generalized overlapping clustering functors can be expressed as projections from weight spaces to clustering domains. Moreover, the theoretical framework allows the proof that no functorial projections exist to cut metrics or tree metrics. Although the injective envelope aspect of clustering domains receives less focus, the study sets out foundational results to elucidate its potential contribution to clustering. Ultimately, the research offers a fresh understanding of clustering domains as the collection of clustering domains of original spaces in a hierarchical sequence of domains enriched with their respective metrics. As domain theory provides a comprehensive understanding of domain structure, future work will delve into examining the hierarchical sequence of clustering domains, facilitated by the presence of morphisms. In addition, the study's new functoriality concept for clustering domains is explored, alongside the introduction of redundant functors that map metric spaces to clustering domains while conserving functoriality. Clustering domains rich in structure have the further benefit of allowing the application of computational tools from domain theory to these structures, enhancing computational efficiency in clustering algorithms. Moreover, the study's initial outcomes reveal the presence of additional equitable partition structures beyond those discovered by Dress, arising from the presence of the order structure influenced by morphisms. Lastly, the research's territorial nature is examined, and the resulting findings establish connections between the related concepts of tree reconstruction and phylogenetic tree reconstruction. Specifically, the study's initial outcomes demonstrate that tree reconstruction is the process of finding the projection from the weight space to the clustering domain associated with the original space, while phylogenetic tree reconstruction involves the projection to the tree domain. As clustering domains generalize previous structures like trees and domains, the research provides a fresh understanding of tree reconstruction and phylogenetic tree reconstruction as the projection from the clustering domain to the tree domain. Tensor completion techniques seek to recover incomplete data in observed tensors by leveraging their low-rank properties, particularly useful in visual data recovery applications. However, when dealing with sequential data such as streams or videos, missing tensor entries can also be contingent on past incomplete entries, compromising existing low-rank-based completion methods' performance. To address this challenge, a novel model called LRNT is proposed, incorporating temporal constraints into a regularization framework to capture temporal dependencies in tensor completion. By incorporating a weighted least squares (WLS) layer to account for correlations between sequential dimensions, LRNT is distinct from traditional low-rank methods. Its combined completion process is defined as a bi-convex optimization problem, which can be efficiently solved using an alternating optimization algorithm. Experimental evaluations conducted on diverse sequential tensor completion datasets demonstrate LRNT's superiority to multiple state-of-the-art approaches. The proposed method is further showcased through a practical video completion example, uncovering new low-rank properties arising from temporal constraints, and yielding robust, superior results. A thorough analysis of its computational efficiency and performance is also provided. The code for this method can be accessed at a publicly accessible repository. By addressing the unexplored area of tensor completion for sequential data, LRNT sets the ground for tackling various real-world visual data recovery tasks. As such, it has wide-ranging potential applications in self-driving vehicles, surveillance, and other fields. In a recent study, researchers employed direct numerical simulations within a triply periodic box, artificially suppressing geostrophic vortices to investigate the properties of turbulent flows. These simulations revealed an inertial wave turbulence that conforms to a specific spectrum first described analytically by Galtier in 2003. Interestingly, it was found that the same underlying mechanisms could either give rise to wave turbulence or stable geostrophic vortices depending solely on the initial conditions, thus further establishing the concept of bi-stability in rotating turbulent flows. We investigate a basic model called Iterative Graph Normalization (IGN) for analyzing weighted graphs, and an adaptation of the model that involves applying a pre-defined function to graph weights before normalization. Research demonstrates that indicator vectors representing maximal independent sets of a graph are the only long-term outcomes of IGN and related versions. We explore the assumptions required for these long-term outcomes to be unique. Firstly, we prove uniqueness under a mild assumption, and establish criteria for this assumption to hold. Secondly, we show uniqueness when the graph's weights fulfill a certain condition, and deduce a direct consequence of this result, which is the convergence of the graph's degrees to a uniform value under specific conditions. Along the way, we establish a significant characterization of the graphs for which the maximal independent sets have unique indicator vectors. Furthermore, we investigate the applications of these long-term outcomes to problems not easily solved by iterative graph pruning, and illustrate the improvements achieved by incorporating a pre-defined function in comparison to standard normalization models. Finally, we discuss connections between the problem of double the maximal independent set and the FP-minimax LP relaxation of the problem of maximal independent set. We show that the long-term outcomes of IGN can be utilized as an algorithmic tool to estimate double the maximal independent set under specific conditions. We observe that these estimations are precise for graphs where the maximal independent set is formed by two equal halves, and propose a criterion for the efficacy of LP relaxation in approximating the problem of double the maximal independent set. We also establish relationships between the prices of LP solutions for maximizing double the maximal independent set and the norms of the indicator vectors representing maximal independent sets. Ultimately, we explore the applications of IGN to the problem of maximizing a cover of a graph, and argue that pricing problems arising from the LP relaxation of this problem are a suitable candidate for the graph's normalization parameter. We show that the prices' lower bound quantifies the complexity of graph normalization, and propose the LP relaxation of IGN as an algorithm to approximate the prices' upper bound. This research studies the impact of a magnetic field on electrically modulated single-layer graphene, aiming to understand the effect of modulation on the thermodynamic properties. The investigation reveals how the periodic electric potential transforms Landau levels into oscillating bands, leading to specific oscillation patterns in response to magnetic field strength. The analysis shows that in electrically modulated graphene, the modulation's influence on thermodynamic properties is more pronounced and exhibits less damping as temperature increases, contrasting conventional 2D electron gas behavior. The distinct thermodynamic behavior in electrically modulated graphene is attributed to changes in work function resulting from applied gate voltage. The research also evaluates and discusses the material-specific work function of single-layer graphene and predicts unique thermodynamic oscillation patterns that can be used to analyze and characterize graphene-based devices and materials. The study further explores how the electric modulation strengthens the magnetic field's influence on the thermoelectric effect, allowing the use of this effect to detect minute changes in magnetic field strength. The research ultimately provides a foundation for understanding the thermoelectric properties of single-layer graphene. Recent findings have identified low-frequency radio emission from systems consisting of small cool stars called M dwarfs, which shares similar patterns to magnetospheric phenomena observed in our Solar System. The radio emission could be driven by a star-planet interaction or an unstable balance in a rotating disk and the surrounding stellar magnetic field. A thorough investigation of GJ 1148, an M dwarf star, was conducted using radio telescopes to test theories about the origin of the radio emission. By analyzing observations from multiple frequencies and timescales, the scientists aimed to determine whether the radio emission is a recurring event linked to the activity in the disk or if it is an isolated occurrence. The research revealed periodic fluctuations in the radio emission every 11.85 days, which coincides with a previous detection of radio emission and an increase in X-ray fluorescence. The scientists propose there are two possible explanations: the radio emission could be a result of an unstable balance in the disk and the changing star-planet distance over an 11.85-day period, which would also cause fluctuations in X-ray emission. Alternatively, the radio emission could be a result of an unstable balance in the disk and an evolving unstable spiral structure, which would also cause the observed fluctuations. The discovery supports a multi-frequency, long-timescale study of activity in brown dwarf and star systems, which could uncover more phenomena similar to magnetospheric turbulence observed in our Solar System. The researchers suggest further observation of GJ 1148 to confirm the origin of the radio emission. The results were based on a collaboration involving the Murchison Widefield Array, the Mullinary radio telescope in South Africa and the Hartraight radio telescope in New Hampshire, which collected data between 2016 and 2019. Our study presents computational findings based on a novel trimer-cluster quantum Monte Carlo simulation approach, which effectively tackles the thermodynamic properties of frustrated two-dimensional quantum antiferromagnets composed of loosely connected three-spin clusters. Specifically, we investigated the thermodynamic behavior of a strongly breathing distorted kagome lattice model and the previously proposed geometric frustration model on a hyperhedral lattice. Observing two-peak specific heat patterns in both models, we validate earlier claims on the formation of spin liquids in both cases, revealing their thermodynamic properties are strikingly similar. Additionally, we demonstrate how the proposed method can be utilized to calculate the lattice energies required to create three-spin clusters within a lattice, thereby aiding the development of theoretical models for related magnetic compounds. Lastly, we outline a potential research direction for generating custom lattice models through cluster-based annealing, encompassing both single- and mixed-spin systems. This approach may serve as a valuable tool to investigate the lattice energies required to create three-spin clusters within lattice structures, thereby shedding light on the lattice models governing the thermodynamic properties of one-third weakly coupled spin chains. This outcome could serve as a valuable starting point for future investigations, particularly regarding the synthesis of corresponding magnetic compounds. Pre-trained language models, exemplified by GPT-3, have exhibited an unexpected capacity for zero-shot learning. Specifically, to accomplish this, users can instruct these models to classify sentiment with untrained examples by prompting them with reviews paired with labels such as "Does the user like this movie?" The model can then be trained to select "yes" or "no" from the subsequent word choices. However, optimizing the zero-shot objective is hindered by the pre-existing training objectives. To improve upon this limitation, researchers have proposed "meta-tuning" - directly fine-tuning pre-trained language models on aggregated datasets to optimize zero-shot performance. In this study, researchers focused on classification tasks and compiled a 43-dataset meta-collection with 441 labeled descriptions. When evaluated on new tasks, models optimized via meta-tuning demonstrated superior performance relative to QA models of similar size and outperformed the previously top-performing system for zero-shot learning tasks. Moreover, doubling the model parameter size resulted in enhanced accuracy with AUC-ROC scores improving by 6.3%. Consequently, evaluating language models in the context of zero-shot learning will now involve considering these models at maximum capacity and with extensive training data. Researchers have also released a dataset meta-collection and the corresponding model family on the AI Forum.
