Voice assistant applications, such as Alexa and Google Assistant, significantly benefit from advancements in semantic parsing, a core challenge in NLP. The latest state-of-the-art semantic parsers employ sequence-to-sequence models, built upon vast language datasets pre-trained on a massive scale of text. Building on these advancements, researchers have explored redefining semantic parsing, resulting in naturally-phrased output sequences within limited language constructs. This breakthrough yields remarkable outcomes, particularly in few-shot learning tasks. To take this development further, we introduce a groundbreaking dataset specifically designed for teaching voice assistants the critical skill of telling stories. The dataset comprises contextual instructions that ask the model to describe a series of imaginary events, a format similar to existing semantic parsing tasks. At the same time, we maintain the output in a free-form, natural language phrase structure. The introduction of StoryParser, a dataset designed for this purpose, allows for comprehensive evaluation of our approach and enables the compilation of a range of benchmark datasets. Conversely, we define a subset of this data, termed Multilingual Explanatory Prompt Translation (MEPT), as a more challenging benchmark due to its nearly flawless translation between languages and the resulting uniformity in label representations. Notably, we discover that directly training on state-of-the-art multilingual models produces exceptional results on both challenges. Ultimately, we share our data, execution code, and relevant machine learning tools publicly in the hope that our contribution stimulates a new wave of multilingual NLP innovation. The data can be accessed at https://github.com/astastef/StoryParser.

Using ALMA's H30α (231.90 GHz) observations of the metal-poor dwarf galaxy NGC 5253, we estimate the galaxy's star formation rate (SFR) and assess the galaxy's physical processes. Based on these observations, the galaxy's photoionizing background radiation's impact on Hα emission is quantified, while H30α measurements allow for the removal of extinction effects and thereby provide an unbiased SFR assessment. Furthermore, the galaxy's SFR is compared to historical estimates made using ultraviolet and Hα luminosity. It was discovered that high-mass, long-lived stellar populations within the galaxy contribute substantially to the galaxy's total luminosity, while the galaxy itself is experiencing a relatively low-level of current star formation. In addition, the galaxy's compact and intense H30α mid-infrared correlation was verified, and the galaxy's supernova rate was determined, all of which provide further insight into the galaxy's star formation processes. Finally, the galaxy's SFR history was reconstructed, and the galaxy's position within the star-forming galaxy density plot was determined. It was observed that NGC 5253's SFR follows that of other late-type galaxies, while its position within the star-forming galaxy density plot is consistent with other metal-poor, isolated galaxies. In contrast, the galaxy's position in the star formation rate vs. stellar mass plot indicates that NGC 5253's star formation has been relatively consistent over 1 Gyr, while its position in the specific star formation rate vs. metallicity plot indicates that NGC 5253's star formation has been relatively slow over the last 100 Myr. It is observed that NGC 5253's star formation has been increasing in recent times. Finally, the galaxy's position in the galaxy interaction parameter plot indicates that NGC 5253 has been in contact with an accompanying globular cluster over the last 1 Gyr, while no current interactions have been detected. In conclusion, by using high-frequency ALMA observations, the galaxy's star formation has been characterized, its history can be understood, and the impact of surrounding environment can be considered. To alleviate the high communication overhead associated with asynchronous online federated learning (AOFLO), we introduced a compressed model sharing approach based on the mutual information framework. This proposed approach optimizes AOFLO through three core strategies: 1) a degree map-based participant selection method to enhance diversity; 2) a gradient quantization technique to reduce dependence on server; 3) a mutual information based compression scheme to replace the traditional token-based compression method and enable accurate data transmission while maintaining security. We have developed a novel method of constructing high dimensional expanders by utilizing covering spaces of simplicial complexes. Building upon expander graphs, high dimensional expanders play a vital role in theoretical computer science but unfortunately, there are only a few constructions available that offer good algebraic expansion. Our research provides a universal framework, incorporating both existing and new methods of construction, thereby significantly enhancing the current theoretical limits on high dimensional expanders. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework by producing new and improved constructions that surpass previous results. Notably, for asymptotically good simplicial complexes, we have achieved approximately 1 in o(log k) probability bounds, representing a significant improvement. Furthermore, for graphs, we have achieved approximately 1 in o(log n) probability bounds, marking a breakthrough with empirical evidences suggesting that these bounds are nearly tight. The tools developed within this framework include a novel proof of the Baker-Liu theorem, a extension of the Liu's theorem, and the introduction of a new invariant, high dimensional expansion, of covering spaces. Moreover, we have successfully applied coverings of expanders to combine the Hall's Marriage Theorem and the Turan's Subgraph Theorem, yielding new insights in counting the number of k-cliques within asymptotically good simplicial complexes. The application of graph embedding for predicting links in complex networks has shown remarkable success, but most real-world networks are sparse, which are currently underserved by this field. We propose the Sparse Structural Network Embedding (SSNE) model, which creates a representation of network nodes suitable for predicting links in these types of sparse networks. Initially, our model converts the network's adjacency matrix into a Sum of Normalized H-order Adjacency Matrix (SNHAM) before passing it through a neural network for a dimensionally-reduced representation. Notably, our neural network-based approach can be considered an alternate method of performing singular value decomposition. Finally, our approach utilizes the generated feature matrix to compute node similarities, which are pivotal in predicting links. Through thorough experimentation using both synthetic and actual sparse networks, our research demonstrates that SSNE outperforms existing models such as structural similarity indexes and other forms of graph embedding methods in predicting links. Two SSNE variations are offered: SSNE-D, which employs a dual-weighted approach in creating SNHAM, and SSNE-M, which multiplies SNHAM with the network's degree matrix. Our empirical findings show that SSNE-M surpasses SSNE-D in predicting links. Additionally, our empirical evaluation reveals that SSNE is more efficient than its close competitor, local graph structural similarity indexes, at a much lower computational expense. Consequently, SSNE has the potential to be applied and further refined in real-world sparse network prediction tasks. As our primary application, we utilize SSNE to predict links in a commercial network, which yields remarkable results. SSNE is offered in an open-source format for further exploration and development by researchers working with sparse networks. We evaluate the precision of a recently proposed nonlinear interference model for a wide range of dual-polarization 4D formats, exhibiting an average disparity with split-step Fourier simulations of no more than 0.1 dB. A novel reinforcement learning method based on the actor-critic type has been developed to tackle portfolio hedging challenges for a variety of financial securities and derivatives using historical data only. Key aspects of this approach involve leveraging various derivative types such as forwards, futures, and options to effectively hedge securities, and incorporating both absolute and relative wealth as key indicators in the actor-critic algorithm. This solution does not require the formulation of a model or a risk management problem being convex. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses alternative reinforcement learning and traditional investment methods in terms of performance and wealth. Furthermore, the algorithm's ability to learn from historical data is also verified by observing that its policy remains unchanged even when market data is not available in real-time. Lastly, the solution's efficacy is also validated by observing no significant increase in computation time as the number of assets increases. Therefore, the proposed reinforcement learning framework is highly versatile and suitable for portfolio hedging problems involving a large number of securities and derivatives. Additionally, the code has been made accessible for immediate use by the community. In particular, the code can be found at the following GitHub repository: https://github.com/bahntoz/RLPortfolioHedging. Key technical details and limitations of the approach have also been outlined in a corresponding supplement. Firstly, the reinforcement learning agent struggles with the initial stages of the training process. This struggle is attributed to the complete absence of any prior knowledge about the environment in which the agent learns to hedge its portfolio. Following an extended period of time, the reinforcement learning agent is able to devise an optimal strategy that effectively matches the one designed by the model-based method. Moreover, the reinforcement learning agent also demonstrated superior adaptability when faced with variations in market conditions. Secondly, the reinforcement learning agent was observed to be prone to over-optimistic policy evaluation due to the presence of negative wealth states. Measures such as importance sampling or a variational version of the model-based method were used to mitigate this over-optimism. Lastly, the reinforcement learning agent was also able to effectively hedge portfolios consisting of a large number of securities, and was even capable of handling a variety of derivative types such as futures and options. In particular, the reinforcement learning agent was observed to leverage the hedging capabilities of these derivative types in order to match the performance of the model-based method. Key technical details and limitations of the approach can be found in a corresponding supplement. Key contributors to this work include Bahman-Teh-Chai, Huanrui Ren, and Jiayi Wu as co-first authors

In today's commercial recommender systems, sequential models play a crucial role. These models predict the items users are most likely to engage with by analyzing their previous platform interactions. Despite their importance, many of these models struggle to grasp the underlying motivations driving users' actions online, making intent modeling vital for user understanding and optimal long-term decision making. We've developed a novel approach to probabilistically model user intent using variational autoencoders and inferred latent variables from user behavior signals. Our approach then adjusts the recommendation policy accordingly, based on inferred user intent. We've validated the efficacy of our approach through offline and live testing on a massive industrial platform. The results show that our method enhances user engagement while reducing friction caused by irrelevant content. Given its success in a industrial setting, we believe this approach serves as a model for other commercial recommendation systems. We've opened source the essential code to facilitate replication in similar environments. Our work highlights the potential for long-term growth through contextualized user understanding, rather than just short-term gains from predictive modeling. The reducible double confluent Heun equation stands out due to its unique unfolding into a Fuchsian equation through a general symmetric process. The Fuchsian equation resulting from the unfolding of this particular DCHE has five distinct singular points: three located near the origin and two elsewhere. To further analyze this equation, we establish its solution near the origin in terms of power series, examining the constraints that the connection formula places on the coefficients of the equation when the three singular points are combined. Additionally, we derive a theorem indicating the necessary conditions for the existence of solutions that grow at most linearly as they approach infinity in a large region beyond the origin. The newly obtained conditions mirror those previously established for the Heun and related equations, confirming our expectation that the Fuchsian equation resulting from the unfolding of the reducible DCHE can be classified as a Heun equation in its extended sense. The analysis is completed by providing explicit solutions for the Fuchsian equation resulting from the unfolding of the reducible DCHE in a large region beyond the origin. The work in this paper forms part of a broader effort to expand the classification of the Fuchsian equations, previously established for the Heun and related equations, in order to facilitate the classification of the DCHE, in particular the irreducible cases. The corresponding classification of the reducible DCHE is scheduled for a follow-up communication. As an aside, we examine the connection between the Fuchsian equation resulting from the unfolding of the reducible DCHE and a linearization of the Painlevii equation P$_\mathrm{IV}$. In this research, we examine the vibrational spectrum of a constrained ring, taking note of its distinct properties that defy symmetry expectations inherent to topological models. A unique characteristic arises due to 2nd-order exceptional points, where an otherwise trivial band structure becomes topologically complex at higher energy levels. Absence of traditional symmetry in the model allows the emergence of fractional boundary states in the system. Moreover, another key aspect of the bulk-boundary correspondence is uncovered, where an extra exceptional point in the bulk material is safeguarded by its connection to boundary states. Lastly, we have discovered a secret to maintaining symmetry within a model while still achieving an exceptional point; this secret lies in the introduction of a special type of boundary condition that is not physical in nature. This novel model is inspired by a nanotube with constraints and can be categorized under synthetic physics. The principles discussed here can potentially be applied to various systems that are currently considered topologically trivial. Since data measurement, rather than physical induction, is primarily relied upon in this research, it can offer a more flexible approach. Furthermore, another key aspect of the bulk-boundary correspondence was discovered, revealing an unexpected similarity between constrained dynamics and time-reversal inversions. By treating the communication links as dynamic processes, our approach adaples to varying network conditions. To address the complexity of distributed MPC, we simplified the innermost optimization problem using the dual decomposition method and applied the gradient projection approach, leveraging the dual variables to share information about the system. Simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed control strategy under diverse network scenarios. Moreover, to broaden the application scope, we modified the approach for non-convex optimization problems using the quasi-Newton method. Detailed comparisons with conventional centralized MPC approaches were conducted to highlight the benefits of the decentralized model proposed. Overall, our approach shows promise in large-scale system optimization. However, its application to real-world systems poses challenges due to the computational complexity of the optimization problem. Consequently, a trade-off must be struck between efficiency and accuracy. Moreover, our approach presented a theoretical guarantee of stability and optimality, which requires thorough verification and validation to ensure the reliability of the model. We've developed a COVID-19 diagnosis framework that uses CT scan image analysis with a double feature extraction technique via BERT. The initial step utilizes a 3D-CNN to extract spatial information from the CT images and then employs BERT for temporal aggregation of these features. A classification model is trained on randomly sampled CT volumes, and subsequent steps utilize the network to extract embedding features from the full scan volume. Averaging these features by segments, a second BERT model aggregates the multiple segments into a unified feature for final classification. By combining both classification stages, we achieve a high validation accuracy of 0.9164 in macro F1 score. Notably, this method outperforms existing models, as seen in multiple trials. Additionally, the features extracted via this approach enable robustness against noise - an advantage not seen in existing methods. We argue this perspective is overly narrow and neglects potential interactions on longer timescales.  We expand the scope of eco-evolutionary dynamics to incorporate slower evolutionary changes which span centuries to millennia.  For instance, feedback loops between changing landscapes and evolving plant life.  We also recognize that rates of ecological and evolutionary changes are influenced by modulators such as genetic adaptation, the direct modification of an organism's traits through natural selection, allorecognition, and other processes including cultural mechanisms.  We aim to bridge the divide between traditional theories of ecology and Darwinian evolution by accounting for adaptations that occur on various timescales.  We draw inspiration from Darwin's own thoughts on the potential for significant changes in landscapes and ecosystems in his time, reflecting the comprehensive nature of eco-evolutionary changes.  Ultimately, considering eco-evolutionary processes that operate on different timescales offers a unified view that incorporates the interactions between ecology, evolution, and speciation.  We recognize that global-scale changes are particularly noteworthy, particularly those resulting in major geological, ecological, and climatic shifts including Snowball Earth events, the emergence of oxygen-producing plants, and the onset of prolonged ice ages.  Furthermore, these major events are not isolated but rather part of an overarching pattern of episodic, stochastic, and unstable transformations spanning all domains of life on Earth.  We define these events of profound transformation as Great Spikes (GS), indicating sudden, significant increases in diversity and biodiversity.  We speculate that GS may serve as critical catalysts driving adaptation through novel ecological pathways such as host-parasite, pollinator-plant, and predator-prey relationships, thereby accelerating the evolution of co-adapted traits in combined and complementary directions.  Conversely, GS may be triggered by the failure of established ecological pathways providing resources necessary for life, leading to the emergence of adapted ecological strategies. Our research focuses on the underlying structure of Automated Market Makers (AMMs), 
a prevalent form of blockchain-based, decentralized exchanges. 
We reveal that the order processing mechanism results in token value diminishment for market liquidity suppliers under circumstances of heightened token price volatility. 
AMMs are adopted predominantly when their supported token combinations have significant use or price movements are strongly interconnected. 
However, the steeper pricing curve actually diminishes the potential for arbitrage during instances of volatility, 
although this effect is softened due to the frequent monitoring of the system, which often results in the intervention of transactions prior to a substantial price disparity developing. 
We expand the boundaries of AMM analysis and investigate AMM dominance by evaluating a comprehensive dataset spanning 12 months. 
We identify the predominant role of AMMs in the Ethereum Decentralized Exchange environment through an evaluation of daily trading volumes, 
providing specific figures for the most popular pairs - USDT and DAI. 
Furthermore, we identify prominent token pairs supported by AMMs as either speculative investments or as fundamental components of a stable cryptocurrency framework. 
Lastly, we identify the predominant role of a specific entity, Sushi, in the analysis, with other prominent DEs examined for their respective dominant tokens. 
Ultimately, we explore the implications of AMM success, pointing out potential drawbacks and investigating the reasons behind their prevalence within the DE setting. 
The research also includes supplementary content regarding the respective roles of AMMs in the Ethereum ecosystem by utilizing co-graph theory. 
Additionally, the paper presents an analysis of a prominent AMM failure resulting from an insufficient liquidity overflow mechanism.

A new analytical framework, referred to as Sensitivity Analysis, evaluates how conclusions based on incomplete data can be affected by uncertainties in underlying assumptions. We develop a straightforward approach for conducting large-sample Sensitivity Analysis when key assumptions regarding missing outcome data are violated. We enhance this method by allowing parameters to fluctuate based on additional external factors. Comprehensive simulations confirm that our technique effectively explores all possible scenarios. We also re-examine the 2010-2011 Salmonella outbreak in England, adjusting the model to accommodate varying contamination levels in different atypical environmental samples, and demonstrate that sensitivity analysis can reveal critical inconsistencies in laboratory testing results. These findings highlight the need for more detailed data and enhanced collaboration between analysts and study designers, particularly in cases involving uncertain model parameters. While our analytical framework is broadly applicable, it is specifically tailored to address the complexities surrounding the Salmonella outbreak, providing insights into causes and contributors of environmental contamination. Furthermore, we develop an open-source software program, sensitivityanalysis.R, which facilitates the implementation of this analytical framework in real-world scenarios. Overall, our technique is versatile and can be easily adapted to various model types and datasets, making it an indispensable tool for individuals working with incomplete data and seeking to evaluate the impact of key assumptions on conclusions drawn from such data. Consequently, this analytical approach is recommended for researchers and scientists to help inform their judgment and decisions. As an example of the utility of this analytical approach, we re-examine the 2000 CDC data, adjusting the model to accommodate changing probabilities of contamination for both environmental and source samples, and demonstrate that sensitivity analysis can uncover critical discrepancies in the original classification of sample statuses. These findings highlight the need for collaborative data sharing and communication between analysts and study designers, particularly in cases involving uncertain model parameters. While our analytical framework is broadly applicable, it is specifically tailored to address the complexities at the time of the Salmonella outbreak, providing insights into causes and contributors of environmental contamination. These findings emphasize that sensitivity analysis can provide valuable guidance on the quality and reliability of data, and can be effectively used as an alternative to Bayesian analysis, while pointing out limitations and inconsistencies in data quality and reliability. This study concludes a comprehensive categorization of $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-symmetries within the larger framework of the quantum toric model. By employing the shift-invariance of the model, the analysis focuses on a reduced set of generators derived from the level-matrices of the Hamiltonians. Although the study is rooted in the quantum case, it is demonstrated that the same method can be applied in the classical model. Previous research by the authors and Bogoliubov is shown to be a specific realization of this broader categorization. An additional investigation into the commutativity of the generators is performed. Several explicit calculations are carried out to illustrate the anomalies that arise when testing the commutativity of the generators, including the Cartan generator, which does not necessarily confer a $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-symmetry. On the other hand, generators associated with the identity are inherently commutative. This research yields a comprehensive understanding of the structure of $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-symmetries within the quantum toric model. Furthermore, the study explores how the shift-invariance of the model can be utilized to construct generalized symmetries, providing a framework for the solution of quantum dynamics on graph-based systems. Examples of how these results can be applied for the manipulation of quantum computers and the simulation of quantum systems on graphs are also provided. Additionally, the study outlines a strategy for the efficient implementation of the generated waves from the highest weight states within the model. In the course of this research, the model was found to possess an extensive array of generating functions that can be utilized to obtain any state within the model starting from a specified initial state, thus achieving the same level of comprehensiveness as the Schrödinger-Heisenberg picture. An additional investigation into the quantum toric model was performed to establish its equivalence to the topological quantum model proposed by Noy. Several explicit calculations were carried out to illustrate the transfer of the topological model to the quantum toric model via the Bogoliubov transformation. Additionally, the study provided explicit examples of symmetries within the topological quantum model that were found to be distinct from those existing within the quantum toric model. Such a comparison is considered novel within the field. As an extension to this research, the study proposed a new topological quantum model defined by the Laplacian matrix within the framework of the quantum toric model. This paper presents an effective approach for locating fixed three-dimensional objects within large-scale metropolitan landscapes using an aggregation strategy for substantial amounts of two-dimensional image data, yielding significantly enhanced precision and robustness. A decentralized decision-making framework forms the foundation of this method, facilitating its capacity to handle large-scale data sets in a distributed and parallel manner. Evaluating this method with extensive image collections covering diverse settings in Atlanta and Chicago, and integrating data from OpenStreetMap and Google Maps, our approach achieves localization within a meter's radius of the truth with minimal total prediction error. Notably, our results show that the accuracy of 3D object location is significantly improved when the objects' orientations are correctly determined as well. Due to its adaptability and relative simplicity, this method can easily process a wide array of metrical data, thereby offering considerable potential for applications including automated driving, metropolitan surveillance, and others. Our code and data are freely accessible at https://github.com/mikkoheinis/3Dlocation. Additionally, our findings have been visualized at https://3dlocation.github.io.

This article investigates the semigroups of composition operators on BMOA-type spaces, specifically on BMOA_p and its analogue VMOA_p. BMOA_p is a part of the family of F(p,q,s) spaces introduced by R. Zhao and serves as the M\"{o}bius invariant subspaces of the Dirichlet spaces D^p_{p-1}. In this context, we aim to comprehend the complete picture of semigroups of composition operators that are norm-attaining. A key finding establishes that a semigroup of operators is norm-attaining if and only if it is idempotent. This study also explores the characteristics of the kernels associated with these operators, discovering novel functions called the generalized Gaussian kernel and the singular generalized Gaussian kernel. A significant relationship was discovered between these new kernels and the well-known singular Gaussian kernel. A hierarchical structure was established in terms of domination, while further analysis delved into the compactness of the semigroup. In a notable conclusion, it was found that a compact semigroup of operators on BMOA_p is necessarily idempotent. This research is a continuation of the author's previous findings on normal, or rather compact, semigroups of operators on BMOA_p. A related paper published in 2020 investigated the normal semigroups of operators on BMOA_p. A subsequent paper published in 2021 explored the compact semigroups of operators on VMOA. This research seeks to expand the known characteristics of operators on Moebius invariant spaces. A public defense of the paper was conducted on December 18, 2021. Understanding universal properties of a critical quantum spin chain model requires identifying key components of conformal field theory, notably the coefficients of operator product expansion, which describe operator fusion. Research suggests that these coefficients can be computed using wavefunction overlaps of low-energy states in the spin chain. We have demonstrated that central charge, conformal dimensions, and operator product expansion coefficients are encoded in wavefunction overlaps, accompanied by universal corrections that rely on representation theory of the SU(2) symmetric group. Additionally, we have derived a universal ratio of wavefunction overlaps, independent of the choice of spin chain representation. This result stems from the symmetries within the SU(2) symmetric group. We have also computed the universal corrections to operator product expansion coefficients, which rely on the dimensions of irreducible SU(2) group representations. Our findings are pivotal in verifying scale-invariance and bootstrapping programs for critical quantum spin chain models. Moreover, we have obtained universal corrections to conformal dimensions by utilizing dimension-normalized wavefunction overlaps. Our analysis also encompasses the universal characteristics of two-point operator correlations, which are essential in scale-invariance and bootstrapping programs for critical quantum spin chain models. Automated part-of-speech (POS) annotation is a crucial task for linguistics and natural language processing, typically addressed as a supervised activity, but for historical languages with limited training data, this approach is impractical. To overcome this challenge, we have developed a method for POS annotation without requiring any prior knowledge of the target language. Although unsupervised POS tagging is a complex problem, we have made significant progress in this area. To validate our method, we have conducted a comprehensive study using 12 languages, including some historical languages, and observed that, in the case of languages with a significant amount of available data, our method yields results close to optimal, whereas, for languages with limited training data, it performs similarly to the best existing solution. Furthermore, we have applied this approach to the POS tagging task involving 11 ancient languages, and achieved satisfactory results in this area. The developed method will be made available to the scientific community under an open-source license. The project also includes a dedicated website (pos tagging historical languages) for the purpose of raising public awareness regarding the language decay phenomenon and gathering hand-annotated data. The developed method has been thoroughly evaluated against state-of-the-art solutions in the unsupervised POS tagging domain. The resulting system, involving 11 ancient languages, has achieved an impressive level of accuracy, on par with the best existing solution, although, in the case of languages with limited training data, we have encountered certain difficulties, such as incorrect handling of capital letters in the case of Greek and Latin, and word segmentation issues in the case of ancient languages, but, overall, we have made substantial progress in this area. The developed method has been successfully applied to the POS tagging task involving 11 ancient languages, and the obtained results have been presented in the form of a confusion matrix for each language. The developed method has further enabled the creation of a dedicated database (dareuropeana) where all the POS-tagged data for the 11 ancient languages are stored in the form of JSON files. The developed method has also facilitated the creation of a dedicated website (europeana) where the POS-tagged data for the 11 ancient languages are freely accessible. The developed method has further enabled the creation of a dedicated video (pos tagging historical languages) where the general public can learn more about the language decay phenomenon and the related project. The developed method has also facilitated the participation of the general public in the project by launching a dedicated crowdfunding campaign (pos tagging historical languages) where the project has been successfully crowd-funded.

This research focuses on developing a method to calculate a utility function from a non-differentiable but locally Lipschitz candidate of a demand function. Using this method, we derive two new criteria that can help determine if a demand function candidate is genuine. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our procedure enables the recovery of an initial underlying preference function.

In essence, we generalize earlier work by Flawsky, Grigoryan, and Kudryakov, which dealt with differentiable demand functions, to handle non-differentiable demand functions. Notably, our results apply to the case where a demand function has infinite values in certain instances. To accomplish this, we draw on concepts related to Lipschitz continuity and multifunctions with upper semicontinuity.

Additionally, we illustrate our findings by applying them to an existing example, showing that a demand function derived from a non-linear, additively-separable (quasi-)concave utility function can exhibit local Lipschitz continuity. This example highlights the significance of our research, as it indicates that such a demand function candidate meets the criteria for being genuine. Finally, we provide an accompanying code that enables users to input a utility function, thereby obtaining the corresponding demand function. This demand function is then used to a partial order on the space of probability distributions, which in turn allows us to generate a simulated preference function. The purpose of providing this code is to facilitate an end-to-end verification of our main theorem's tenets. In essence, we want to ensure that our utility function output aligns with the original utility function input. While this process does not constitute a formally optimised process, it does represent an important advancement. Ultimately, we plan to utilise these preference functions, along with other techniques such as deep learning, to develop a novel method for generating synthetic data that maintains the original characteristics of a given utility function. This is particularly important in cases where a utility function has infinite values in certain instances. As smart cities expand, they generate an increased need for automated conversion of human-specified demands into precise, machine-readable specifications. Nevertheless, human requirements often extend beyond available, standardized data sources. We introduce CitySpec, an innovative AI-powered system for converting non-standard urban requirements into machine-readable specifications utilizing diverse datasets. The proposed approach involves two stages: the joint learning and representation of similar, related requirements allows for effective generalized specification creation; while secondary, low-dimensional learning enables the preservation of original requirement nuances. Our approach excels in extracting relevant city-related information from lengthy, open-text human requirements, yielding a 78.72% exact match rate, a 3.84% improvement over current methods. The systematic evaluation of various techniques further confirms the robustness and superiority of our solution. CitySpec is now accessible online, with the code and data residing at a dedicated GitHub repository. We envision CitySpec as a valuable tool for supporting smart city planning and facilitating efficient, automated requirement matching in city administrations. Furthermore, our approach could be easily adapted for other similar applications, such as processing requirements from social media platforms. The ongoing research also aims to expand the proposed approach to encompass additional, complex urban scenarios for promise detection and requirement specification. The resulting technology has the potential to emerge as a foundational component of intelligent assistant systems for future smart cities. These services include urban waste sorting and minimum energy consumption. Our research presents an innovative technique for accelerating variational quantum algorithms based on hidden inverse methods to counter coherent errors. By incorporating inverse gate implementations, noise levels are diminished and the robustness of the training process is enhanced. This approach proves effective across multiple quantum noise scenarios. Our findings also reveal that for small coefficient values, implementing the inverse gate is superior to the explicit inverse method in reducing error rates. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this error mitigation strategy can efficiently mitigate the adverse effects of readout noise in measurements. This hidden inverse method presents a cost-effective solution for mitigating noise within variational quantum algorithms, thereby accelerating quantum optimization simulations. Additionally, we reveal the intriguing phenomenon of noise-dependent overparameterization, which may have significant implications for the robustness of quantum algorithms. These findings are rooted in numerical simulations using the Qiskit platform and our developed open-source code. Moreover, these results have been successfully applied to a quantum circuit designed for optimizing quantum circuits, specifically, the quantum approximate optimization algorithm. We outline both an algebraic and a geometric approach to this method, with the latter presented here for the first time. Moreover, we discovered an additional momentum map, resulting in a dual pair of momentum maps, which under specific conditions can represent the process of Lie-Poisson systems collectivization. Consequently, applying symplectic Runge-Kutta methods to solve the system in its canonical form leads to integrators preserving coadjoint orbits and Casimirs precisely. We provide two case studies: the Kida vortex, which corresponds to Lie-Poisson systems on $\mathfrak{so}(2,1)^{*}$, and the heavy top, which corresponds to Lie-Poisson systems on $(\mathfrak{se}(3) \ltimes \mathbb{R}^{3})^{*}$. These examples illustrate the algorithm's efficiency in identifying the target Hamiltonian and its Casimir constraints in both cases. Furthermore, we successfully generalized the method for systems not strictly constrained by integrals but rather by Casimirs. In doing so, we encountered some inconsistencies when applying integration methods, which led to Casimirs also being disregarded. Once again, the two mentioned examples serve as proof of the algorithm's efficacy, with additional examples confirming its broader applicability. Ultimately, we discovered that integrating the target system with the additional momentum map and its Casimirs leads to integrators preserving coadjoint orbits and Casimirs. Consequently, we may consider the method an efficient means of simulating highly nonlinear systems by approximating conservative systems resulting from a similar method of Lie-Poisson systems collectivization. Moreover, we may consider the method an efficient alternative to integrating the target system with higher precision in order to integrate Lie-Poisson equations in a higher order. Currently, the most trusted diagnostic tool for COVID-19 is RT-PCR, which
takes several days and sometimes produces incorrect results. Computed Tomography
scans can provide valuable assistance with COVID-19 diagnosis, although they expose
patients to a significant amount of radiation, which can be detrimental to those
requiring multiple scans. To address this issue, we studied low-dose and ultra-low
dose scan protocols, which minimize radiation levels while maintaining image
quality suitable for diagnostic purposes. Since the availability of labeled COVID-19
data is extremely limited, we developed a simulation tool to generate synthetic data.
This enables the training of a pre-trained 3D U-Net model to classify COVID-19 positive
or negative based on either simulated or actual data. To validate our approach,
we successfully tested it on two distinct datasets. One consisted of synthetic images
derived from dual-energy scanner images of chest organs, providing 1100 instances
of COVID-19 positive and negative data. The other was real DECT data comprising
COVID-19 positive or negative patient scans, totaling 450 instances. The model's
evaluation metrics revealed an impressive accuracy of 0.891, followed by
recalls of 0.860 and 0.840, respectively. By applying our approach to lung infection
detection, we achieved an accuracy of 0.891, recall of 0.860, F1 score of 0.872,
supporting the effectiveness of low and ultra-low dose CT scans for diagnostic
purposes. Moreover, the model trained on actual data produced outcomes rivaling
those derived from simulated data. Ultimately, this method may aid clinicians in
making informed decisions regarding COVID-19 diagnosis using dual-energy CT scans. 
Although the tool is currently restricted to use with DCCT scans, its adaptation to
other modalities could be feasible in the future. This work has the potential to
substantially reduce radiation exposure for both patients and healthcare workers. 
To foster future research, the code and data used in this study have been made
available for the public at https://github.com/ericsilveiro/COVID19-DECT.

As numerous satellite constellations in the low-Earth orbit region are scheduled to launch, effectively arranging the space occupied by each satellite in their operational trajectories is essential to prevent collisions and reduce critical encounters. Here, the term "space occupancy" is defined as the area an individual satellite covers during its orbit, taking into account external perturbations and a specified timeframe. Following the discovery of a strong connection between space occupancy in the zonal problem and the principles of frozen orbits and proper eccentricity, frozen orbit satellites can maintain a constant space occupancy size over time. Furthermore, frozen orbits can be designed such that the space occupied by a satellite remains within a predetermined bounded area, depending on the orbit and observation time constraints, thus allowing for an efficient occupancy schedule to be established among the satellites in a constellation. This schedule enables each satellite to maintain a minimum distance from its neighbors, both in terms of orbital configuration and observability, by assigning unique frozen orbits to each satellite. Here, the concept of space occupancy is introduced, its key features analyzed, and its applicability demonstrated through computational simulations of specific orbital configurations. Lastly, a method for merging multiple orbit designs into a unified system is provided as an additional tool for managing and optimizing low-Earth orbit satellite constellations. Interestingly, the findings in this study also connect to historical frozen orbit developments, providing a meaningful contribution to the engineering of orbit systems. Specifically, the concept of space occupancy can be utilized during the critical phase of deployment to minimize collisions and damages when multiple satellites are launched simultaneously, whereas the merging method offers strategies for adjusting and refining satellite orbits over time. Research in the past few years has seen significant advancements in creating machine learning models that can withstand malicious data manipulations. A robust learning model is defined as one that relies solely on examples and gives special importance to instances that are hard to alter without being detected. However, existing methods for robust learning rely heavily on certain sensitive data features that require special protection, which poses a problem for their application in domains where such features are not present. A robust learning model's effectiveness also heavily depends on how well it can identify and utilize challenging instances, which in turn depends on the model's ability to recognize test examples that contain unaltered versions of these instances. A robust learning model's ability to do this is facilitated by the presence of local membership queries, which allow the model to verify the unaltered state of test examples with high confidence. Therefore, for the application of robust learning models in domains that contain sensitive data features, the development of robust learning models that are based solely on data examples and local membership queries and do not rely on any protected data features, is of significant importance. Our paper presents an algorithm that is robust to any data manipulations and only relies on local membership queries and data examples. It is an in-demand learning model that can be applied to any domain. Our algorithm's only interaction with the data is through local membership queries and it can identify the hardest instances based on the number of queries it takes to correctly classify these instances. It is an natural idea that points to the connection between robustness and the model's ability to identify hardest instances, which in turn corresponds to data examples that contain sensitive features. Our algorithm's effectiveness also demonstrates the connection between robustness and the model's ability to identify hardest instances, which is an concept that can be utilized in training methods that aim to enhance the model's ability to identify these instances. It is an intrinsic property of the data and can be captured through equivalence relations, which do not rely on any specific data features. Our algorithm's design also shows the connection between equivalence relations and the model's ability to identify hardest instances, which is an concept that can be utilized in training methods that aim to enhance the model's robustness. Our experiments conducted on standard datasets from the field of natural language processing and computer vision, yielded results that demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach. It establishes a framework for the application of robust learning models in any domain. Our work's connections and contrasts with previous research on robust optimization methods that aim to minimize the model's reliance on sensitive data features, is an area that warrants further exploration

By showing that multiplying these matrices with vectors can be achieved in $O(N)$ operations and demonstrating their closure under specific operations like scaling and Hadamard product, and being a subset of linear operators that can be inverted in $O(N)$ time, we reached this conclusion. Furthermore, this class of matrices enables the development of fast and reliable algorithms for solving kernel matrices and an emerging research area on solving linear systems in $O(N)$ time, thus opening new avenues for the advancement of these matrices. We also derive a novel proof for the fact that an iterative algorithm for solving kernel matrices converges, provided the target vector can be reached as a limit, which appears as a corollary in a different context. Young stars emitting intense X-ray and UV radiation can drastically alter planetary atmospheres, influencing both mass loss and chemistry. Observing AU Mic, an 22-million-year-old star hosting a closely orbiting planet, provides us with a unique chance to study these effects in evolution. AU Mic's X-ray spectrum appears abnormal and has shown considerable variations in recent studies, contradicting flaring activity patterns seen in other young stars. A space mission called NASA's TErPS aimed to capture high-resolution X-ray spectra of low-mass stars, including young stars like AU Mic, to gain significant insights into their behavior. However, the TErPS mission was terminated prematurely after a launch failure. We analyzed the limited number of TErPS observations collected before the mission failure, focusing on how the spectral characteristics of AU Mic compare to other stars, especially those in the hibernation phase. We also calculated the high-energy flux level emitted by AU Mic and the effect of this radiation on its planet's atmospheric mass transport. Our analysis shows that the X-ray spectrum of AU Mic has a distinct magnetic topology and emits less energy in the high end of the X-ray spectrum than other stars. We observed significant variations in the high-energy X-ray flux emitted by AU Mic on short timescales. If we assume that the X-ray flux level detected by TErPS represents the level emitted by AU Mic in the hibernation phase, then the planet trapped in a 5.2-day period experiences a mass transport of 2.8e8 kg per day due to evaporation, which is primarily caused by the effect of high-energy radiation emitted by AU Mic. Furthermore, the total mass transported each day is roughly 2.8 times the mass emitted each day from the planet's lower atmosphere. We observed the level of high-energy radiation emitted by AU Mic to decrease by a factor of 2 during the period when we observed a lower X-ray flux level, which indicates that the star has a long-lived high-energy emission episode. We compared the X-ray spectrum of the magnetic region on the surface of AU Mic to equivalent spectra obtained from other stars. We observed the equivalent width of the magnetic lines from the two other stars to be approximately three times higher than for AU Mic, which indicates that AU Mic has a relatively low surface magnetic activity compared to other stars. We calculated the star's rotation period to be roughly twice that of its orbital period based on magnetic region modeling. We proposed a theoretical model to explain the significant variations in the high-energy flux emitted by AU Mic.

The dynamics of a liquid film on a fiber heavily depend on the boundary conditions at the liquid-solid interface. This understanding has led to a theoretical model that uses the axisymmetric Stokes equations to examine the effect of liquid-solid slip on a film coated on a fiber undergoing the Rayleigh-Plateau instability. The new theoretical model reveals that slip leads to a higher rate of instability and longer wavelengths than predicted by previous models. Consequently, larger drops tend to form on fibers with high slip coefficients. The accuracy of the theoretical model is supported by numerical simulations and experimental results from a study conducted by Haefner, et al., published in 2015 in Nature Communications. This theoretical model provides a clear understanding of the effect of liquid-solid slip but neglects factors such as gravity, electrostatic forces, and interactions with surfaces, which are essential components of a comprehensive theoretical model. Additionally, an analytical model derived in the late 19th century by Plateau is revealed to be applicable even at small scales due to the decoupling of surface tension and gravity at small lengths. While surface tension dominates at very small lengths, gravity begins to play a role at longer lengths, demonstrating that the dynamics of capillary instability on a liquid film are largely governed by a systematic power-law decay of the growth rate with increasing surface wavenumber, regardless of slip or gravitational conditions. Lastly, an experimental investigation was conducted to examine the effect of liquid-solid slip on a liquid droplet growing inside a gas-filled capsule. The study employed electrostatically-generated bubbles in a superhydrophobic environment and found that liquid-solid slip has no effect on the bubble growth process, contradicting the theoretical model and power-law model derived from numerical simulations. This discrepancy highlights that liquid-solid slip has an insignificant impact on bubble growth but emphasizes the importance of considering surface boundary conditions in microscopic processes. Conversely, a subsequent study on droplet growth in nanoscale films using a superhydrobic surface also revealed an insignificantly large effect of liquid-solid slip on film instability. Ultimately, both studies suggest that there is minimal potential for significant slip effects in nanotechnology, microelectronics, biomedical engineering, and other related fields, although localized slip may still have an essential impact on surface reactions and film formation. Ultimately, an understanding of the dynamics of liquid films requires comprehensive theoretical and simulation models that can accurately describe film dynamics at both large and nanoscale lengths. Specifically, this involves exploring collections of handwritten manuscripts and early printed materials. Acquiring suitable datasets for research on historical documents employing various machine learning methodologies necessitates identifying appropriate datasets. Unfortunately, selecting datasets from the diverse pool of data, varying in script, format, degradation level, label representation, evaluation processes, and benchmarks poses a significant challenge. To address this issue, this research conducts a meta-analysis on available datasets. A thorough, systematic selection process yielded 219 features, descriptions, testimonials, and experimental results from 85 datasets. These datasets comprise 38 collections of handwritten work, 29 early printed materials, and 18 collections of documents in mixed categories. Moreover, datasets from pre-printed forms and synthetic documents are also present. A comprehensive review of these datasets is provided, including their characteristics, difficulties in image analysis tasks such as layout, structure, and content understanding, and visual degradation. Moreover, an explicit compilation of evaluation methods and benchmarks from these datasets is conducted, incorporating classification, detection, location, and verification tasks. This research paper is intended to serve as a definitive reference for choosing datasets for applied research in document image analysis. Finally, an analysis of research publications is performed using automatic data mining techniques to highlight prominent datasets in the field. These datasets are also made publicly accessible through a dedicated web application for researchers and practitioners to choose appropriate datasets for their work in document image analysis. The application of deep neural networks in medical image classification has shown great promise due to their advanced learning capabilities. Despite this, current methods rely heavily on a vast quantity of high-quality labels, which are often marred by imperfections and noise. Various studies have sought to rectify this by employing transfer learning and semi-supervised methods, but these methods are limited by the reliance on clean labels. To overcome this challenge, we propose a innovative method referred to as label cleaning, which integrates with the training process of medical image classification for the purpose of eliminating noisy labels. This is made possible through the use of a unique network design comprising clean and noisy label branches, which simultaneously trains the model and identifies and eliminates incorrect labels. To facilitate this process, two regularization techniques are employed, resulting in the estimation of clean labels, which are then utilized to refine the model. This method possesses certain advantages, primarily because it does not require the acquisition of additional data or the creation of a separate clean dataset. Furthermore, the model trained using this method possesses improved resistance to misclassification, which is a valuable attribute for medical imaging applications. The efficacy of this method is evaluated on multiple datasets comprising a diverse range of environmental conditions and noise, which demonstrates its state-of-the-art performance, with the model trained using this method achieving up to a 6% greater accuracy than those trained via traditional methods. Comprehensive comparison experiments reveal that this method boasts a 15% greater efficiency than existing methods and achieves 12% reduction in the number of incorrect labels. Thorough ablation studies further confirm the robustness of this method across a wide range of noisy label densities and dataset quality. Furthermore, the method possesses certain benefits over existing label rectification methods, primarily because it does not require the utilization of model-specific modifications or the modification of loss functions. All the experimental results are made publicly available via an online data platform, which facilitates the reproduction of these results. The proposed method holds considerable potential for the application of deep neural networks to medical image classification even in the presence of noisy labels. It is anticipated that this method will find utilization in the training of the model utilizing only a small portion of diverse labels from medical imaging datasets prone to noise. The proposed method can be accessed at: https://github.com/fzhangmlgi/LearnToCleanLabels. The Sgr A East supernova remnant, located near the center of the Milky Way, poses a mystery with age estimates ranging from extremely young, around 1-2 thousand years, to a significantly older, 10 thousand year estimate. Our objective is to create a straightforward simulation of a supernova event replicating the shape, dimensions, and placement of Sgr A East, which was achieved using a simplified hydrodynamic model that simulated the interaction of a supernova explosion with surrounding interstellar gas. The resulting remnant matched observations of the Sgr A East cloud's cloudiness and the change in X-ray brightness from its center to edge, indicating an age of approximately 10 thousand years. This matches earlier predictions that classified Sgr A East as an intermediate-age cloud. Our simulation also showed that the angular expansion of Sgr A East, based on its assumed age and speed, wouldn't have been visible from Earth in its early stages. Consequently, the likelihood of remaining radio emission from an older supernova remnant like Sgr A East, positioned near the center of the galaxy, isn't as high as some scientists have suggested. Yet, our simulation still supports the idea that the supermassive black hole at the galaxy's center influenced the cloud's rotation and movement over its lifetime. Furthermore, the simulated evolution of Sgr A East, extending over 10 thousand years, failed to explain variations in clouds within the Sgr A East region that appeared in 1.3 mm wavelength observations conducted by the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA). Nonetheless, the simplicity of our hydrodynamic model allowed it to forecast that Sgr A East would continue expanding at millimeter wavelengths, aligning with predictions from other studies. Despite our simulation not fully matching observations at millimeter wavelengths, the simplicity of our model provided solid grounds for additional research into more intricate interactions between the supermassive black hole, accretion flow, and millimeter brightness of Sgr A East. Specifically, the likelihood of the supermassive accretion rate occurring above 10 times its typical rate could contribute significantly to understanding this process, as it might also realign the center of the Sgr A East cloud, turning its current symmetrical shape into an irregular figure. Ultimately, the simplicity of our hydrodynamic model enabled the simulation of a relatively low and steady suppression of Sgr A East's millimeter brightness, as well as estimates of its age, but a more intricate model would be needed to fully match observations at millimeter wavelengths.

The study examines various oversampling methods to classify multi-class topics, particularly focusing on the performance of SMOTE, a popular method for generating new samples based on minority class examples, and its two variants along with random oversampling in text classification tasks. The research assesses the efficiency of SMOTE, its Borderline and ADASYN modifications, and random oversampling in conjunction with machine learning algorithms such as k-nearest neighbor, support vector machine, and different types of neural networks, using text representations. The outcomes suggest that using oversampling methods enhances the accuracy of classification and indicates that the performance of KNN is significantly improved when combined with the ADASYN algorithm, whereas the use of random oversampling achieves comparable results to SMOTE and Borderline SVM. The study also explores the impact of oversampling methods on the accuracy of different SVM kernels, revealing that the use of these methods is insensitive to specific kernel types. The findings ultimately demonstrate that the use of oversampling methods offers a reliable approach for handling class imbalance data. The proposed algorithms are published on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/amanmandal22/Class-Imbalance-Text-Classification. The study's data is released under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License. 

Keywords: oversampling, class imbalance, text classification, KNN, SVM, neural networks. 

Abstract:
The application of machine learning in text classification has been an active area of research for classifying multi-class topics. The study examines the performance of oversampling algorithms, including SMOTE and its variants, in improving text classification accuracy when classes have uneven balances. The research assesses the efficiency of SMOTE, a popular oversampling algorithm, and its modifications, in conjunction with machine learning algorithms, using text representations. The outcomes reveal that the use of oversampling algorithms increases classification accuracy and suggests that the performance of KNN is significantly improved when combined with the ADASYN algorithm, in contrast to the performance of SVM algorithms, which shows no sensitivity to the oversampling algorithms used, yet exhibits a positive interaction with kernel types. The study ultimately demonstrates that the use of oversampling algorithms, along with the chosen algorithms, can be a reliable approach for handling data with uneven class balances. The research also highlights the potential of using undersampling algorithms, though less effective than oversampling methods, as an alternative to improve classification accuracy when data are densely sampled in the minority class. The findings are released under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License at https://github.com/amanmandal22

This study analyzes data from an online monitoring system of U.S. local news to explore connections between COVID coverage, regional case and death rates, and characteristics of news outlets. Using a distinct dataset of over 850,000 articles from over 300 outlets between April 2020 and February 2021, our results show that local news outlets initially covered COVID at a rate influenced by national death rates but ultimately became less correlated as other issues like the U.S. elections dominated headlines. Additionally, our findings reveal that local news COVID coverage varied based on the area's politics, with Democratic regions devoting more space to COVID stories and Republican regions giving more prominence to other storylines like the U.S. elections. Moreover, our data indicates that local news outlets largely serve and reflect their respective communities, with correlations between COVID coverage and local case rates strengthening over time. These findings have implications for understanding and limiting the spread of infectious diseases via media messaging and raise important ethical considerations about local news role in informing residents about vital health issues. Finally, our data shows that smaller and rural news outlets devote a higher proportion of space to COVID stories, whereas larger and urban news outlets gradually decrease their COVID coverage, aligning with their readers' growing awareness of the pandemic. This study contributes to existing research by enabling comparison of local news influences on distinct diseases and outbreaks, such as SARS, Ebola, and influenza. Ultimately, our results indicate that local news play a pivotal role in informing residents about vital health issues. Therefore, governments, health organizations, and public relations experts should develop strategies to leverage local news to disseminate crucial information about infectious diseases and vaccines, potentially enhancing vaccination rates. Conversely, local news also provide an opportunity for advertisers and pharmaceutical companies to reach key audiences and boost sales by promoting relevant products. Moreover, our data shows that smaller and rural news outlets surpass their larger urban counterparts in local COVID coverage awareness, suggesting a potential resource gap in disseminating essential health information. Lastly, our results indicate that local news play a distinct information-positivity role in influencing regional case and death rates, contrasting with the national level's limited effectiveness in curbing the pandemic. Ultimately, our results highlight the significance of local news role in fighting infectious diseases via messaging strategies. While local news do not entirely determine COVID outcome, they do have a considerable impact on individual perceptions which, in turn, affect the pandemic's progression. Local news can effectively collaborate with health organizations to raise awareness, especially in rural areas, by targeting demographics with relevant content. Local companies and advertisers are advised to promote relevant products

Smoothed particle hydrodynamics possesses innate conservation capabilities, which are confirmed in this paper for energy, angular momentum, and kinetic energy. The study reinforces the knowledge that mass and linear momentum conservation are maintained in SPH, which was previously documented. Evidence of moment conservation is also provided, followed by validation through explicit simulations of energy, angular momentum, and kinetic energy preservation in both incompressible and compressible fluids at rest. Additional tests involving the inclusion of artificial viscosity have been conducted to demonstrate the preservation of energy and angular momentum in scenarios where viscosity effects are present. Artifical inflation of densities is another beneficial characteristic of SPH, which has been shown to effectively conserve mass. However, preserving kinetic energy may not be achievable when artificial viscosity is in operation. To address this shortcoming, a new, conservative numerical scheme has been developed, which achieves precise integration of artificial viscosity and thus enables the preservation of kinetic energy. The scheme has been validated through simulations of hydrostatic levels and is compatible with existing SPH implementations. The code is freely available for download at https://github.com/nsadati/SPH-KES. The implementation of the new scheme does not incur additional computational costs, which makes it an attractive solution to researchers. The authors are currently working on extending the scheme to account for thermodynamic processes and anisotropic viscosity for its eventual application in planet-scale modeling. The development of the new scheme has the potential to widely distribute reliable SPH coding practices. We develop a novel, yet efficient, method for augmenting existing data to enhance the learning capacity of reinforcement and imitation learning from expert examples. The policy-generated synthetic data is designed to supplement real-world data, and its effectiveness is pinpointed to a specific set of states. We derive a strict boundary for the minimum number of synthetic examples required to guarantee reliable imitation, and also establish that policy-generated data falls short of providing adequate training data for certain environments. Rather than relying on optimal policies, we propose a template-based approach to creating synthetic data and provide optimal bounds for its efficacy. Ultimately, we present empirical evidence validating our theoretical findings and highlighting the potential benefits of incorporating synthetic data into various learning frameworks. Furthermore, our research identifies several key factors influencing data efficiency and provides insight into optimizing imitation through the choice of synthetic data states. In a preliminary move, we also begin exploring the broader implications of data efficiency in the context of reinforcement learning. The paper's code can be accessed at https://github.com/benoitz/synthal. Atomic magnetometers that utilize self-oscillating technology and driven by resonant modulation demonstrate enhanced sensitivity and dynamic range capabilities.
This technology, in conjunction with phase-coherent feedback, enables the detection of modulating signals at very low levels.
The atomic magnetometer's ability to detect these signals is explained by a mathematical model that describes its behavior according to the principles of nonlinear physics.
It is found that the mathematical model used to describe the over-damped nonlinear system of the atomic magnetometer matches a statistical mathematical model developed as part of a different theory.
These findings lead to the creation of a mathematical model that connects the system's physical behavior to its statistical properties.
Using this mathematical model, it becomes possible to predict a wide range of characteristics of the atomic magnetometer, including its capacity for dynamic range and sensitivity.
It is hoped that this approach, in which the predictions are made in a reverse order of events, will contribute to the development of advanced modulation detection systems. Furthermore, it is proposed that this new theoretical approach could facilitate the development of new methods for analyzing statistical data. As an example of its feasibility, this approach is applied to predict a new characteristic of the atomic magnetometer.
Additionally, it is found through this approach that there exists a optimal set of parameters that maximizes both the dynamic range and the sensitivity of the atomic magnetometer.
These optimal parameters are identified and their values are determined.
Using these findings, it becomes possible to enhance the performance of the atomic magnetometer by adjusting the driving parameters.
Finally, it is found that the predictions made using this approach can be used to forecast features of the atomic magnetometer in scenarios where the system is no longer in a state of quasi-equilibrium. As an example of its applicability, this approach is applied to the study of a local Co wire which is under the influence of a magnetic field. The main contributions of this study include developing an Efficient Polynomial-Time Approximation Scheme for finding the minimum surface topography (genus and non-orientable genus) for complex network graphs that are densely connected. Densely connected networks are defined by an edge to vertex ratio greater than 1.33 times the square root of the number of vertices. Although a simple, constant factor approximation algorithm exists for this type of graph, removing which vertices makes the remaining subgraph connected only with loopy networks. To overcome this challenge, we adapted a well-established method for closely approximating surface topography in the form of a loopy network, thus refining our understanding of network structure in densely connected networks. Furthermore, we devised an efficient method for converting any vertex arrangement in the loopy network into an efficient edge arrangement in an equivalent embedded graph, resulting in a precise surface topography determination for densely connected networks. Notably, since densely connected networks can be distinguished by their topological characteristics from those that belong to a specific family (which include well-known examples like complete graphs), our algorithm may be used to determine whether a network belongs to this family with high accuracy. In addition to developing algorithms for determining surface topography in densely connected networks, we also refined our understanding of which vertices contribute to denseness, contributing to the solution of a long-standing problem in the field. The development of efficient algorithms relies heavily on the integration of combinatorial and geometric approaches, as well as the novel introduction of a new algorithmic technique called array splitting. Array splitting is a flexible method that can be applied across various mathematical domains and is thus likely to have far-reaching applications in fields beyond graph theory. The efficient determination of surface topography in densely connected networks has significant practical implications, including the automatic identification of malicious nodes in network security systems, which relies on the determination of minimum surface topography in densely connected networks to identify loopy-oven attacks, a newly discovered threat in which an attacker can manipulate the topography of a network by adding loopy-oven nodes without being detected by current security systems. Our algorithm may also be used to determine network efficiency by converting any vertex arrangement in the loopy network into an efficient edge arrangement in an equivalent embedded graph, which could help to detect inefficient networks. A stochastic Newton algorithm for distributed convex optimization tasks is proposed, which utilizes individual machine capabilities to calculate gradient and Hessian-vector products for the same shared objective between communication intervals, significantly minimizing required communication rounds. Convergence analysis and performance preservation are demonstrated for quasi-self-concordant objectives like logistic regression, backed by empirical results. As an improvement, this approach surpasses smaller communication intervals, often resulting in decreased total computation through smarter resource allocation, unlike existing methods. Moreover, its efficiency in handling large-scale vision tasks such as image-based gender prediction is effectively showcased. Our algorithm, named DistNW, has exhibited superior performance in various tasks, outdoing a well-established method when the tasks demand the least possible upper bound of gradient evaluations per step. This new approach, however, relies on accurate measurement of local objectives, which may not always accurately reflect the size of shared objectives, especially in asymmetric learning where individual contributions to the shared objective are not always equal, an issue observed in certain image-based tasks such as large-scale gender prediction. Consequently, a modified version of the algorithm, named DistNW-B, was proposed, which uses a weighted average instead of simple last-updated rule for combining local results at communication intervals, effectively mitigating the negative impact of inaccurate measurement of local objectives on the final outcome. This modified version, however, requires advanced mathematical derivation of weighted average convergence, which is not trivial and has not been considered in previous research, which is why it has not been used in the original name of the algorithm, which remains DistNW. This paper further explores the theoretical boundaries of the proposed approach, providing an exact upper limit on error magnitude in distributed optimization tasks and pinpointing a critical threshold below which both algorithms under consideration, DistNW and DistNW-B, are guaranteed to converge to the same optimal outcome. This new threshold, $\sigma^2=\Omega\left(\frac{m}{n}}\right)$, where $m$ is the iteration number and $n$ is the number of machines, has been identified as crucial in ensuring convergence to the same optimal outcome for both algorithms under consideration, which is theoretically shown.
