Since their introduction in the 19th century, little has been known about the link between their dynamic behaviors and geometric properties of the underlying spaces they're defined within. To address this gap, a numerical method was proposed for determining geodesic distances in Gaussian random field manifolds, involving two main components: deriving the underlying metric (a specific first-order matrix), and computing the necessary Christoffel symbols from the derived system. These calculations are used to solve the resulting system of differential equations through iterative approaches, such as Runge-Kutta. When applied to different scenarios, this method demonstrated its capability to estimate distances while also uncovering intriguing connections between random field dynamics and the geometric characteristics of the associated manifolds. Furthermore, it provides a practical tool for analyzing complex systems governed by random differential equations, offering valuable insights into the dynamic systems under consideration. This approach is also the first to tackle geodesic distance calculations on complex surfaces characterized by spatial variations, moving beyond the limitations of flat surfaces. It's essential to note that in some instances, the connection between the random field's characteristics and the resulting geometric properties may lead to suboptimal outcomes, as evident in the considered examples. By extending the principles of optimal mass transport to random field manifolds, this method opens up the possibility of studying geodesic distances across various categories of random fields (including stand-alone, Gaussian, and linear combinations of these fields) and derives the corresponding geometric characteristics based on the underlying random field type. It also introduces a novel algorithm for computing the first-order partial derivatives of the geodesic distance metric with respect to the underlying random field, offering opportunities for inverse problems inversion and high-dimensional computational optimization. In the realm of experimental physics, we identify future objectives aimed at replicating the conditions of our astrophysical experiments, probably including the development of laboratory models representing the final stages of compact binary mergers, similar to those occurring in the cosmos. A graph on n vertices is called pancyclic if it has a cycle of every possible length from 3 to n. In 1992, Fiala established a bond between the pancyclicity of a graph and the clique number and the size of its coloring. Specifically, he demonstrated that a graph with a clique number of r (and at least 2r + 2 vertices) is pancyclic if it is k-colorable and k is greater than or equal to 3. In 2014, this relationship was further refined by taking into account the structure of the coloring. In this research, we examine the applicability of these generalizations to Hamiltonian graphs specifically, and we also provide a counterexample to show that the previously made assumption that a Hamiltonian pancyclic n-graph with a clique number of r exists has a clique whose diameter does not exceed (r - 1) + 2 is false. Moreover, we identify cases where the previously made assumptions that a Hamiltonian pancyclic n-graph with a clique number of r has a Hamiltonian cycle induced by a clique of diameter not exceeding (r - 1) + 2, or at least (r - 1) + 3) is false. In these instances, we describe a Hamiltonian pancyclic n-graph with a clique number of r in which no such Hamiltonian cycle can be found. In addition, we provide a description of pancyclic Hamiltonian graphs with specific structures, such as a main block and a number of isolated vertices, or a main block and a number of isolated edges. In these cases, the graph's clique number equals the size of the main block plus one. In further research, we investigated the possibility of embedding two pancyclic graphs in a third one under certain constraints. In particular, we demonstrated that for any given integer k greater than 3, there exists a k-colorable and pancyclic graph with 2k^2 +8k vertices. In this graph, the pancyclic property is preserved even after dividing it into two components with a minimum distance of k+1. In addition, we identified a Hamiltonian pancyclic graph with 14 vertices and showed that for any given integer k greater than 3, there exists a pair of pancyclic graphs with k colors and a product of n number of vertices, which when combined into a third graph with the same number of vertices, preserves the pancyclic property with a minimum distance of k+1. This review provides an overview of quantum mechanics history with a specific focus on addressing the theoretical difficulties in explaining ionization within the framework of stationary state quantum mechanics. The fundamental principles of stationary state quantum mechanics and the concepts of resonance parameters are then explored, leading into an in-depth examination of the Schrodinger-Krahler problem, which is a theoretical model designed to elucidate the process of autoionization. The review includes a discussion on how to effectively apply quantum mechanics theory and algorithms, particularly those grounded in the complex quantum mechanics theory, to solve problems related to resonance parameters. The practical utility of the approaches outlined is demonstrated through the solution of a range of problems, from basic to complex, involving various types of potentials, including the Maxwell boundary conditions, which are relevant in the study of multiphoton ionization. The algorithms discussed are adaptable and can be readily implemented in a range of physical phenomena, such as photoionization, where the boundary conditions are both non-Roentgen and non-Dirichlet. The review concludes by highlighting the key insights and the significant advancements that have been achieved in the field, as well as the prospects for further study and the possibility of the development of new technologies and understanding of quantum mechanics and the behavior of matter at the atomic and subatomic level. The final outcome of the review is the demonstration that quantum mechanics theory is a powerful and efficient tool for the study of the ionization process. The review includes additional documentation in the form of four appendices that expand on the methods and approaches discussed, as well as a comprehensive bibliography containing over 300 entries. The paper is the first of a series of three reviews on quantum mechanics and the study of quantum systems, the second of which will focus on the numerical methods in vacuum quantum electrodynamics and the scattering theory, and the third will focus on the application of quantum mechanics to the study of vacuum quantum electrodynamics and the gravo-thermoelectric effect. The paper is accompanied by a code library containing over 40 algorithms in the form of working programs that demonstrate the application of quantum mechanics theory to the study of resonance parameters, and over 30 contributions from approximately 30 reviewers that expand on the topics covered. TERS is an essential technique for analyzing surfaces with subnanometer resolution. Yet, accurately simulating specific TERS signals is computationally difficult. Our innovative method combines the primary factors driving the effectiveness of TERS, the electromagnetic and chemical interactions, into a single quantum simulation. The electromagnetic influence describes the sample's interaction with highly localized, inhomogeneous electric fields produced by the plasmonic tip, a focal point of many mechanistic studies. Conversely, the chemical interaction accounts for the distinct responses between the apex tip and sample under extremely close-range, highly position-sensitive chemical interactions. Our study focuses on a SnPc sample molecule paired with a single silver atom, modeling the chemical interaction using a time-dependent density functional theory description. By incorporating the electromagnetic influence using a series of point charges simulating the plasmonic Ag nanoparticle, we examine the resultant Raman responses across the entire 3D grid, achieving the precise spatial resolution inherent to TERS. Our simulation uncovers the underlying Raman signals and identifies how the electromagnetic and chemical interactions are intertwined, particularly evident in monolayer SnPc where significant intensity enhancements and depolarizations arise due to the chemical interaction, manifesting as non-zero polarizability in all directional axes. Conversely, our mechanistic analysis of the biomolecular rod-like SnPc also indicates a distinction between the electromagnetic and chemical dominance based on the molecule's orientation. Specifically, our simulation reveals a possible explanation for depolarization effects observed in TERS, showing that the chemical interaction contributes substantially to the non-zero polarizability in direction perpendicular to the sample molecule axis. Hence, our approach allows for the quantitative analysis of the combined electromagnetic and chemical influences defining the TERS spectrum, paving the way for mechanistic understanding and simulations of this Raman spectroscopy technique. The simulation code used within this study has been made publicly accessible via GitHub, incorporating the necessary modifications to the quantum simulation software Wien2k. Furthermore, our discussion includes discussions on the capabilities and necessary improvements for the simulation of specific TERS signals. As quantum calculations confirm the significant impact of the electromagnetic influence in TERS, they also underscore the chemical interaction's prominent role in the monolayer subunits of SnPc, implicitly pointing out its implicit presence in typical TERS experiments. To mitigate systematic measurement errors on quantum computers, current methods employ counteractive postprocessing techniques known as measurement error mitigation (MEM). A key limitation of these techniques is the tradeoff between scalability and validity: methods that handle a large number of qubits tend to produce negative probabilities, whereas those that guarantee a correct probability distribution cannot be scaled. To address these concerns, we propose a new scheme that combines both principles. Specifically, we adapt and implement a standard iterative Bayesian unfolding approach commonly used in high-energy physics experiments in a way that scales effectively with the number of qubits. Our approach is validated by successfully mitigating measurement errors in experiments involving up to 127 qubits and 26 qubits using Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger and Bernstein-Vazirani algorithms, respectively. Furthermore, we employ our technique in a real-world context by leveraging the computational power of the IBM 127-qubit quantum computer to solve the multicore Max-Planck Institute problem, thereby surpassing its previous limitations. When humans operate robot arms, it is frequently necessary for the robot to infer the task the human is attempting to accomplish. Current research on assistive teleoperation and shared control focuses on developing methods for the robot to determine the desired task based on human joystick inputs. Typically, this is done by using an internal map that links joystick inputs to specific tasks: for instance, pressing the joystick to the left indicates the desire to move a plate, while pressing it to the right signifies a cup should be moved. While this method works well after the user has learned the robot's operating conventions, it can be confusing for users at the beginning. Furthermore, users may believe that pressing the joystick somewhat to the left or right should result in the plate or cup being positioned at a corresponding intermediate location. Our study shows that users commonly hold this belief and proposes that robots should indicate the relationship between joystick inputs and tasks through dynamic highlights on a decision-making map. Our findings confirm the benefits of this approach and suggest that robot explanations should be considered an essential aspect of assistive teleoperation and shared control. Our conclusion also suggests potential designs for integrating these explanations into existing shared control frameworks. Our study utilizes kinesthetic training and highlights the necessity for user education on the robot's operating conventions. Ultimately, the method proposed in this paper can improve the training process by increasing user understanding of the robot's operating conventions. Our study also compares the utilization of the robot's operating conventions against the robot's policy and finds they are not always in agreement. Our data suggests that robots should at least be informed of their operating conventions. Our study also demonstrates the method's implications for vision systems and shows that using highlights for training is feasible. Our study was conducted using a Worcester Polytechnic Institute teleoperation laboratory where three tasks were performed by a robotic arm. Our data reveals the common misconception among users that intermediate joystick inputs should result in the intermediate placement of objects. Our study also discovered the reasons behind this misconception through questionnaires. Our data indicates that educating users about the robot's operating conventions through highlights significantly improves their understanding. Our study also found that highlighting the robot's operating conventions does not compromise the efficiency of the task. Our study also compared the utilization of the robot's policy against the robot's operating conventions and found that the robot's policy achieves higher task performance. For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drifting and produce a unified global map for navigation. Unfortunately, implementing these systems on a large scale can be challenging due to their tendency to deviate and slow build-up times. In response to these limitations, a novel map representation called HiTMap is presented, featuring a unique hierarchical structure that focuses solely on a local metric map for obstacle avoidance while keeping the representation lightweight. Furthermore, HiTMap detects frontiers, integrating them into the map as an attribute to guide navigation, and includes a path-planning module to evaluate the representation's feasibility and efficiency. The system's performance was validated through simulation testing and a real-world demonstration, and its source code is available openly for public use. When dealing with multi-variable data sets that change over time, we anticipate observing interconnected patterns. Common characteristics of such data sets frequently include seasonal trends, variations, and interconnected components. However, it's also possible for true relationships with other data sets to be nonexistent, resulting in randomness. While interconnected components are often non-random, they may be accompanied by random fluctuations. That being said, true connections might sometimes be hidden by recent, isolated occurrences or the influence of significant, sporadic events. Multi-variable data often presents these dynamics in a more complex and controlled environment, facilitated by technologies such as sensor networks, patient monitoring equipment, healthcare systems, and the field of knowledge discovery for better understanding the data. In order to effectively analyze data that evolves over time and may also be affected by other factors, we require methodologies that take into account the context in which the data was collected, making the classification process still rather challenging. The promising potential of extracting valuable insights from Electronic Health Records (EHRs) has emerged as a crucial area of study, as machine learning models can assist healthcare professionals in decision-making to enhance overall healthcare quality. Advances in recent years have seen the development of sequential or graph-based models aiming to tackle this goal. Despite the complexity and diversity of EHR data, which can be visualized as a multi-layered, interconnected network (heterogeneous relational graph), past studies have neglected these essential aspects of the data. Moreover, existing methods that do address complexity often prioritize simplification, resulting in the loss of critical information. Our new approach, the Flexible Heterogeneous Relational Graph Network (FRGN), aims to address these issues by leveraging the effective representation of EHR data as a heterogeneous relational graph. By incorporating both low-level and high-level features, our model aims to provide a coherent and comprehensive understanding of this data. Our framework, which builds upon the Multi-layer Percedptron (MLP) framework, is unique in that it represents each "entity" within the graph with a set number of features, while "relations" between entities are represented by specific features as well. Our framework, which can be applied to a broad range of diagnostic tasks, utilizes an attention-based approach to focus on the most relevant entities and relationships for an specific task, before providing a final diagnosis. Our new model outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques on three diagnostic datasets for diagnosis and patient outcome prediction. Our model and code are openly available on the repository located at https://github.com/grasp-llm/FFRGN. Our results indicate that our approach enhances diagnostic performance by 5-15% when compared to the use of simplified graphs, while allowing for more detailed understanding and interpretation of the data by healthcare professionals. Our model's ability to provide interpretability is critical, as it can result in the improvement of overall healthcare quality. Our model's ablation studies reveal the crucial role of the multi-layered representation of the graph for FRGN's effectiveness. From a free energy model, we calculate the electrostatic potential and number of water and ions within the boundary by solving coupled differential equations, taking into account how each variable affects the others. We then use these results to find the capacitance of the boundary, focusing on how capacitance varies in response to different electric potentials. Our study shows that neglecting solvent effects in favor of fixed charges leads to significantly overestimated estimates of the electrostatic potential near the boundary. Additionally, we find that conventional models that treat solvent effects as negligible significantly deviate from predicted behaviors when accounting for this factor, but these deviations are reduced as the size of the solvent molecules approaches that of the ions. Important advances in our understanding of electrolytes involve incorporating both moving particle sizes and solvent effects into these models, allowing these systems to be modeled in non-equilibrium conditions. Overall, our study provides a comprehensive framework for modeling electrolytes in diverse settings. We have also discovered that a specific type of electrical double layer, characterized at the boundary of an asymmetric redox flexible material with high concentrations of redox molecules, displays behaviors not previously seen, including a shift in their characteristic time scales from Debye lengths to the values related to their self-exchange rates. We then use these results to predict electrical responses based on their sizes and capacitances. We have conducted a series of capacitor-like experiments using optical measurements of the flexible material's redox-based capacitor, validating our predictions for the observed frequencies. These results show that in the very low and high frequency ranges, the material exhibits behavior that is consistent with a pure capacitance and inductance. In the intermediate frequency range, the material displays behaviors not predicted by conventional models. We have observed a response that is similar to a resistor-capitance-inductance circuit in an area, for the first time. We have extended the scope of this study to understand the capacitor-like behavior of the flexible material in a variety of situations, including when it is exposed to other factors that help explain its different responses. We have used these results to create an analytical model, allowing predictions to be made about the information that can be extracted from the measurements of the flexible material's redox-based capacitor. These predictions show that conventional methods for extracting such information may produce results that are biased. A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local densities of states for precise analysis. Utilizing the theoretical framework, 60 Scrimpscott, Schmitt, and von Döbner (SDV) states have been identified within the YSR spectrum, including zero-energy states. To validate the theoretical predictions, a scanning tunneling spectroscopy experiment was conducted on Fe impurities on the Nb(110) surface. Upon comparison of the theoretical and experimental findings, an almost perfect correlation between the two was observed. Consequently, a new, efficient scanning technique has been proposed, allowing the identification and characterization of magnetic Scrimpscott, Schmitt, and von Döbner impurities on superconducting surfaces by analyzing their zero-energy states. Additionally, a graphical guide illustrating the orbital dependencies of the YSR states, particularly those related to Scrimpscott impurities, has been developed and presented. As a result, the development of this theoretical framework and the proposed scanning technique will facilitate further research into the unique properties of Skimpscott, Schmitt, and von Döbner impurities in superconducting materials. Furthermore, the theoretical framework will provide valuable insights into the varying orbital dependencies of the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states in different magnetic impurities. In conclusion, the research offers significant opportunities for exploring the unique properties of quantum bits in their basic forms. Furthermore, the techniques developed in this research will facilitate the detection of magnetic signals at ultra-low concentrations, a capability that will contribute to the advancement of quantum computing technologies. Moreover, the analysis of Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states in their various forms will pave the way for the development of more efficient scanning techniques, thus accelerating research in this field. Ultimately, the research has the potential to pave the way for the mass production of quantum bits, a key requirement for future large-scale quantum computing systems. However, the techniques developed in this research are not limited to the analysis of Scrimpscott impurities, as similar techniques can be applied to other magnetic impurities that exhibit Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states. For instance, the techniques can be used for the analysis of Schmitt impurities, as the orbital dependencies of the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states for these impurities have been extensively documented

Subjecting solid materials to an ultra-intense, high-flux X-ray pulse gives rise to electron dynamics involving highly nonlinear processes. In examining these dynamics via time-resolved X-ray spectroscopy, researchers have discovered a phenomenon where the materials under investigation alter their electronic structure in response to the X-ray flux. As a result, we achieve improved explicit Laplace transforms, surpassing a prior theorem by Cai et al. and yielding increased efficiency through numerical studies. Additionally, we demonstrate that our best outcome can be attained by treating the Merton option as a special case of a power-mean option, allowing for a unified view of options pricing. Furthermore, we show that certain power-mean options have explicit Laplace transforms via a direct process analysis, and showcase this via numerical studies of the power-mean option. Lastly, we apply the CTMC framework to tackle the challenge of Monte Carlo simulation speed in Asian options pricing. By exploiting the property that the future process is equally distributed to a past process, we develop a universal method for constructing ancestral processes from present processes in a straightforward manner. This in turn enables the acceleration of Monte Carlo simulations, an improvement which is illustrated through numerical examples of option pricing scenarios.

Understanding how complex visual models work is crucial, and developing techniques to explain these models can be particularly challenging. To address this issue, a framework called LaViSE is proposed to enable convolutional neural networks to describe their internal workings in plain text. By using generic image data, this approach creates a link between visual and semantic information, allowing for its application across different domains without specific training. The LaViSE framework has a flexible structure, making it possible to analyze any network, regardless of its location. Furthermore, it can be used as a tool to measure the coherence of the internal structure within a network. As an example of its application, this approach explains how a dog classifier identifies its target as a dog. Additionally, it highlights key features such as the presence of fur, a tail, and eyes. This information is validated by conducting user studies on various models and datasets, including the CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet datasets. The LaViSE framework has been made available for public access at the URL: https://lavise-neurips-2022.net/. Finally, it is worth noting that this approach can identify biases within datasets, as it was observed during the user study that the generated text-based explanations for the 'frog' class contained a clear bias towards the presence of ants, a creature not typically found in this class. This insight confirms that LaViSE can serve as a powerful tool to investigate the internal workings of artificial neural networks. The abstract of the paper can be found at: https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.10213. The LaViSE framework's source code has been hosted on GitHub at: https://github.com/brosing1/LaViSE_NEURIPS22. A video introducing the LaViSE framework is available at: https://youtu.be/8Bq2tQO8B9E.

The equilibrium problem described by the Nikaid\^o-Isoda-Fan inequality encompasses several key problems like optimization, variational inequality, and others, as specific instances. This paper aims to provide a clear outline illustrating the connection between the equilibrium problem and monotone variational inequality problems. Moreover, it offers a straightforward example that clearly demonstrates the equilibrium problem has no solution, along with a straightforward, full analysis of a particular monotone variational inequality problem. Calculations demonstrating the efficiency of the Shapley coefficient for convex games via Monte Carlo simulation are also presented. Finally, this paper announces a full general analysis of the essential smoothing algorithm for solving equilibrium problems. This algorithm has previously been found to be convergent under the assumption of bounded level-below maps when the underlying function space is finite-dimensional. Our analysis relaxes this assumption, requiring only that the maps be upper semicontinuous and convex. Under these more general assumptions, we demonstrate the convergence of the essential smoothing algorithm for monotone equilibrium problems when the underlying map is twice differentiable. These findings have been proven through a novel approach to proving convergence in monotone variational inequality problems. They have also been proven through a novel full general analysis of the essential smoothing algorithm for solving monotone variational inequality problems. These findings have been published in a separate paper. Our analysis also proves that, for compact convex cones, a particular full general analysis of the essential smoothing algorithm for solving monotone variational inequality problems can be reduced to a specific instance of monotone equilibrium problems. This finding has also been published in a separate paper. Our calculations also show that a particular full general analysis of the essential smoothing algorithm for solving monotone variational inequality problems can be reduced to a specific instance of optimization problems when the underlying map is a classical convex objective function. These findings have also been published in a separate paper. Using the outlined methodological contributions, we have verified the convergence of the essential smoothing algorithm for solving monotone variational inequality problems in a range of realistic applications across optimization, game theory, and extended contact problems. These findings have also been published in separate papers. Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have brought about a significant transformation in the field of reversible steganography. A key foundation of reversible steganography relies on predictive modeling that can be achieved using deep neural networks. However, critical inaccuracies persist when dealing with data outside the scope of a model's training and noisy data. To address this challenge, we introduce the concept of uncertainty in predictive models rooted in the theoretical framework of Bayesian deep learning. Bayesian neural networks are essentially intelligent systems that recognize their own shortcomings. To accurately quantify uncertainty, we approximate the posterior predictive distribution by leveraging Monte Carlo sampling combined with stochastic forward passes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that predictive uncertainty can be separated into aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties, both of which can be learned through unsupervised methods. Experimental findings show that the application of Bayesian uncertainty analysis results in improved steganographic performance with regard to capacity-distortion metrics. To facilitate reproducibility and evaluation, we release an open-source extension of the popular DeepSteganography-Challenge platform, referred to as BayesDeepSteganography-Challenge. This repository contains implemented techniques and data that can be accessed via the following link: https://github.com/Bayesian-Dynamic/BayesDeepSteganography-Challenge. Our research presents a new frontier for reversible steganography by integrating concepts of uncertainty and Bayesian deep learning. Ultimately, we deliver state-of-the-art steganographic performance with the lowest distortion observed to date. The debate on turbulent effects influencing magnetic activity in the Sun and stars persists. The mean-field theory provides a widely applied framework to link these effects to fundamental magnetohydrodynamics, although it's not possible to directly observe these effects from observations or simulations with resolved magnetics. To bridge the gap, we utilize global simulations of the Sun that resolve the magnetic field and yield turbulent effects through the calculation of transport coefficients based on the Alexei Kitchatinov's model. By incorporating these effects into a global Charley Townes model, we explore how solar cycle fluctuations are influenced by different geometric configurations of turbulent effects. The results indicate that turbulent effects in the interior and surface of the Sun are necessary to reproduce the observed period of the solar cycle. The effects showing the largest impact are related to the combination of the Sun's rotation rate and tangent-angle parameter. The dependence on the tangent-angle parameter highlights the importance of interior and surface turbulence interaction through the tachocline. The results also reveal that turbulent effects in the convection zone have an unexpected role in the solar dynamics, one that could be tested by astero-seism data. The code used to calculate transport coefficients and solve the mean-field equation is available at https://github.com/eilifhuq/solar_dynamo. Portfolio managers assess investment success in relation to market standards, specifically using the Standard & Poor 500 index as a benchmark. Our revised assessment combines two key measures: the portfolio's absolute value and its performance relative to that of a chosen benchmark. The traditional Merton problem, however, solely focuses on the portfolio's absolute wealth. In contrast, our proposed model encompasses both absolute and relative wealth in a comprehensive utility function. The utility functions, derived from power law equations, allow for flexibility with varying exponents to suit individual benchmarks or market scenarios. The outcome provides an explicit solution and is compared to the original Merton problem solution, with implications for the Capital Asset Pricing Model framework. The observed insights suggest that investment behavior may significantly differ when considering a relative wealth objective versus an absolute wealth objective. The choice of utility function exponent has a substantial impact on portfolio allocation among the three investment options. A high exponent leads to heavy investment in the relatively best asset, whereas a low exponent results in heavy investment in the most probabilistically favorable asset. Furthermore, in relative wealth objectives, portfolio allocation tends to be riskier, with higher allocations to the risky asset, as compared to the absolute wealth objective scenario. The observed behavior also presents an interesting contradiction to the predictable outcome of a relative wealth objective, as compared to the absolute wealth objective. The power utility functions, allowing for a wide range of behavior, provide a clear understanding of investment allocation among the three options. The model's ability to generate explicit solutions highlights the significant implications of utility function properties. The explicit solution obtained in this model is essential for a relative wealth objective, as it would be difficult to derive in a model with a utility function over a continuous probability space. The comparison of our model to the original Merton problem, as well as the obtained results, is crucial in a relative wealth objective, as it would not produce such explicit solutions. The model's first-order stochastic differential equation can be modified to incorporate multiple time periods, enabling the analysis of long-term behavior. The model's first explicit solution demonstrates its practical applicability to the relative wealth objective, as the traditional Merton problem solution cannot. The model's versatility is further shown by its ability to be extended to a multi-period setting with multiple time periods, as well as its ability to be interpreted in a partial equilibrium model. By reducing the complex model into a non-interacting chain with varying site potentials, we map it to a standard quantum comb. The quasiparticle stability is influenced by both its width in the beam and the detuning from the mean energy. These conditions result in a set of sharp resonances in absorption spectra. The width of the quantum comb corresponds to the dispersion of quasiparticles, and detuning represents an external influence. Quasiparticle stability is enhanced when its dispersion is low and it is centered at its mean energy. In the context of strong fermion-boson coupling, this model is applicable to systems such as strongly correlated high-temperature superconductors or cold atom setups, where stability of quasiparticle can be described through a change in Heisenberg matrix elements, dependent on distance. Utilizing crowdsourcing platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk to acquire top-tier human annotations proves more complicated than initially thought, influenced by several key factors, including task instructions and annotator compensation, among others. To prevent inaccurate annotations which could mislead machine learning systems, it's crucial to select high-quality annotators while minimizing financial costs. In this research, we investigate using real-time annotator monitoring during data collection to maintain quality control. Through a test involving 156 annotators, we evaluate the efficacy of hiring criteria and payment methods in recruiting reliable annotators. Moreover, we assess the effectiveness of paying annotators extra for superior performance, as well as the impact of providing explicit evaluation criteria, in maintaining quality. Ultimately, by integrating these strategies, we achieve a consistent quality standard among our annotations at a minimal additional cost. We release the code for this process on GitHub. Previous studies, such as those by Gulati et al. in 2019 and 2020, have also explored similar topics, however they did not combine all the techniques demonstrated here. Additionally, we are releasing the dataset consisting of 5,525 high-quality annotations of 1,403 named entities. This dataset can be accessed on the GitHub repository. In conclusion, by employing real-time monitoring and combining hiring criteria, payment methods, and providing explicit evaluation criteria, we are able to control the quality of annotations made using crowdsourcing platforms. Such a method could also be applied to other types of data, like text annotations. Their work in 2020 shows that providing explicit evaluation criteria increases the task's acceptance rate and maintains its quality. Our research builds upon these findings, providing a comprehensive solution to maintaining high-quality annotations. Text-video retrieval, a rapidly developing field, faces challenges from discrete video segments with varying lengths, leading to uneven textual features for each video clip.
This issue prompts the proposal of TS2-Net, a novel token shift module designed to dynamically adjust the number of textual features per video segment for accurate matching during retrieval tasks.
Comprised of an encoder, token shift module, and a shared learning aggregator, TS2-Net synergistically leverages textual features from distinct video clips to enhance overall representation accuracy.
To further improve performance, a multi-clip decision module is also developed to determine the most informative video segments for retrieval purposes.
Experimental results demonstrate that TS2-Net achieves superior outcomes compared to existing methods on TextVid-7M and TextVid-1M datasets. The associated code can be found on the GitHub repository https://github.com/HiProtopath/TextVid-7M.git. 
This research is one of the first to address token shift across video clips for accurate retrieval. It introduces a pioneering solution in this area, outperforming existing methods by integrating a novel technical approach. To address the topic, a custom-designed dataset is developed with 7 million video clips, introducing a new research direction in this area. One of the major challenges encountered during this research includes reducing the computational costs associated with the proposed method. To overcome this issue, the system architecture of TS2-Net was optimized to improve its efficiency. We also developed a multi-stage training approach to allow the model to converge during the retrieval process. These optimizations significantly reduced the computational costs of TS2-Net. To evaluate the model, three distinct metrics were used including recall, precision, and F-beta score. These metrics were utilized to compare the performance of the proposed method against existing approaches. We also developed a decision module to determine the optimal number of video segments for accurate retrieval. To further improve the model's generalizability, the proposed method incorporated a learning aggregator that can accumulate and enhance the textual features across multiple video clips. These features were then merged using a shared decision module to form the final textual feature which represents the video content. In response to the intricacies of network data, a new type of hybrid network is suggested that blends rules for preferential attachment and uniform attachment.  This hybrid network creates edges according to a mixture of these rules.  Specifically, at each edge creation step, a new node is chosen with probabilities based on the preferential attachment rule, or with equal likelihood as existing nodes, following the uniform attachment rule.  Numerical analysis confirms that this hybrid network closely replicates the characteristics of actual networks, including the distribution of node degrees and the development of network connectivity over time.  Additionally, a new method for generating hybrid networks has been developed based on a simple and intuitive idea.  Finally, an investigation into the effects of differentiating the parameters that govern this hybrid network on resulting node degree distributions is conducted.  The findings indicate that a hybrid network offering slight favoritism to preferential attachment has the most satisfactory outcomes.  Conversely, overemphasis on either rule is found to yield unrealistic node degree distributions.  These results imply that a hybrid network combining rules for preferential attachment and uniform attachment may be the most effective approach for accurately modeling real-world networks.  Consequently, such a hybrid network could serve as a useful tool for generating synthetic networks that accurately replicate the characteristics of actual networks.  Specifically, a new type of synthetic hybrid network has been developed that combines the preferential attachment and uniform attachment algorithms.  The synthetic hybrid network was generated using the following formula: $P(i,j) = (\frac{n_i(n_t-1)}{2n_s} + cI_{i=j})$, where $i$ and $j$ are nodes in the network, $n_i$ is the number of incoming edges for node $i$, $n_t$ is the total number of nodes, $c$ is a parameter that balances preferential and uniform attachment, and $I_{i=j}$ accounts for self-loops.  The parameter $c$ is set to 0.1 in order to generate a synthetic hybrid network that accurately models real-world networks.  The synthetic hybrid network was found to closely replicate the degree distribution of real networks.  The synthetic hybrid network was also found to well approximate key features of real networks. All AI systems inevitably make mistakes, characterized by their unpredictability and distinctness from human errors. A critical objective is to rectify these AI errors without compromising their established abilities and ideally without requiring direct human intervention. This work introduces a groundbreaking approach where an AI system detects and corrects its own errors using only its own internal data, without any external guidance. Employing mathematical justification, we confirm that this self-correction process minimizes the overall performance loss and prevents the accumulation of persistent errors. Through practical testing, we demonstrate that our method effectively learns from the corrections and generates more accurate outcomes, and we observe that the probability of corrections decreases over time as the model becomes more reliable. This innovative self-correction method offers new avenues for enhancing the efficiency and reliability of AI systems. It serves as a unique model for naturally managing errors that differ from human mistakes, and it facilitates the collaborative problem-solving capabilities of AI systems. Additionally, it contributes to the ongoing advancement of AI by assessing the quality of its own internal data, thereby validating the utility of using synthetic data for supervised machine learning. At present, there is limited understanding of the interaction between synthetic and real data. Therefore, we are compelled to ask: Can AI benefit more from the information contained within fewer high-quality examples than from the presence of a larger quantity of low-quality examples? This research aims to clarify this uncertainty and presents a potential application of using synthetic data in the context of self-driven vehicles learning to avoid pedestrians and obstacles. Results indicate that the AI system is capable of effectively avoiding pedestrians and obstacles using data solely from the view of the vehicle's driver. Importantly, it performs substantially better than a baseline method that utilizes real images from various perspectives. This study paves the way for the possibility that AI systems may ultimately surpass human capabilities, and it underscores the critical need for ongoing mathematical justification in the ongoing advancement of AI, particularly in the science. A accompanying video can be found at: https://youtu.be/6Bq1Xn2X1qA. A publicly accessible demonstration of the study's code can be found at: https://bandcamp.comot.com/production-of-self-adaptive-recurrent-networks/.

However, test code can be compromised by suboptimal design or implementation choices referred to as test smells. These shortcomings can significantly undermine the quality of software systems by exacerbating difficulties in comprehension, amplifying maintenance complexities, and making systems more susceptible to bugs and errors. Prior studies have investigated the likely consequences of test smells on test code. Despite their focus, a knowledge gap remains regarding the perspectives of developers regarding these issues. This paper investigates the existence and uniqueness of solutions to a modified version of the sweeping process, first proposed by J.J. Moreau in the early 1970s as part of plasticity theory. The proposed modification involves a novel combination of the classical ODE autonomous sweeping process and an integral forcing term, initially introduced by H. Brezaoui et al. in 2015. The objective is to prove that the described evolution equation has a single, unique solution within a suitable space, building upon Leiba R. Rockafellar's work in 'Convex Cones' published in 1974 and the author's previous findings in 'Second Order Sweeping Process' published in 2018. The developed approach can be applied to diverse systems of differential type, and it even confirms the equivalence of the described process to a modified version of the classical Stokes equation when applied in the context of viscoelastic fluid flow modeled by the Loewner-Kichline integrated type integral equation model. The work in this area stems from the collaboration with C. Grujic in 'On Isolated Singularities of Steady Viscoelastic Fluid Flows' published in 2016. The general approach considered here can likely be used in diverse fields of research. Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals can provide early warnings for cardiovascular diseases. However, identifying IBIs from noisy signals is difficult, especially when they are heavily distorted by motion noise, which is common in individuals who are highly active. Researchers working on remote health monitoring and wearable devices have identified signal denoising and IBI estimation as a significant area of focus. Recent breakthroughs have involved the use of deep learning, which has significantly improved signal quality assessment and IBI estimation accuracy. We have developed a deep learning approach based on conditional variational models to tackle the two associated problems simultaneously, improving estimation accuracy and signal quality when noise levels are severe, as demonstrated by testing on the ActiveECG dataset. Our approach outperformed state-of-the-art models, increasing average IBI estimation accuracy by more than 10% and signal quality metrics by 15%, with particular success in interpreting motion noise. We also analyzed the effect of our proposed model on other performance metrics and discovered that better signal denoising significantly boosts IBI estimation accuracy. Our findings have the potential to improve remote health monitoring and wearable device devices, which are essential for monitoring cardiovascular diseases. To utilize contemporary computing systems efficiently, an important consideration is reducing the communication cost associated with data transfer, especially when calculating the tensor singular value decomposition (t-SVD) in just a few data passes. The prevailing t-SVD approaches have either restricted computational resources or necessitate a large number of data transmissions. In this study, a novel data transmission schedule called L-GT-SVD has been introduced and validated to work efficiently on a wide variety of tensor dimensions. L-GT-SVD was formulated specifically to minimize data exchange during t-SVD computation. An alternating least squares-based algorithm for t-SVD has been modified to implement L-GT-SVD, and our results demonstrate that L-GT-SVD requires only a small initial data transfer and subsequent iterations involve minimal data exchange. Recent experiments conducted on a IBM Blue-Gene/P system have shown that L-GT-SVD can take advantage of its hardware capabilities by computing the t-SVD in fewer data transfers than existing methods. Moreover, our data compression results for the lin-global tensor singular value decomposition (lin-GT-SVD) of a 9-way tensor in just 10 data passes exceed the previous best outcomes for this problem. These findings highlight the effectiveness of L-GT-SVD in reducing data exchange costs for a variety of tensor computations. Finally, our latest analysis introduces a new three-way tensor classification method based on the t-SVD, which has been tested and validated on the Blue-Gene/P system. An open-source implementation of L-GT-SVD can be obtained at the website https://github.com/L-GT-SVD/long-scheduling-t-SVD. Additionally, this implementation supports computations on tensors of any order or dimensionality. Moreover, our latest analysis introduces a new three-way tensor classification method based on the t-SVD, which has been tested and validated on the Blue-Gene/P system. An open-source implementation of L-GT-SVD can be obtained at the website https://github.com/L-GT-SVD/long-scheduling-t-SVD. Additionally, our code has been configured to work efficiently on other contemporary high-performance computing systems, allowing t-SVD computations to be optimized for maximum performance. Network analytics heavily relies on embedding static graphs in low-dimensional vector spaces to enable node classification, link prediction, and visualization, but this approach struggles to accommodate dynamic behavior exhibited by real-world networks. These networks often undergo changes in their topological structure, feature evolution, and spreading dynamics over time. To capture such dynamics, researchers have proposed various techniques for embedding dynamic graphs over time. These methods face challenges related to modeling temporal changes, incorporating temporal characteristics, and adjusting to varying levels of granularity. This overview survey provides a comprehensive analysis of dynamic graph embedding by detailing its fundamental aspects and latest developments. We formally define dynamic graph embedding and categorize it into problem settings and a novel taxonomy of input and output. We also discuss different dynamic phenomena and categorize them according to topological changes, feature evolution, and network processes. In addition, existing methods and a classification of algorithmic approaches, ranging from matrix factorization to deep learning, are discussed, as well as common challenges and potential solutions. Ultimately, this work aims to provide a thorough understanding of dynamic graph embedding and a clear perspective on its various aspects, paving the way for future research in this rapidly evolving field. The survey specifically targets network analysts interested in dynamic graph embedding using traditional or deep learning algorithms, giving an overview of existing methods and linking theoretical aspects to implementation. We also outline practical challenges and recommended research directions in this dynamic and evolving field. Dynamic graph embedding has numerous real-world applications across visualization, classification, link prediction, and measure estimation. These techniques are widely employed in various domains such as social network analysis, biomedical study, power grid transmission, and drug resistance research. Consequently, we give recommendations for choosing a particular approach based on the underlying network characteristics and provide directions for potential research avenues. Dynamic graph embedding is a sophisticated concept, and working with real-time network data and machine learning approaches necessitates considerable expertise in both subject areas. In an effort to make this survey most useful, we provide explicit implementations of our method in Figure 10 and Figure 11 and Appendix C, allowing readers to better comprehend the technical aspects by comparing different approaches and their performances on standard datasets. These implementations, written in popular programming languages such as Python and R, demonstrate approaches like deep dynamic graph factorization and temporal deep network embedding. Furthermore, the provided code serves as a starting point for researchers to develop new methods, test existing ones, and select the most suitable technique depending on the underlying network characteristics. We hope that our code and this survey provide valuable insights, motivating future research directions and scenarios in which dynamic graph embedding is most applicable

Our investigation into a $^7$H resonant state treated as a five-body system with a $^3$H core and four neutrons involved, involved constructing an effective neutron-$^3$H potential to reproduce the $^7$H bound state energy in a $^7$H+$^4$N system. Utilizing the asymptotic behavior of the $^7$H wave function, we determined the quantum numbers of the $^7$H bound state to be $s_{1/2}$ with angular momentum J=7/2. We further observed a resonant state at approximately 9 MeV above the $^3$H+4n threshold, which we identified as having ground state configuration (n'n'n') with quantum numbers $l_m=$3,21 respectively. We then analyzed the $^7$H bound state as well as the resonant state under the effects of the centrifugal term for both a neutron-$^3$H core and four neutrons, ultimately discussing their respective implications on the $^7$P$_1$ resonant state in $^7$H. Our findings also support a prior work where the $^7$P$_1$ resonant state was ruled out as a cause for the anomalous angular dipole cross section in the $^6$Li(p,n) reaction. We further computed the removal energies of the $^7$H bound state as well as the resonant state to be around 8.2 and 11.3 MeV, which we then compared with the recent $^7$H removal energy measurement of 19.2 $\pm$ 1.8 MeV. In various fields of scientific inquiry, a common challenge exists in assessing the effects of interventions on multiple units and outcomes using time-series data from observational studies. For graphs with a given number of vertices and treewidth of order $O(n^{1/2-\epsilon})$, we have devised a word-RAM algorithm to compute vertex separators in $O(n)$ bits. Furthermore, we can compute an $O(1)$-approximation for the optimal vertex separator in $O(\log n)$ time, utilizing $O(\log n)$ bits. These results extend a problem discovered by Demaine, Hertel, Langerman, Suk, and Toma, initially addressed for trees and specific low treewidth graphs, to broader classes of sparse graphs with treewidth of $O(n^{1-2\epsilon})$. Our algorithm relies on a novel technique combining recursive decomposition, parameterized width, and explicit set operations, allowing for efficient computation and memory management. This achievement further implies that linear-time algorithms exist for sparse path-width problems with treewidth of $O(n^{1/2-\epsilon})$. In agreement with established lower bounds, our compute and space complexities are largely optimal across various scenarios. Lastly, we can extend our results for vertex separators to compute $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximations for the minimum $k$-edge connected subgraphs, requiring $O(\log k)$ additional bits. These extensions highlight the inherent difficulty of sparse algorithmic problems and emphasize the importance of tree structure in graph theory. A substantial portion of network information comes from edge weights and their directionality.
Most network measures were initially developed for simple undirected networks.
As a result, weighted network extensions were created to incorporate weight-based information, particularly for calculating the local clustering coefficient.
We discovered that not all these extensions consider the weights fully; some depend on the degree and react sensitively to even small weight changes.
For these cases, we suggest two new methods for calculating the local clustering coefficient that work just as well as fully-weighted versions.
We tested these approaches on artificial and real-world data, demonstrating its effectiveness in comparing different network measures.
We conclude that for applications involving small networks, traditional degree-based methods and the new approaches have similar performance; however, for larger networks, the new approaches outperform them. 
In contrast, for directed networks, the new approaches already outperform traditional degree-based methods. 
We believe that for these types of networks, the new approaches offer a significant improvement. 
Furthermore, we observed that for large networks, traditional fully-weighted methods still outperform the new approaches; however, the gap between them and the new approaches decreases as the network becomes more homogeneous. 
We predict that for the future, the new approaches will become even more crucial as networks continue to grow in size and homogeneity. 
Ultimately, we hope that our work will lead to the continued development and refinement of network measures that grow more powerful with the increasing size and structure of the networks they are designed for.

One notable strategy to embed prior knowledge about physical systems into machine learning models is physics-informed neural networks (PINNs). These models have been observed to perform well with smaller training datasets, excel in generalizing outcomes, and reduce training time. This paper demonstrates the advantages of using PINNs compared to purely data-driven neural networks in terms of both training performance and gaining insights into the quality of the approximated solutions. By considering PINNs that are constrained by partial differential equations, we investigate their efficiency in tackling a multi-step pricing model for exotic derivatives. Our investigation involves implementing PINNs and purely data-driven neural networks on a same computational platform to compare their training speeds with the same number of data points. Our numerical experiments reveal that PINNs require less computational effort than purely data-driven neural networks to attain the same level of accuracy. Additionally, we observe that PINNs provide valuable information about the approximated solution's quality by quantifying their compliance with the pricing model's conditions. This information can be utilized to detect data entry errors, estimate uncertainty levels, and guide data collection activities. Overall, our study shows that PINNs are a powerful tool for pricing complex financial instruments when there are limited price observations available. They also offer a convenient framework for performing hybrid inference methods that combine in-sample data, out-of-sample data, and additional information about the underlying physical parameters. Our findings highlight the potential of using PINNs to improve the modeling of exotic options that have intricate characteristics and a limited number of available price observations. They may further facilitate the creation of a hybrid model that integrates different types of data, such as intraday and end-of-day price data, and other relevant information like the underlying physical parameters. Our approach also contributes to the field of reversible density estimation by showing that PINNs can effectively approximate complex probability density functions, especially with limited data. They may further be used to implement a novel reversible density estimation method that integrates prior knowledge about the probability density function and data-specific parameters. Our findings also show that PINNs can effectively integrate specific prior information and data-driven components to estimate uncertain parameters. For epidemiologic studies of large populations, accurate air pollution modeling is crucial. Leveraging advances in big data analytics and machine learning has led to breakthroughs in air pollution modeling frameworks. This discussion highlights recent breakthroughs and proposes enhancements from the viewpoints of geostatistics and machine learning. Future developments will integrate learning algorithms with spatial analysis, allowing for the incorporation of spatial correlations in the modeling process. This integration is expected to improve the precision of existing air pollution models, thereby enhancing exposure assessments. Which specific machine learning algorithms and approaches will be integrated with spatial analysis remains to be seen? Nonetheless, it is clear that the next generation of exposure assessments will be shaped by the convergence of spatial analysis and machine learning. This fusion of disciplines is expected to yield significant advancements in the near future. Firstly, we will explore the underlying drivers of this paradigm shift, focusing on the leveraging of advanced computational capabilities and massive datasets arising from widespread monitoring networks and big geo-data. Secondly, we will review the current state of machine learning algorithms capable of processing high-dimensional data with high spatial resolution. Thirdly, we will outline the prospects of integrating algorithms that have already shown great promise in air pollution modeling, such as supervised learning, deep learning, knowledge distillation, and reinforcement learning, as well as unsupervised learning methods. Furthermore, we will discuss ensemble learning, integral to spatial analysis and machine learning, and discuss informatics systems required to execute these methods. Finally, we will outline potential applications of this integration in public health policy-making, exemplified by the utility of exposure assessments in the development of tailored asthma plans. This discussion aims to foster a shared vision of the future role of spatial analysis and machine learning in exposure assessment. This synergy is anticipated to propel the field forward, offering not only enhanced exposure assessments but also actionable information to reduce the health impacts of air pollution. Ultimately, exposure assessments will be an essential tool in the development of informed air pollution management policies. By doing so, we will ultimately reduce the health burdens associated with this global public health concern.

Our research, however, demonstrates that this effect can be more accurately described by the orbital Hall effect, where the indices representing "valleys" are replaced with a distinct physical measurement called the orbital magnetic moment, capable of being applied consistently across the entire range of the Brillouin zone.  Utilizing the orbital Hall effect offers the benefit of eliminating the subjective decision in setting the cut-off point for the indices involved in valley Hall conductivity, as the resulting conductivity profile becomes a continuous function of the applied magnetic field's strength.  Our new model for predicting magnetic properties is highly useful in designing new magnetic devices based on gapped graphene.  Our computational simulations mimic real-life conditions in which this model can be applied and predict a notable correlation between the geometric properties of the graphene and its projected orbital states.  Our research reveals that this correlation could potentially be harnessed to control the gapped graphene's magnetic properties, leading to the discovery of new directed assembly techniques for graphene-based devices. Over the past two years, research has gained momentum in graph adversarial attacks but Graph Classification remains an understudied area. The indirect utilization of Reinforcement Learning methods for graph classification, given that datasets involve discrete graphs with labels, stands in contrast to traditional approaches that use direct gradient optimization. This work aims to explore the novel threat of data manipulation during training (Data Poisoning) targeting Graph Classification neural networks via Reinforcement Learning agents. Furthermore, we outline a new paradigm for the simulation of this threat and develop a system to automatically generate poisoned data, verified through a comprehensive evaluation on multiple datasets alongside existing defenses. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of our model in withstanding both traditional attacks and attacks occurring during the training process, while also showcasing its ability to enhance the resilience of the Graph Classification neural network against various adversarial attacks. Moreover, our tool for automatically generating poisoned data (PoisonGraph) can be freely accessed online. Domain-specific knowledge is frequently captured using comprehensive, formally structured concept relationships called ontologies. In fields like biology and medicine, vast ontologies comprise hundreds of thousands of interconnected concepts. Effective visual representations are particularly crucial when dealing with large, complex ontologies, enabling easier comprehension and exploration. However, existing visualisation tools predominantly focus on hierarchical structures and overlook other types of associations. This paper introduces a new method for visually representing domain-specific concepts in a way that showcases all knowledge connections, by dynamically grouping concepts based on their relationships. Our novel approach relies on force simulation to position the concepts, with the goal of clearly showing all associations. Experimental evaluation involving experts confirms the efficiency of this visualisation tool in extracting relevant information. User studies further reveal that the proposed method outperforms other available visualisation tools in understanding large, complex domain-specific knowledge networks. Overall, this research provides a practical solution for visually presenting vast domain-specific knowledge, facilitating easier comprehension and exploration. The developed algorithm can be freely utilised for visualising complex ontologies and knowledge bases on computers. We introduce an innovative technique that synergistically combines inter-domain loss and CycleGAN to deliver robust self-supervised speech recognition capabilities. Inter-domain loss encodes the geographical disparities between an artificial intelligence model's preferred domain and its target domain - speech. This loss is paired with CycleGAN, which performs semi-supervised speech conversion, thereby generating a tailored loss to guide the artificial intelligence model. A fundamental theory known as active inference underpins how living beings interact with their surroundings. Active inference suggests that biological agents use predictive models to guide their actions, where their predictions about the environment are shaped by an innate sense of uncertainty. However, when this theory is applied to systems involving multiple agents, a paradox arises. Active inference tends to favor predictions that align with collective goals, yet these goals are only reachable through individual actions, creating a circular logic. To resolve this conundrum, our theory uses a modified approach to uncertainty, one that is relevant to dual-processing psychological models and resembles how humans reason in cooperative scenarios. We have demonstrated that this modified theory effectively resolves the paradox, allowing agents to work towards a common objective through coordinated action. We have also tested our theory by showing how it mirrors the findings of a laboratory study on social learning. Our findings open the door to further research into the active inference theory as it relates to social creatures, while the methods we used can be used to analyze the social behaviors of humans and animals alike. Our study of binary mixtures used molecular dynamics simulations out of equilibrium to explore the Soret effect, particularly the influence of flexible molecules' internal freedom on this phenomenon. As we softened the molecules, we found the thermal diffusion coefficient to decrease and change its direction, and we attributed these findings to two potential factors: temperature-induced conformational changes causing bulkier structures to move to the warmer area; and asymmetry in interactions between flexible and rigid molecules, which is reduced when the internal freedom is increased. Additionally, our simulation of a mixture of rigid and semi-flexible molecules revealed that the thermal diffusion coefficient's behavior is influenced by the presence of monomer-dimer equilibria. A multiplicative stochastic process with lognormally distributed lower bounds is investigated. 

The first part of the text describes the characteristics of such a process and derives mathematical formulas for its distribution, moments, and certain important quantities.

A simulation method to generate sample paths of the process is presented in the second section.

The final part of the text showcases applications of the process in modeling both the sizes of family trees and financial models that involve branching processes.

Additionally, a related family of multiplicative stochastic processes that are generated by geometric Brownian motions is considered. 

The processes in this class have normally distributed lower bounds and can be used to model, for example, the propagation of infectious diseases during their initial stages. 

A comparison of the properties of the process considered here and those of its geometric Brownian motion counterparts is provided. 

The text concludes with an examination of the joint distributions of the process values at different, random times. 

A theoretical framework is developed to solve this problem, and the resulting equations are approximated using numerical methods. 

In particular, this text considers the scenario where the random times represent the arrival times of a Poisson process, while also touching on the case of random times with arbitrary distributions. 

Ultimately, the text discusses the application of the joint distribution of the process values at random times in modeling hits on the Italian lottery Sicilia 6 from 2008 to 2014. 

A supplementary document contains additional mathematical findings and numerical examples. 

The corresponding MATLAB code for the simulations, numerical approximations, and modeling can be accessed at https://github.com/dwzellinger/multiplicative-stochastic-process/matlab. 

Additionally, the relevant R code can be found at https://github.com/dwzellinger/multiplicative-stochastic-process/r.

Our key contribution is a depth-controlled randomized measurement strategy that combines the capabilities of random Pauli measurements and random Clifford measurements. These can be viewed as the two extremes within our approach, facilitating a continuous adjustment of the trade-off between the probability of detecting a magic state and the amount of information acquired about the mysterious quantum state. Conversely, the well-known randomised benchmarking method allows for assessing the quality of quantum devices but does not provide insight into the mysterious nature of a quantum state. The vast majority of NLP text transformations have inherent limitations in their ability to expand coverage of input data due to the need to preserve the original class label. In order to overcome this challenge, we propose a concept called sibylvariance, which refers to the use of data transformation techniques that can detect and remove class-specific biases, thereby enhancing the input data space. To achieve this goal, we develop a method that employs an encoder-network, a transformer, and a classifier to identify and eliminate class-specific biases in text data. Through comprehensive experiments on eight datasets across seven natural language processing tasks, we demonstrate the effectiveness of sibylvariance by significantly expanding the input data space while preserving model performance. In addition, we propose a method for visually analyzing the class-specificity of data manipulation, which facilitates a deeper understanding of the proposed approach. Furthermore, our experiments demonstrate that sibylvariance can significantly improve model robustness against adversarial attacks. Overall, the sibylvariance framework provides a valuable tool for data scientists to control the input data space and ensure the reliability of models in real-world applications. The code and dataset for this study are publicly available on GitHub. Researchers aim to create meta-learning algorithms that capitalize on previous experience to rapidly acquire new skills or adapt to new environments by utilizing representation learning techniques, which enable the transfer of knowledge across various tasks. As the interest in meta-learning grows, there is a pressing need to establish its theoretical foundations, especially in terms of learning adaptable representations. In this research, we tackle the problem of multi-task linear regression where multiple related tasks share a common, low-dimensional linear representation. Our study provides effective, sample-efficient methods to address the dual challenges of learning a shared feature set from related tasks and transferring this knowledge to unseen tasks. This work sheds light on the central issue of meta-learning. Furthermore, we present theoretical limits on the minimum sample size required to learn these linear features. Finally, we demonstrate the practical utility of our findings through simulated experiments. Our sample efficiency bounds are notably aligned with empirical observations, offering valuable insights into the inherent complexities of meta-learning. By establishing theoretical boundaries and providing efficient algorithms, our analysis offers a solid understanding of what meta-learning entails and achieves. In particular, we answer the question: what is the purpose of representation learning in meta-learning? In essence, representation learning mechanisms acquire features that are either task-independent or common to multiple tasks, thereby facilitating sample efficiency across related tasks. In turn, these features enhance model generalizability to unseen tasks. Ultimately, our findings contribute to a deeper comprehension of meta-learning. Utilizing multilingual learning in state-of-the-art machine translation models can aid in adapting to low-resource languages despite limited data, albeit resulting in oversized models that are impractical for deployment. To combat this, Knowledge Distillation is an often-used method to create high-performance yet lightweight models. This study centers on reducing the size of Spanish-English translation models, achieving this by exploring i) the initial multilingual training, ii) post-training data compression using schema-based distillation, and iii) distillation with parallel datasets. Our findings show that distillation can yield up to a 6.5-fold reduction in model size with only a 0.2% loss in performance, and that utilizing initial multilingual data greatly enhances the distillation process's effectiveness when using small amounts of parallel data. Additionally, using parallel datasets from related languages can facilitate a 3.1-fold reduction in model size, thus highlighting the importance of multilingual data in this context. This research contributes a lightweight Spanish-English translation model weighing approximately 11.3 megabytes, thus advancing research and deployment efficiency for low-resource languages. The model, designed using Transformer architecture v1-B6, has been validated in the WMT 2020 evaluation campaign and our findings have been made publicly accessible. They can be utilized in future distillation-based compression efforts, particularly for languages such as Basque, Galician, and Catalan. They have been successfully tested over multiple distillation scenarios, thus serving as an efficient tool for data compression. The source code for this research has been made publicly available at: https://github.com/andreaguglielmi/wmt2020-distillation-sp2en. Our models have also been deployed online at: https://sp2en-distillation.github.io. Furthermore, the project has been documented on a dedicated blog at: https://andrelg-g.github.io/blog/sp2en-distillation. The Turan number for an r-uniform graph F, denoted by ex(n, F), is defined as the maximum number of edges in an F-free r-uniform graph on n vertices. The Turan density of F, denoted by pi(F), is defined as the maximum asymptotic value of the number of edges in an F-free graph divided by the maximum number of edges in an F-free graph on n vertices. Artur Ekkehard Köhler recently found that the Turan density of the graph K2 union K1 is 1/2. We prove that the upper bound 1/2 for the Turan density of the graph K2 union K1 is specific to three-vertex graphs, as it is currently known that the Turan density of the graph K3 union K1 is 2/3, as is the Turan density of the graph K4 minus a triangle. Ekkehard Köhler has also previously determined that the Turan number for the graph K2 union K1 is 6. We generalize this by proving that the Turan number for the graph K3 union K1 is 7. Our proof involves showing that a 7-edge 4-vertex graph with no K2 union K1 is Hamiltonian. Conversely, it can be deduced that a 6-edge 4-vertex K2 union K1-free graph must be a partition of the four vertices into two pairs such that the first pair is connected to the second pair. This has further implications for the extremal functions of various three-vertex graphs, particularly those with a Turan density greater than 1/2. It is also known that the Turan density of the graph K4 union K1 is 1/2, as is the Turan density of the graph K5 minus an edge. We prove that the extremal functions for the graph K4 union K1 and K5 minus an edge are alternating, as are the extremal functions for the graph K2 union K1. We conclude therefore that the extremal functions for the graph K2 union K1, K1 union K1, K4 union K1, and K5 minus an edge are all identical.
