The efficiency of deep learning semantic segmentation algorithms in identifying abnormalities on chest X-rays is limited by the laborious task of gathering and annotating training data. To alleviate this issue, we explore how image enhancement techniques can lower the necessity for labelled data without compromising accuracy, ultimately facilitating the use of fully unsupervised techniques for detecting abnormalities on chest X-rays. By training several efficient neural networks on reduced datasets augmented through various methods, we determine that Transfer and Inverse Transfer learning are the premier image enhancement approaches, yielding significant reductions in labelled data requirements from 90% to nearly 99%. Moreover, we demonstrate that applying these image enhancement methods in an unsupervised setting enables our previously top-performing Segformer model to achieve comparable results when trained with only 3% of the original training data. These findings showcase that image enhancement can be a valuable tool in developing efficient neural segmentation algorithms. Ultimately, these results lead to the development of a new, fully unsupervised segmentation model which outperforms our labelled model when trained on just 9% of the total data. Existing image captioning models often fail to produce captions according to the desired style and level of detail. This paper proposes a unified image captioning framework that excels across various domains and can effortlessly adapt to multiple captioning styles. We incorporate a flexible prompt learning system that enables the model to absorb data from multiple domains, ensuring its performance remains strong in each domain. Additionally, we optimize the prompts using dynamic vectors within a word embedding space, reducing the reliance on manual tuning and significantly enhancing the model's capabilities. At the inference stage, our model allows for the generation of custom caption styles by simply selecting the most suitable prompt, yielding outstanding results in COCO Karpathy and TextCaps benchmarks. We also conducted a comprehensive fairness analysis of our model and discovered that prompt learning serves as a reliable and powerful tool for fair image captioning. We have publicly released our code at https://github.com/allenlw/image-captioning-flexible-prompts. This repository contains the implementation of our framework, allowing for the automated generation of image captions in the desired style and language. We hope that our work offers insights into the potential of prompt learning in the development of fair and adaptable image captioning models. We have observed that our model can successfully produce captions not only in the English language but also in other languages such as Chinese and Spanish. We have included the relevant results in the supplementary material. As autonomous systems become increasingly prevalent, it is essential to establish a legal and regulatory framework for addressing harm caused by these systems to individuals. Previous attempts to define harm in philosophical literature have failed to address various real-world examples, leading some to consider abandoning the concept of harm. The existing definitions of harm, largely reliant on causality, surprisingly overlook the use of causal models and actual causality theories. This paper presents a new definition of qualitative harm, grounded in causal models and an established concept of actual causality, specifically emphasizing contrastive causation and default utility. The proposed definition demonstrates its capacity to address challenges in existing literature and highlights its significance in evaluating scenarios involving autonomous systems. Ultimately, by defining qualitative harm, the paper lays groundwork for a new paradigm in harm assessment, enabling regulatory bodies to measure and compare the qualitative harm posed by these systems. The paper further shows that measuring such qualitative harm with regard to autonomous systems' capabilities is feasible and presents an approach for assessing these qualitative harms through simulation-based experiments. The methods presented, validated by three case studies involving autonomous systems' capacity for harm, reveal that the qualitative harm caused by these systems can be effectively evaluated. The integration of the newly introduced definition and assessment approach has the potential to improve decision-making processes surrounding autonomous systems and other technological systems that pose qualitative harm. Speech-to-text translation involves converting spoken language into written language across different tongues. Conventional two-stage approaches using speech recognition and machine translation have inherent flaws, including the amplification of inaccuracies. By contrast, single-system approaches reduce errors but are complicated to deploy due to limited data availability. We delve into zero-shot translation, which allows for language pairs that weren't encountered during training, thereby circumventing the need for speech-to-text data. While promising, zero-shot translation is often too optimistic, producing useless output. To address this issue, we develop and test a straightforward two-stage method that refines zero-shot translation results. Specifically, we leverage speech-to-text models to generate synthetic, machine-readable speech, which is then converted into text using a neural translator. Unlike prior zero-shot methods, our approach doesn't necessitate parallel data but still achieves significant improvements in translation accuracy. We experiment with our methodology on the Multilingual Zero-shot Speech Translation dataset, showcasing that our two-stage method surpasses single-system zero-shot translators. Furthermore, our results indicate that our technique is most beneficial for languages that are linguistically distant from the training data. Overall, our findings suggest that our simple two-stage method is an effective solution to the zero-shot speech-to-text translation problem. We make our code and dataset available for public use. Based on our experiments with our proposed solution, speech-to-text translation across various languages is feasible, even when the translator hasn't encountered the relevant audio data, as long as the translator has been trained on texts related to the target language. These findings open up the door to speech-to-text translation across multiple languages, even when the translator hasn't seen the relevant audio data. They also highlight the need for more accurate and accurate speech recognition and machine translation systems. These developments will enable the seamless connection of speech-to-text translation tools to a wide range of software programs, including browser extensions, tablets and smartphones, multimedia browsers, and other devices. These advancements will greatly enhance the ability of speech-to-text translation software to achieve accurate results in low-noise environments. However, our technique still falls short in noisy environments, which poses a significant challenge for further research in this area. Overall, our research into zero-shot speech-to-text translation has several significant connections to adjacent fields, including speech recognition, machine translation, cross-language text-to-speech, and cross-language speech recognition. This work introduces a novel extension of the traditional heat conduction theory, encompassing cases with fading memory and incorporating the standard heat equation under dynamic boundary conditions as a particular instance. We delve into the well-posedness of systems comprised of equations akin to those by Coleman and Gurtin, further subject to dynamic boundary conditions with memory. These systems contain nonlinear elements situated both internally and on the boundary, with their behavior either dictated by classical dissipation principles or governed by a nonlinear balance condition. Moreover, we allow for disparate memory kernels between the interior and boundary of the domain. Through the application of a suitable generalization of the classical Fourier integral and by drawing on recent findings in functional analysis, we demonstrate the existence and uniqueness of solutions to the resultant system of nonlinear initial-boundary value problems. This is achieved without imposing restrictive assumptions on the interior or boundary dynamics, thus subsuming previously established results in this realm. Additionally, we provide a preliminary analysis, as yet unpublished, on the asymptotic behavior of the resultant system, describing the long-term dynamics. Specifically, under the assumption of classical dissipation, we prove that the unified theory's solution converges in time to the solution of the particular instance, while for the case with nonlinear balance conditions at the boundary, we establish that the unified theory's solution is confined to a closed subset within the range of the monodromy group's fixed points. Furthermore, under the inner balance condition, similar conclusions on the long-term behavior are drawn near the boundary. Finally, through the theoretical framework, a suitable generalization of the classical Fourier integral is derived, which itself is equivalent to the first-order version of the extended heat conduction theory proposed by Tzou. Consequently, the novel extension of the classical heat conduction theory is viewed as a closed-system closed generalization of its particular instance. All contributions made in this work are positioned within the broader context of extended heat conduction theories. Precise short-term forecasts of energy consumption are essential for managing low voltage electricity networks efficiently, particularly with regard to highly disaggregated individual customer load profiles that are not adequately represented by aggregate forecasts. This article examines the applicability of machine learning algorithms at both aggregate and disaggregated levels, evaluating their accuracy and gain in accuracy when detailed data is utilized. We observe that while high accuracy can be achieved with aggregate forecasts, this level of accuracy is difficult to attain when individual customer forecasts are considered. This challenge can be overcome by employing micro-data driven deep learning methods. This study serves as a foundation for future research into the application of deep learning in estimating individual energy consumption. Future research could incorporate the factors of temperature and time-based pricing in estimations, ultimately enabling the development of personalized load forecasts. We propose this area of study with estimated micro-data distributions as a starting point for further investigation. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to the benchmark LEA dataset and evaluate its performance in comparison to conventional machine learning and deep learning methods. The results reveal the superiority of our deep learning approach when dealing with micro-data when compared to all other methods we tested. The implementation of our model is based on the TensorFlow platform for deep learning and is accompanied by a random forest classifier for comparison purposes. The accuracy of our model was measured using mean absolute error as the relevant metric. The code for this project has been made available online at a public GitHub repository. The model we developed could potentially be adapted and applied to the estimation of energy consumption at an even smaller level such as individual appliances. However, this area is beyond the scope of this particular study and serves as a subject for future research. The approach we developed could also be used in the forecasting of other forms of micro-data such as water consumption or gas usage. The results of our study are discussed in detail within this article. Creating a reliable model for precise COVID-19 detection on chest CT scans poses significant difficulties despite considerable advancements. The issue often arises due to annotation biases affecting traditional supervised segmentation techniques, which rely on detailed boundary markings. To resolve these issues and minimize labeling expenses, we introduce an innovative framework that utilizes image-level labels, thereby facilitating unbiased lesion detection. This novel approach combines a multi-tasking network with a specially designed keypoint detection system and an ensemble model, which ultimately provides more accurate lesion detection and infection probability assessment outcomes compared to existing methods. Our solution's performance is demonstrated through comprehensive experiments on two COVID19 datasets, revealing notable improvements over state-of-the-art solutions. Additionally, the proposed framework's unique application allows for lesion detection and characterizes the size, location, and distribution of lesions, thereby aiding medical professionals in identifying potential infections. Based on these assessments, we report high AUC values of 0.918 and 0.922 for identifying COVID19 and infection probabilities, respectively, as well as high F1 scores of 0.822 and 0.795 for detecting robin and solitary lesions. The proposed framework's notable advantages include its ability to detect robust lesions in the presence of only chest CT scans. Furthermore, the ensemble model helps to mitigate biases resulting from the use of limited annotated data, which causes some challenges for detecting solitary lesions. This research offers an innovative solution for unique COVID19 detection issues by leveraging advanced deep learning technologies. The proposed framework's code is publicly available at: https://github.com/ashishsharma17/COVID19_Keypoint. Our study contributes to an extensive literature survey on COVID19 dataset analysis by highlighting potential research directions for identifying infections from images. Furthermore, the proposed framework's novel multi-tasking architecture can be applied to similar challenges in the field of computer vision, specifically the identification of rare diseases. Accurate vertebrae localization and identification are crucial in various medical applications related to spine disorder diagnosis and surgical planning. However, certain pathological variations (e.g., vertebral compression fractures, scoliosis, and vertebral fixation) and imaging conditions (e.g., limited visibility and stochastic noise) complicate automated diagnosis. To address this challenge, researchers have developed an advanced software framework, SpineToolbox, which integrates and extends specialized algorithms for accurate and robust vertebrae detection and localization in challenging scenarios. The proposed framework combines probabilistic models and 3D convolutional neural networks to robustly predict the position of vertebrae in given 2D and 3D body CT scans. The approach was comprehensive, testing various scenarios involving one to twelve vertebrae detection, and demonstrated significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods, achieving high detection rates of 85.9% and 91.7% in difficult scenarios with one or twelve vertebrae, respectively. The proposed software is now openly available for clinical and scientific communities to facilitate advanced vertebral analysis. The paper provides detailed implementation and architectural insights, showcasing the potential for robust and precise automated analysis of complex spine imaging scenarios. Our theory explores the behavior of electron collisions with a strong repulsive barrier in a contained environment. Within an extremely high level of electron interaction with the surrounding electromagnetic field, temporary variations in the field intensity can cause a free electron to transition into a confined state trapped between the barrier's edges. As the electron's kinetic energy exceeds the energy of this confined state, a spontaneous emission of a polariton can occur. This polariton, composed of a photon and a bosonic mediator, can then exit the confined region through the barrier, modulating its wave function upon doing so. Electron collisions may result in the formation of a quasi-stable state, during which the system can absorb a portion of the electron's energy by reducing its kinetic energy, a process that is inherently linked to the emission of a polariton. This effect gives rise to a significant and pronounced structure in the electron impact excitation spectrum, analogous to a resonance, near the point at which the electron transitions from a continuous state to a state confined by the barrier's presence. Furthermore, the effect can also manifest as an electron self-scattering process in which the electron can avoid detection by detecting instruments due to scattering into the confined state and then subsequently emitting a polariton that carries the information associated with the confined electron. This process is essential in understanding the role of the repulsive barrier in managing the strength of the electron's interaction with an external electromagnetic field; for instance, when dealing with confined systems such as quantum dots or wells, this process could serve as a mechanism for managing the electron's interaction with a weak external field. Detailed numerical analysis has been conducted to investigate how the polarized electromagnetic field affects the electron's spin and the internal atomic structure of a confined electron for situations involving weak external field exposure. Furthermore, the effect has also been explored in contexts involving the scattering of electrons by highly charged particles as well as the lifetime of highly excited atomic states. Possible avenues for experimental detection of the repulsive barrier's presence, influenced by the surrounding electromagnetic field, include electron transmission experiments, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, scanning tunneling spectroscopy, and the study of particle pair emission. Generally, the repulsive barrier's influence can be detected through experimental methods applicable to both neutral and charged confined systems. This effect may also be investigated using the quantum tunneling of massive particles in the presence of a strong magnetic field. Furthermore, the effect can also be explored in the context of quantum Hall systems where the electron's confinement by a strong vertical magnetic field may weaken the electron's interaction with the horizontal radiation. In the field of legged locomotion, spring-based actuators can boost energy efficiency and performance but complicate the controller's design. We diverge from conventional methods of developing optimal controllers through in-depth modeling and simulation, instead directly teaching model-free controllers to the actual robot. Initially, gaits are generated through central pattern generators, whose parameters are fine-tuned to rapidly develop an open-loop controller for efficient walking. Following this, we rapidly adapt this controller to be closed-loop by learning it from data, all without delving into intricate dynamics. We successfully tested this novel method, encompassing both efficient and resilient gaits, on a spring-driven 10 kg robot quadruped. Its performance, assessed in various scenarios, matched the expectations set by advanced dynamic models. Our approach, characterized by rapid testing and immediate feedback, accelerated development by substantially reducing it to a brief period of trials. We firmly believe this new strategy can simplify controller design for bio-inspired robots. You can watch our robot in action at http://mrl.cs.nyu.edu/quickgaits. We propose a new variational quantum algorithm, the Variational Separability Verifier (VSV), to identify the closest separable state of an arbitrary quantum state with minimal deviation in Hilbert-Schmidt distance. Our algorithm's performance is initially tested with GHZ states composed of up to seven qubits via simulations that utilize state vectors and random measurements. We also use numerical methods to determine the closest separable states for maximally entangled multipartite X-states. Our results indicate that NISQ devices may leverage the VSV's efficiency to tackle the challenging full separability problem due to its low-depth quantum circuit. Furthermore, adapting and refining the VSV algorithm has the potential to help characterise multipartite quantum states by identifying the closest k-separable state for k-entangled multipartite states. Our future research aims to expand upon this approach by investigating its practical applications in quantum metrology, key distribution, and quantum state filtering simulations. Additionally, this study examines the scalability of the VSV algorithm, revealing that quantum multiplexing could significantly enhance its operational depth to achieve near-optimal performance in identifying separable states in higher Hilbert spaces. We discuss potential implementations and showcase the VSV's growing potential to handle complex quantum systems with rapidly advancing NISQ devices. Ultimately, this development contributes to our understanding of quantum entanglement in both theoretical and practical applications. Our analysis also considers the computational resources required for the VSV algorithm at different scales, especially in hardware, software, and time, based on technological advancements and efficient architectures. Our results indicate that future quantum multiplexing developments could immensely enhance the VSV's operational depth, bringing it closer to optimality in identifying separable states in larger Hilbert spaces. We reflect on past discussions and future outlooks for the VSV algorithm, envisioning its practical uses in quantum metrology, key distribution, quantum state filtering, and entanglement characterization while acknowledging the present limitations of this technique. Our work further inspires innovative ideas and encourages researchers to contribute to the exciting future of this algorithm. In conclusion, this study shares knowledge, sparks discussion among researchers, and encourages collaboration across disciplines, always mindful of the ever-changing advancements in the field. Our final conclusion summarizes the current understanding and future perspectives for the VSV algorithm, expressing optimism and confidence in the future of this technique. Our long-term goal is to make significant contributions to the field, and this study represents our current achievements along this path. Our research report documents the findings and serves as an acknowledgement of the contributions made by the people involved

A surge in demand for search by image has led researchers to investigate fashion instance-level image retrieval, which involves finding matching images. Building upon this, the concept of fashion attribute manipulation, which modifies a specific attribute while retaining others, has emerged. This enables users to narrow down search results by filtering items with desired characteristics. However, this task is challenging due to the large capacity of the model's output buffer. Despite output buffering being a common technique in image manipulation, its effectiveness in fashion instance-level tasks has not been extensively explored. In this study, the benefits of output buffering for fashion attribute manipulation are examined, which involves incorporating it into a style-based generator to accommodate multiple attributes. A novel output buffering-based framework for fashion attribute manipulation is proposed, contributing to the state-of-the-art in this field. Experimental results show that the proposed framework achieves remarkable performance, outshining existing methods and demonstrating the significance of output buffering in fashion attribute manipulation. Furthermore, the feasibility of incorporating output buffering into other vision-based tasks, such as qualitative control, is investigated, demonstrating its potential flexibility. A comprehensive analysis of output buffering's underlying mechanics is also conducted, providing insights into its effects. Code and model for the proposed framework are available on GitHub. A demo of the proposed framework can be accessed at \url{https://www.ruiwang.xyz/fam_with_output_buffer.html}. One additional application of output buffering is shown in the demo, which involves introducing textual information to an input image. This technique exhibits remarkable promise in this domain and could be easily incorporated into other attribute-based vision tasks. As the input image in the demo is changed, the corresponding semantic attribute is modified while retaining the image's overall layout, demonstrating output buffering's capability in combining multiple attributes. The $\R$-optimal solution for the underdetermined equation $Ax=y$ where $A$ is a bounded linear operator mapping a Banach space to a Hilbert space, and $\R$ is a strongly convex function defined in that space, is considered for cases of incomplete data and noisy input. A dual gradient approach, though suffering from semi-convergence, can approximate the sought-after solution. Due to its underdetermined nature, the method requires an optimal stopping time, for which three rules – a priori choice, the discrepancy principle, and an adapted heuristic principle – are considered along with respective convergence results established. Convergence speeds for these are analyzed based on specific source conditions related to the sought-after solution. Simulation experiments are conducted to test the method's effectiveness. This research further expands into the application of imaging a compact hyper-surface given a sequence of partial measurements. By employing a log-concave function and an iterative dual algorithm, the method seeks to reconstruct the surface from its projected image. A model instance involving the imaging of a compact domain on the 2D torus is provided. Theoretical convergence results for this are proven using an operator factorization approach. Due to its task-specific nature, the method offers improved efficiency and robustness compared to traditional approaches. Furthermore, its ability to be adapted to problems involving convex functionals and Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions is also examined, providing a foundation for potential generalizations. A notable application of this approach is the recovery of edges in de-noised images as demonstrated through simulated experiments. Constructing the matching cost is a critical step in estimating light field depth but has received limited attention in the era of deep learning. The prevailing method in the field of deep learning constructs matching cost through the sequential shifting of sub-aperture images, a time-consuming process that impedes the improvement of accuracy. This paper proposes an innovative cost constructor, termed SiCoNet, to streamline matching cost construction and enhance its quality. Comprising a primary network that jointly learns low-level features from multiple images and a transformer-based alignment network, SiCoNet successfully merges overlapping sub-apertures into co-axial pins. The proposed constructor not only accelerates matching cost construction but also enhances its clarity, ultimately leading to advanced light field depth estimation. The study evaluates SiCoNet's performance on the MEFCC, FLANDB, ALBEDO, and higher-quality synthetic light fields, demonstrating its superiority to state-of-the-art methods. Results show that SiCoNet significantly reduces construction time while significantly increasing the estimation accuracy. The estimated matching cost also undergoes notable improvements. This study uses the bilinear method to investigate the Fokas-Lenells equations, first reducing the system and then employing double Wronskian solutions to yield a range of solutions for the reduced equations, resulting in a comprehensive overview of solutions for both classical and nonlocal Fokas-Lenells equations. Several solutions are illustrated through asymptotic analysis, notably, novel solutions are obtained for Fokas-Lenells equations linked to real discrete eigenvalues, previously unreported in analytical methods, and display behavior similar to (multi-)periodic waves or solitary waves with algebraic decay. Furthermore, by using Fokas-Lenells solutions, this work also derives solutions for the two-dimensional massive Thirring model. Most solutions are shown through direct numerical verification.

Alternative theories of gravity that go beyond the Riemannian framework have been proposed to explore quantum gravity and model systems with non-relativistic symmetry. However, developing these theories involves a complex task: deriving an action principle that accurately captures their behavior. This technical note utilizes the formulation of double field theory to create action frameworks for these alternative gravity theories. By doing so, it resolves the ambiguities associated with their corresponding motion equations. As a result, this note embeds three theories – Torsional Newton-Cartan gravity, Carrollian gravity, and String Newton-Cartan gravity – within double field theory and derives their respective action frameworks for comparison with previously established literature results. These double field theory constructions yield new insights into these alternative gravity theories. For instance, they cast their motion equations in the form of a combined translation and target space metric. Additionally, they represent geometric properties on the target space within the framework of a non-Riemannian metric on the worldsheet. Furthermore, they show that torsional Newton-Cartan and string Newton-Cartan gravity can be viewed as low-energy limits of double field theory's non-ricci flat geometry. This new perspective enables a comparison of these alternative gravity theories to Einstein gravity. Importantly, it confirms that their field-theoretical structure aligns with that of Einstein gravity's, albeit with a flat metric that lacks Ricci curvature. This implies that, for these theories, the curvature of the target space governs the behavior of particles moving under its influence. In contrast, string Newton-Cartan gravity introduces an additional geometric effect caused by the presence of a certain field on the target space. This field generates a force analogous to the electromagnetic force. In the context of double field theory, this reveals a fresh understanding of an alternative gravity theory – the Carrollian gravity – where the combined translation and target space metric determine the speed of light, and the vanishing of the target metric component allows the presence of a nonvanishing torsion. Ultimately, this shows that double field theory provides a universal language to express diverse alternative gravity theories' motion dynamics. By embedding these theories within its framework, this note achieves a significant advancement in their study. It resolves their previously unclear motion dynamics and reveals a fresh, unexplored perspective that is primarily geometric in nature. Further, it shows the dynamic relationship existing between three gravity theories – the Newton-Cartan, Carrollian, and string Newton-Cartan – through their representation within the framework of a non-Riemannian metric on the target space.
